abstract: Paediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the leading cause of chronic liver disease in children and adolescents worldwide and is increasing alongside rising rates of paediatric obesity and type 2 diabetes. Paediatric MASLD most often arises in the setting of obesity and metabolic dysfunction but can occur without obesity and is influenced by early life exposures, genetics and environmental factors. Paediatric MASLD and youth-onset type 2 diabetes are tightly linked given the shared and bidirectional pathophysiological mechanisms. Hepatic steatosis often develops early in the course of insulin resistance, even in preschool-age children. Epidemiology in children varies by sex and ancestry and carries major prognostic implications, with a higher MASLD prevalence in male and Hispanic youth, more severe liver disease when MASLD coexists with impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, and an alarming increased risk of mortality in late childhood and young adulthood. Paediatric MASLD is distinct from adult disease, with 20-25% of affected youth demonstrating clinically significant fibrosis on histology, distinct periportal (zone 1) patterns unique to childhood disease, and more severe liver histology in those with impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes. Early life determinants, such as maternal obesity and diabetes, are associated with childhood steatosis beginning early in life. Further, puberty represents a critical window of vulnerability, as physiological insulin resistance, sex-specific effects of androgens, and obesity-related metabolic stress drive sharp increases in both MASLD and youth-onset type 2 diabetes, with distinct sex differences in prevalence and severity. Current management for MASLD in paediatrics is evolving, relying primarily on lifestyle modification and targeted screening but with emerging evidence supporting the benefits of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery in selected youth with obesity, type 2 diabetes and related comorbidities, underscoring the urgent need for paediatric-specific therapeutic trials.

title: Perioperative Nutritional Optimization in Total Joint Arthroplasty: From Screening to Supplementation
abstract: Background: Malnutrition and suboptimal nutrient status are increasingly recognized as modifiable risk factors influencing outcomes after total joint arthroplasty (TJA). Older adults and medically complex patients are particularly vulnerable to perioperative catabolism, impaired wound healing, and delayed functional recovery. This review synthesized current evidence on perioperative nutritional optimization, including biochemical screening, micronutrient correction, essential amino acid (EAA) supplementation, and adjunctive metabolic strategies, to support recovery in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty.

Methods: A targeted narrative literature review was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar databases. Search terms included combinations of "total joint arthroplasty," "total knee arthroplasty," "total hip arthroplasty," "malnutrition," "albumin," "vitamin D," "vitamin C," "essential amino acids," "HMB," "arginine," "glutamine," "bioflavonoids," "micronized purified flavonoid fraction," "carbohydrate loading," and "GLP-1 receptor agonists." Priority was given to randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and large observational studies with direct relevance to arthroplasty populations.

Results: Vitamin D deficiency (13 to 63% of TJA patients) is consistently associated with increased complications, impaired functional scores, and higher infection risk, with favorable outcomes observed after targeted repletion. Vitamin C improves collagen synthesis, decreases inflammatory markers, reduces pain, and lowers the incidence of complex regional pain syndrome. Magnesium supports vitamin D activation, analgesia, and collagen stability. Bioflavonoids, particularly micronized purified flavonoid fraction, demonstrate high-quality evidence for reducing postoperative swelling and improving early motion after total knee arthroplasty. The use of EAA supplementation preserves quadriceps muscle mass, improves strength recovery, and accelerates return to activities of daily living. Carbohydrate loading mitigates postoperative insulin resistance, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists offer metabolic benefits but require individualized perioperative management.

Conclusions: Perioperative nutritional optimization, including vitamin D repletion, vitamin C, magnesium support, micronized purified flavonoid fraction therapy, and structured EAA supplementation, represents a safe, accessible, and evidence-supported strategy to enhance recovery after TJA. Integrating targeted nutrition into prehabilitation pathways may help reduce complications and support faster functional gains.

title: The First Triple Agonist for Antiobesity: Retatrutide
abstract: The prevalence of individuals with overweight and obesity has increased by 18% since 1990 and it is projected that by 2030, nearly 50% of US adults will have obesity. Lifestyle modifications, such as diet and exercise, typically lead to approximately 3-5% weight loss, whereas 5-15% weight loss is necessary to significantly impact obesity-associated comorbidities and improve overall health outcomes. In addition to lifestyle modifications, pharmacotherapy has been utilized as an adjunctive treatment to increase weight loss and improve health outcomes. The Food and Drug Administration has currently approved 6 drugs to treat overweight and obesity, with the recently approved drugs surging in popularity after demonstrating superior weight loss outcomes. Additionally, a number of agents are in the pipeline, offering promise of unprecedented degrees of weight loss. One such drug is retatrutide, which is a triple agonist targeting the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor, and glucagon receptor. Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials have demonstrated the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of retatrutide in patients with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes. The pharmacokinetics of retatrutide were dose proportional and its mean half-life of approximately 6 days supported a once-weekly dosing. The safety profile was similar to GLP-1R agonists and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor/GLP-1R co-agonists, with gastrointestinal disorders being the most common adverse effects reported. Each trial demonstrated greater weight loss with retatrutide treatment in comparison to placebo, with greatest efficacy at higher doses. Overall, these clinical trials have demonstrated the superior efficacy of retatrutide as a weight loss medication in patients with overweight and obesity.

title: Semaglutide in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: Exploring Recent Evidence in Therapeutic Potential for the Obese Population
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is an increasingly prevalent condition, particularly among the aging population in the United States, and is associated with significant challenges due to its complex pathophysiology and limited therapeutic options. Historically, few pharmacological therapies have successfully mitigated HFpEF, making the emergence of effective treatments particularly significant. This review evaluates recent evidence on the therapeutic potential of semaglutide for managing HFpEF, especially in the obese population. Results from the STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM trials demonstrate that semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist originally developed for type 2 diabetes but now also approved for obesity treatment, significantly improves clinical outcomes such as symptom scores, body weight, exercise capacity, and inflammation markers in the obese population suffering from HFpEF. These improvements are attributed to both the weight loss induced by semaglutide and its direct effects on the congestive pathophysiology of HFpEF. The efficacy of semaglutide offers new hope for addressing a condition that has long lacked effective pharmacological interventions.
keywords: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

title: Postbiotic of Bifidobacterium breve i1088 alleviates type 2 diabetes by promoting GLP-1 secretion: identification of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid as a key active metabolite
abstract: Objective: The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is intrinsically linked to the suboptimal secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). While postbiotics have emerged as a compelling therapeutic modality for metabolic modulation, the precise bioactive effectors and their underlying mechanisms remain largely elusive. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of Bifidobacterium breve i1088 (B breve i1088) lysate on GLP-1 secretion and identify its key active molecules.

Methods: The GLP-1 secretory activity of i1088 lysate was assessed in human enteroendocrine NCI-H716 cells. Subsequently, the metabolic benefits of the lysate were validated in a T2DM mouse model. Untargeted metabolomics was employed to profile the bioactive substances of the lysate.

Results: In vitro, B breve i1088 lysate exhibited a robust, dose-dependent capacity to stimulate GLP-1 secretion. In vivo, high-dose lysate (HL) not only recapitulated the glucose and lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory efficacy of live bacteria (LB), but also demonstrated superior stability. Mechanistically, HL treatment profoundly reprogrammed the intestinal incretin axis by upregulating preproglucagon (GCG) and proprotein convertase 1 (PC1), thereby enhancing endogenous GLP-1 synthesis and preserving pancreatic islet function. Crucially, we identified 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) as the pivotal bioactive signature within the B breve i1088 lysate. Cellular assays confirmed that 5-HIAA directly triggered GLP-1 release and upregulated the mRNA expression of both the GCG and PC1 genes, serving as a key molecular messenger in the B breve i1088-mediated metabolic recovery.

Conclusion: HL enhances GLP-1 synthesis via the upregulation of the GCG/PC1 pathway and alleviates T2DM, with 5-HIAA serving as a key functional metabolite in this postbiotic-mediated response. The potent efficacy of the B. breve i1088 lysate highlights its potential as an innovative postbiotic therapy for T2DM management.

title: Characteristics and Treatment Utilisation Patterns of Individuals Using Tirzepatide for Type 2 Diabetes in Germany
abstract: Introduction: This study describes real-world characteristics and utilisation patterns of tirzepatide among adults with type 2 diabetes in German office-based practice.

Methods: This retrospective observational study analysed data from the CompuGroup Medical Healthcare Database. Cohort 1 initiated tirzepatide between 1 December 2023 and 31 March 2024 and cohort 2 between 1 July and 30 September 2024. A subgroup of cohort 1 with ≥ 6 months' follow-up data and uninterrupted tirzepatide use (cohort 1a) was also analysed. Descriptive statistics summarised baseline characteristics, prior therapy, and dosing patterns.

Results: Cohort 1 included 1223 individuals and cohort 2 included 2300; mean (± standard deviation) age was 59 ± 12 and 60 ± 12 years, respectively, and approximately 54% were male. Comorbidities, especially hypertension and dyslipidaemia, were frequent. Most individuals had prior insulin and/or glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) treatment (cohort 1, 72.1%; cohort 2, 59.6%). A total of 458 individuals had 6 months' follow-up (cohort 1a). The most common starting dose was 2.5 mg (71.2%). Use of higher doses gradually increased over time, with 5.0 mg becoming the most prevalent; at 6 months, 35.9% of individuals received 5.0 mg and 18.6% received 10.0 mg.

Conclusion: This first comprehensive real-world study of tirzepatide use in Germany showed tirzepatide initiation primarily after GLP-1 RA and/or insulin therapy. Most individuals remained on 5.0 mg, with a notable proportion escalating to 10.0 mg. Cohort characteristics were generally similar to those in the SURPASS trials, supporting the relevance of trial findings to clinical practice.

title: Real-world effectiveness of tirzepatide among youth with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity: a multicenter analysis
abstract: Objectives: Tirzepatide has demonstrated efficacy for adults and youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and adults with obesity, but real-world pediatric data remain limited. We evaluated clinical outcomes among youth prescribed tirzepatide across three academic centers.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of patients aged ≤21 years with T2D and/or obesity who initiated tirzepatide and had at least one follow-up visit. Primary outcomes were changes in hemoglobin A1c (A1C), body mass index (BMI), BMI z-score, and weight at first and second follow-up.

Results: The cohort included 74 patients. Median age was 18.4 years, 45.9 % were female, 86.5 % had T2D, and 78.4 % had prior GLP-1 RA exposure. At first follow-up (median 102 days [IQR 74, 133]), BMI decreased from 42.7 to 42.0 kg/m2 (n=69; p=0.003), BMI z-score from 2.9 to 2.8 (n=69; p<0.001), weight from 126.2 to 123.9 kg (n=69; p=0.001). In those with T2D, A1C decreased from 8.0 % to 7.2 % (n=58; p<0.001) and basal insulin dose declined from 59.7 to 43.9 units/day (n=24; p=0.008). At second follow-up, A1C, BMI, BMI z-score, and weight remained significantly lower than baseline. In multivariable regression analysis among patients with T2D, prior GLP-1 RA use and partial nonadherence were associated with smaller A1C reductions, while higher baseline A1C and higher tirzepatide dose were associated with greater A1C reductions.

Conclusions: In this multicenter real-world cohort, tirzepatide use among youth with T2D and/or obesity was associated with reductions in BMI and, in those with T2D, reductions in A1C despite prior GLP-1 RA exposure.
journal: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM

title: Neuropsychiatric Outcomes Associated With GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use in Medicare Beneficiaries With Type 2 Diabetes: Variation by Treatment Pattern and Obesity Status
abstract: Aims: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors are expressed in brain regions governing mood, reward and stress, yet the neuropsychiatric effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) therapy remain poorly characterized. We estimated associations between GLP-1 RA use and neuropsychiatric disorders and variation by obesity status and treatment pattern.

Material And Methods: This population-based cohort study used claims data from Medicare enrolees with Type 2 diabetes mellitus. GLP-1 RAs were compared with other second-line glucose-lowering medications and evaluated across four treatment patterns: monotherapy, switch, escalation and augmentation. Eight neuropsychiatric outcomes were examined using 1:1 propensity score-matched, covariate-adjusted stratified Cox regression with time-varying covariates.

Results: GLP-1 RA use was associated with a small increase in aggregate psychiatric disorder risk (Hazard Ratio [HR] = 1.04; 95% Confidence Interval: 1.03-1.06; 1.7 excess events/1000 person-years), of uncertain clinical significance given the large cohort size. Risk was elevated for depression (HR = 1.11; 3.0 excess events/1000 person-years) but reduced for substance use disorders (HR = 0.84; 4.1 fewer events/1000 person-years), dementia (HR = 0.87; 2.8 fewer) and suicidal/self-harm (HR = 0.81; 0.4 fewer events/1000 person-years). Associations varied by treatment pattern: monotherapy showed elevated psychiatric (HR = 1.43) and elevated emotional symptom (HR = 1.32) risks; escalation also exhibited elevated psychiatric risk, whereas switch and augmentation demonstrated reduced or null risks.

Conclusions: Rather than a uniform class effect, the neuropsychiatric profile of GLP-1 RA appears context-dependent, differing by treatment pattern, obesity status and outcome examined. Elevated risk with monotherapy or escalation may reflect baseline clinical differences rather than pharmacological effect. Reduced risks of substance use disorders, dementia and suicidal/self-harm are reassuring.

title: Trends in metabolic risk factor control and medication use among adults with type 2 diabetes in Taiwan, 2015-2024
abstract: Background: To evaluate 10-year trends in metabolic control and guideline-directed pharmacotherapy among adults with type 2 diabetes in Taiwan.

Methods: Using Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database (2015-2024), we analyzed annual trends in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and medication use. Blood pressure (BP) was assessed via a nationwide Pay-for-Performance registry. Trends were evaluated overall and across subgroups with cardiovascular disease (CVD) or chronic kidney disease (CKD).

Results: The treated population expanded from 1.58 to 2.27 million. Target achievement improved significantly: HbA1c <7.0% rose from 42.5% to 55.3%, and LDL-C <100 mg/dL from 54.3% to 69.0% (both p-trend <0.001). Among patients with all three measurements available, triple-factor control reached 18.2% by 2024. These gains coincided with rapid sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) uptake (from 3.3% in 2016 to 38.0% in 2024) and increased statin use. However, 23.5% of young adults (20-44 years) maintained poor glycemic control (HbA1c ≥ 8.5%). SGLT2i use was higher in patients with CVD (43.1%) or CKD (43.8%) than in those without the respective conditions (34.7% and 36.6%), while glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use remained below 4%.

Conclusions: Metabolic control in Taiwan improved substantially alongside adoption of newer therapies. Gaps among younger adults and high-risk cohorts highlight the need for targeted, risk-stratified management.
journal: Journal of the Formosan Medical Association = Taiwan yi zhi

title: Precision medicine approaches in diabetic cardiomyopathy: from molecular mechanisms to personalized therapeutic strategies
abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a distinct myocardial disease defined by the existence of abnormal myocardial structure and performance in diabetes mellitus patients without hypertension and coronary artery disease. DCM has been identified as a major cause of heart failure, hospitalisation and cardiovascular mortality with increasing global burden of diabetes. However, there is a large interindividual variation in disease susceptibility, disease progression and response to therapy, highlighting the limitations of conventional management strategies that are applied uniformly. Precision medicine provides a transformational approach through the integration of genomic, molecular, imaging, clinical and lifestyle data to allow for personalized risk assessment, early diagnosis, prognostication and treatment. This review presents the recent advances in the field of precision medicine for DCM with a focus on the molecular pathological mechanisms including metabolic disorders, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, fibrosis and microvascular injury. We discuss the relevance of genomics, pharmacogenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics and epigenomics in the context of disease heterogeneity and identification of novel therapeutic targets. Emerging biomarkers including circulating microRNAs, non-coding RNAs, inflammatory mediators, fibrosis-related markers and extracellular vesicles are discussed for their potential in personal diagnosis and prognosis. We also consider the increasing role of advanced cardiac imaging, digital phenotyping, wearable technologies, artificial intelligence, and machine learning in enhancing early detection and clinical decision-making. In this review, the therapeutic advances, including sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, anti-fibrotic therapies, mitochondrial-targeted interventions, regenerative medicine, gene therapy, and RNA-based therapeutics, are discussed, with a focus on the precision medicine approach. Finally, we present current challenges in data integration, clinical validation, cost-effectiveness, and ethical issues, and highlight future directions in digital twins, multi-omics integration, and AI-driven personalized cardiology. The combination of these technologies has the potential to revolutionize the prevention and management of diabetic cardiomyopathy and improve cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes.
journal: Journal of molecular and cellular cardiology

title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders treated with antipsychotics: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Weight gain and impaired glucose metabolism are common complications of antipsychotic treatment in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD). While beneficial in other populations, the efficacy and safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in SSD remain unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating GLP-1 RAs versus placebo in SSD patients treated with antipsychotics. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched until January 2026. Random-effects models were used to pool mean differences (MDs), standardized mean differences (SMDs), and risk ratios (RRs), as appropriate. Seven RCTs including 481 participants were included. Compared with placebo, GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD -6.98 kg; 95% CI -10.53 to -3.43), BMI (MD -2.51 kg/m²; 95% CI -3.51 to -1.51), waist circumference (MD -5.05 cm; 95% CI -6.66 to -3.44), HbA1c (MD -0.32 percentage points; 95% CI -0.38 to -0.26), and fasting blood glucose (MD -0.54 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.83 to -0.25). Heterogeneity was substantial for body weight (I²=93%) and BMI (I²=80%). No significant effects emerged for blood pressure or lipid parameters. Psychiatric symptom severity did not differ between GLP-1 RAs and placebo (SMD -0.05; 95% CI -0.36 to 0.25). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with GLP-1 RAs than with placebo, while overall study drop-out did not differ between groups. GLP-1 RAs improve short-term anthropometric and glycemic outcomes in SSD patients treated with antipsychotics. However, the limited number of trials, substantial heterogeneity in weight-related outcomes, and relatively short follow-up warrant cautious interpretation and further large-scale RCTs.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology

title: Parasympathetic dysfunction assessed by deep-breathing CVR-R is associated with early discontinuation of oral semaglutide in type 2 diabetes: A multicenter retrospective study
abstract: Aims/Introduction: Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are widely used for type 2 diabetes, gastrointestinal intolerance frequently leads to early discontinuation. Predictors of oral semaglutide discontinuation remain poorly defined, and its formulation-specific dependence on gastric conditions may influence tolerability. We examined whether the coefficient of variation of R-R intervals (CVR-R) was associated with discontinuation within 6 months.

Materials And Methods: In this multicenter retrospective study, 203 consecutive patients initiating oral semaglutide between February 2021 and December 2024 were screened, and 61 were analyzed after exclusions. The Discontinuation Group (n = 21) discontinued because of nausea and/or vomiting within 6 months, whereas the Maintenance Group (n = 40) continued for ≥ 6 months. CVR-R was assessed at rest (CVR-R_rest) and during deep breathing (CVR-R_DB). Associations with discontinuation were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression; exploratory machine learning and time-to-event analyses were performed.

Results: CVR-R_DB was lower in the Discontinuation Group than in the Maintenance Group (median 1.93% vs 3.26%, P < 0.001). CVR-R_DB remained independently associated with discontinuation after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 0.191; 95% CI 0.071-0.512; P = 0.001; AUC 0.832) and further adjustment for neuropathy stage. The AUC was numerically higher for the age- and sex-adjusted model containing CVR-R_DB than for that containing CVR-R_rest (0.832 vs 0.699; DeLong P = 0.085). An internally derived CVR-R_DB cutoff of 2.55% stratified 6-month persistence (43.3% vs 87.1%; log-rank P < 0.001), and machine learning analyses prioritized CVR-R_DB.
Conclusions: Lower CVR-R during deep breathing was associated with early oral semaglutide discontinuation due to nausea and/or vomiting. CVR-R_DB may support risk stratification at initiation.

title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists for antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background: Antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation are highly prevalent among patients with severe mental illness. Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial metabolic benefits in the general population, their efficacy and safety in antipsychotic-treated patients remain unclear. This review aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of GLP-1RAs in patients with antipsychotic-related overweight and metabolic dysregulation.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating GLP-1RAs in adults receiving antipsychotic treatment. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 13, 2026. Primary outcomes included changes in body weight, body mass index (BMI), HbA1c, and total cholesterol. Random-effects models were used to pool mean differences (MDs) and risk ratios (RRs). This study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261290294).

Results: Eight RCTs involving 535 randomized participants were included. GLP-1RAs treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight (MD = -6.54 kg, 95% CI: -9.80 to -3.29, P < 0.001, I2 = 92%), BMI (MD = -2.34 kg/m2, 95% CI: -3.34 to -1.34, P < 0.001, I² = 85%), HbA1c (MD = -0.32%, 95% CI: -0.39 to -0.26, P < 0.001, I² = 52%), waist circumference (MD = -5.22 cm, 95% CI: -6.55 to -3.88, P < 0.001, I2 = 27%), visceral fat mass (MD = -0.31 kg, 95% CI: -0.46 to -0.16, P < 0.001, I2 = 11%), and LDL-C (MD = -0.16 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.31 to -0.01, P = 0.03, I2 = 54%), whereas no significant effects were observed for total cholesterol, triglycerides, or HDL-C. Weight reduction was greatest with semaglutide, followed by liraglutide, and increased with longer treatment duration (both P for subgroup differences < 0.05). GLP-1RAs were associated with higher risks of nausea (RR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.20 to 2.16), vomiting (RR = 2.10, 95% CI: 1.32 to 3.35), and constipation (RR = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.23 to 4.47), but not of diarrhea, serious adverse events (RR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.49 to 1.06), all-cause discontinuation (RR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.60 to 1.85), or discontinuation due to adverse events (RR = 2.14, 95% CI: 0.72 to 6.33). Psychiatric adverse events were infrequent and could not be pooled.

Conclusion: GLP-1RAs significantly improve weight-related and glycemic outcomes in antipsychotic-treated patients, at the cost of an increased risk of gastrointestinal adverse events. Their psychiatric safety could not be established owing to sparse data. Longer-term trials with standardized safety reporting are warranted.

title: Metabolic biomarker levels before and after initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment among individuals with schizophrenia: interrupted time-series analysis
abstract: Background: Randomised controlled trials have demonstrated that treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) reduces body weight, waist circumference and haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in patients with schizophrenia. However, because of participant selection in clinical trials, it remains unclear whether the beneficial metabolic effects of GLP-1RAs for patients with schizophrenia extend to real-world clinical settings.

Aims: We investigated whether GLP-1RA treatment initiation was associated with reductions in HbA1c, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and triglyceride levels (the latter two as proxies for weight loss) in individuals with schizophrenia.

Method: We used the Danish nationwide registers to identify individuals with schizophrenia between 1996 and 2023. Among those, we identified individuals initiating GLP-1RA treatment. The main outcomes were changes in HbA1c, LDL and triglyceride levels following initiation of GLP-1RA treatment. Changes in HbA1c, LDL and triglyceride levels were visualised graphically and quantified with interrupted time-series analyses.

Results: We identified 3042 individuals with schizophrenia who initiated a GLP-1RA. Initiation of GLP-1RA treatment for diabetes was followed by reductions in HbA1c, LDL and triglyceride levels of 11.4, 6.2 and 14.8%, respectively. Initiation of GLP-1RA treatment for overweight was followed by reductions in HbA1c, LDL and triglyceride levels of 3.4, 4.9 and 12.7%, respectively. All level changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Initiation of GLP-1RA treatment was followed by clinically meaningful reductions in HbA1c, LDL and triglyceride levels among individuals with schizophrenia. These findings suggest that the metabolic benefits of GLP-1RA treatment found in randomised clinical trials in schizophrenia extend to real-world clinical settings.
journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science

title: A rare diagnosis during evaluation for metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease: Glycogen storage disease type Ia presenting during adolescence in a male with severe obesity
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a common comorbidity of pediatric obesity that predisposes patients to hepatocellular adenomas (HCAs). HCAs however are nonspecific to MASLD and warrant further evaluation. We present a case of a 16-year-old male with severe obesity, and persistently elevated liver enzymes, initially evaluated for MASLD. Imaging revealed multiple hepatic lesions consistent with HCAs, prompting further genetic evaluation. Trio exome sequencing identified biallelic variants in the glucose-6-phophatase gene, confirming a diagnosis of glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSD Ia). This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by overlapping features of MASLD and GSD Ia, particularly hepatic steatosis, HCAs, and metabolic syndrome. Initial management of MASLD with glucagon-like peptide-1 therapy was discontinued given risk for hypoglycemia, and the patient continues glucose monitoring and cornstarch therapy. This case emphasizes the importance of including inborn errors of metabolism in the differential diagnosis for multifocal HCAs and concerns with obesity treatments.

title: Skeletal effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in adults with overweight or obesity: a systematic review
abstract: Unlabelled: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for weight management, yet their skeletal effects remain unclear. This systematic review of eight randomized controlled trials (n = 493) evaluating dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-derived bone mineral density reports findings separately for each agent, without pooling, because the trials evaluated four pharmacologically distinct agents differing markedly in weight-lowering potency. The evidence is sparse for every agent and is insufficient to establish the skeletal effects of GLP-1 RA therapy in this population.

Purpose: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for weight management, yet their skeletal effects remain uncertain. We systematically reviewed the randomized evidence on bone mineral density (BMD) and bone turnover markers in adults with overweight or obesity, reporting findings separately for each individual agent.

Methods: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review (INPLASY202630076) searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Google Scholar (January 2015 to July 2026). Eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolled adults aged ≥18 years with mean baseline body mass index (BMI) > 25 kg/m², compared a GLP-1 RA with placebo or another antidiabetic therapy for ≥12 weeks, and reported BMD assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Because the included trials evaluated pharmacologically distinct agents that differ substantially in weight-lowering potency, results were synthesized narratively and reported separately by agent; no meta-analysis was performed.

Results: Eight RCTs (n = 493) were included. Three trials were at low risk of bias (Eriksson 2019; Hygum 2020; Hansen 2024) and five raised some concerns, principally regarding the randomization process and selective reporting; no agent is supported by more than one trial at low risk of bias. (Cai 2021 contributes two treatment arms assessed separately, giving nine comparisons in the risk-of-bias assessment.) Evidence was unevenly distributed across agents: semaglutide and dulaglutide were each evaluated in one trial, liraglutide in two, and exenatide in five. Five of the eight trials enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes, including all four that randomized an insulin comparator arm; three enrolled adults without diabetes, of which one was defined by obesity alone. By study-level mean baseline BMI, five trials lay in the obese range ( ≥ 30 kg/m²) and three in the overweight range (25 to <30 kg/m²). The single semaglutide trial (Hansen 2024; n = 64; low risk of bias), which produced the largest weight loss of any trial (estimated treatment difference [ETD] -6.8 kg vs placebo), reported reduced lumbar spine BMD (ETD - 0.018 g/cm², p = 0.007), reduced whole-body BMD (mean difference [MD] -0.02 g/cm²; 95% CI - 0.03 to -0.01), and increased C-terminal telopeptide (CTX; MD 166.50 pg/mL; 95% CI 66.60 to 266.40). Liraglutide was evaluated at two doses with divergent results. At the weight-management dose of 3.0 mg daily, in the only trial conducted in adults with obesity and without diabetes (Jensen 2024; ETD - 6.7 kg vs placebo), lumbar spine BMD (MD - 0.019 g/cm²; 95% CI - 0.034 to -0.004) and total hip BMD (MD - 0.013 g/cm²; 95% CI - 0.024 to -0.002) were reduced. At the diabetes dose of 1.8 mg daily (Hygum 2020; -3.8 kg), no site changed materially (lumbar spine MD 0.00 g/cm²; 95% CI - 0.01 to 0.01). Exenatide trials were inconsistent, ranging from 0.03 g/cm² (95% CI 0.02 to 0.03) at the lumbar spine (Renyuan 2015) to -0.04 g/cm² (95% CI - 0.15 to 0.07; Akyay 2023). Certainty of evidence was very low for every agent.

Conclusion: The randomized evidence is too sparse and too clinically heterogeneous to determine the skeletal effects of GLP-1 RA therapy in adults with overweight or obesity. Each agent has been evaluated in at most five small trials, most conducted in adults with type 2 diabetes rather than in adults with obesity alone. The two trials producing the largest weight loss, one of semaglutide and one of liraglutide 3.0 mg, both reported reduced lumbar spine and total hip BMD at closely similar magnitudes of weight loss, and the semaglutide trial additionally reported increased bone resorption. This convergence warrants dedicated evaluation rather than extrapolation across the drug class. Adequately powered, agent-specific trials with fracture endpoints are required.
Protocol Registration: INPLASY202630076.

title: Gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's disease: neuroinflammatory mechanisms and immunopharmacological interventions
abstract: Despite being defined pathologically by amyloid-β plaques, chronic neuroinflammation and neurofibrillary tangles, the drugs that target these processes directly (lecanemab and donanemab) have only modest effects on the clinical course of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and significant safety concerns have been identified, so there is renewed interest in upstream, systemic contributors to disease. This review aims to provide a synthesis of the latest mechanistic and clinical evidence that gut microbiota dysbiosis is associated with Alzheimer's disease with a specifically immunopharmacological focus. We will explore how the gut-brain axis pathways (vagal, immune, endocrine and microbial-metabolite signaling) converge to trigger microglial and astrocytic activation via toll-like receptor 4/NF-κB and complement-primed NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, which is also directly activated by amyloid-β and tau. Then we review the immunopharmacological interventions intended to break this axis - probiotic supplementation (some consistent benefit - although mild) and sodium oligomannate, with strong preclinical and case report signals that need human trials (in 2026) and polyphenols and GLP-1 receptor agonists, which have a persistent disconnect between mechanistic promise and clinical efficacy, including a definitive null result for semaglutide in 2026. Translative directions are addressed to nanotechnology-based delivery systems for improving bioavailability and blood-brain barrier penetration, as well as emerging precision-medicine, AI-driven approaches in the selection of treatments based on microbiome information. It is our opinion that because the gut-brain-immune axis is a mechanistically supported and potentially highly scalable therapeutic target, complementary to amyloid and tau therapies, the development of future therapies should match the inflammatory, metabolic and microbial phenotypes.

title: GLP-1-based therapies in cardiovascular disease: outcomes, mechanisms, and emerging clinical applications
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have shown cardiovascular benefits beyond their established role in treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This review evaluates recent clinical evidence, potential mechanisms, and the expanding use of GLP-1-based therapies in cardiovascular disease.

Methods: We reviewed major randomized clinical trials assessing cardiovascular, kidney, and heart failure outcomes, along with related mechanistic studies and clinical guidelines published through July 2026.

Results: Early trials, including LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, and REWIND, reported 12%-26% reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with T2DM. More recent trials have extended these findings to other populations. SELECT showed a 20% reduction in MACE among individuals with obesity and established cardiovascular disease but without diabetes, while FLOW demonstrated a 24% reduction in its primary kidney composite outcome. SOUL reported a 14% reduction in MACE with oral semaglutide, and SUMMIT showed a 38% reduction in cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure with tirzepatide. SURPASS-CVOT found tirzepatide to be noninferior, but not superior, to dulaglutide for MACE. These benefits likely involve several mechanisms beyond glucose lowering and weight loss, although gastrointestinal adverse effects still remain a concern.

Conclusions: Growing clinical evidence supports the use of GLP-1-based therapies beyond diabetes management, particularly in patients with cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or obesity-related heart failure. Further studies will be needed to understand their mechanisms better, long-term safety, and optimal use in clinical practice.

title: Pharmacotherapy for MASLD: current evidence and challenges in clinical practice
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is characterized by a complex pathophysiology driven by intertwined metabolic and hepatic pathways, enabling the identification of multiple therapeutic targets and a rapidly expanding drug development pipeline. This review summarizes the current and emerging therapeutic landscape for MASLD and discusses key challenges for clinical implementation. The imminent availability of several new therapies is expected to pose important clinical challenges, particularly in accurately identifying patients most likely to benefit. Currently, resmetirom and semaglutide are the only two drugs conditionally approved for patients with fibrosis stages 2-3, pending final phase 3 outcomes, and represent the main liver-directed and metabolic-focused therapeutic strategies, respectively. Treatment selection should follow a phenotype-based approach integrating metabolic profile and liver disease stage. Non-invasive tests are central for assessing treatment eligibility; however, strategies incorporating metabolic risk profiling and longitudinal monitoring will be essential to optimize real-world management of MASH.

title: New Horizons for Incretin-Based Therapeutics
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies marked a major breakthrough in obesity pharmacotherapy, while subsequent advancements targeting multiple entero-pancreatic hormones now deliver weight loss previously achievable only with bariatric surgery, alongside improvements in obesity-related complications. Despite this progress, significant challenges persist, including reduced efficacy in diabetic populations, gastrointestinal adverse effects, and high costs that drive a real-world adherence gap. Consequently, next-generation therapies, including receptor polyagonists, oral formulations, and small-molecule incretin mimetics with optimized pharmacokinetic profiles, are being developed to enhance efficacy, tolerability, and accessibility while maintaining safety. However, weight regain after treatment cessation remains a critical hurdle. Growing evidence underscores the importance of sustained lifestyle interventions and muscle mass preservation to facilitate weight stabilization. Concurrently, research is heavily focused on identifying the biological drivers of weight regain, such as altered neuroregulation, metabolic adaptation, and adipose tissue remodeling. This review examines the current landscape, limitations, and emerging strategies of obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Lessons from dog lifespan therapeutics for their human companions
abstract: The growing evidence that existing cardio-renal-metabolic therapies, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors, confer all-cause mortality benefits has positioned them as the first wave of potential gerotherapeutics. However, repurposing these drugs for a lifespan extension indication remains constrained by trial duration, misaligned incentives, and the lack of a viable regulatory path. We highlight two parallel strategies to address these barriers: (1) identifying and validating precise surrogate endpoints, and (2) modifying the 505(b)(2) pathway to allow accelerated approval of already-approved drugs with demonstrated mortality benefit and favorable post-marketing safety. Veterinary medicine's expanded conditional approval framework already applies these strategies, offering precedent for human gerotherapeutics development.

title: Dissecting polycystic metabolic ovarian syndrome heterogeneity (PMOS): multi-omics, AI subtyping, and precision management
abstract: Polycystic metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is the most common endocrine disorder, affecting 8-12% of women of reproductive age and increasing the risk of infertility, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease. However, traditional symptom-based diagnostic criteria do not fully capture the underlying biological diversity of PMOS. Recent research using multi-omics and artificial intelligence (AI) has revealed that PMOS is best understood as a syndrome with multiple subtypes. Data-driven clustering of clinical variables consistently identifies four major subtypes: HA-PCOS, OB-PCOS, SHBG-PCOS, and LH-PCOS. Each subtype shows unique hormonal, metabolic, and genetic features, including distinct patterns in lipid, amino acid, and energy metabolism. Immune system disruptions and impaired blood clot breakdown in the ovarian environment are also notable features. Novel findings suggest that altered lactate metabolism and changes in histone lactylation may contribute to granulosa cell dysfunction, although further studies are needed to confirm these mechanisms. Machine learning models that integrate clinical, metabolic, and genetic data have achieved high diagnostic accuracy and can provide interpretable results. Potential targeted therapies, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, N-acetylcysteine, and NK3R antagonists, have been proposed for specific subtypes, but have yet to be validated in clinical trials. Remaining challenges include small and homogeneous study cohorts, limited long-term data, and barriers to care in low-resource settings. Overall, recognizing PMOS as a syndrome with distinct subtypes highlights the promise of AI-powered, personalized approaches for more effective and equitable management.

title: Targeting the gut-liver axis and gut microbiome in pediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: current evidence and future directions
abstract: Unlabelled: Pediatric metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease in children, closely linked to the rising prevalence of childhood obesity and metabolic syndrome. Increasing evidence highlights the central role of the gut-liver axis and the gut microbiome in disease pathogenesis, offering potential targets for therapeutic modulation. This review aims to summarize current evidence on interventions targeting the gut-liver axis and the gut microbiome in pediatric MASLD and explore emerging strategies in this field. This narrative review was undertaken after searching PubMed and Embase databases for available up-to-date literature on pediatric MASLD and therapeutic interventions targeting the gut microbiome and gut-liver axis, including dietary therapy, prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and pharmacological therapies. Dietary interventions, including low-free-sugar and Mediterranean-style diets, improve hepatic and metabolic outcomes, although microbiome-mediated benefits remain unproven in children. Probiotics and synbiotics show modest and variable effects, with heterogeneity in strains, dosing, and outcomes limiting definitive conclusions. Evidence for FMT in pediatric MASLD is absent, with only indirect evidence from adolescent obesity and other pediatric diseases. Pharmacological therapies, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and farnesoid X receptor agonists, have demonstrated metabolic and hepatic benefits primarily in adult populations, while effects on microbial metabolism, intestinal barrier integrity, and bile acid signalling provide potential mechanisms linking these therapies to the gut-liver axis. Although microbiome-mediated mechanisms have been proposed, direct evidence linking these therapies to microbiome changes in pediatric MASLD is currently lacking. Emerging approaches such as precision nutrition, engineered probiotics, and bacteriophage therapy offer potential avenues for targeted modulation of disease-relevant pathways.

Conclusion: Therapeutic modulation of the gut-liver axis and the gut microbiome represents a biologically plausible and evolving strategy in pediatric MASLD. Current pediatric evidence remains limited, and robust, well-designed clinical trials incorporating microbiome profiling and clinically meaningful endpoints are needed to establish efficacy and enable personalized, therapeutic strategies.

What Is Known: • Pediatric MASLD is increasing in prevalence, and alterations in the gut-liver axis and the gut microbiome are known to contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease by influencing various disease-relevant pathways such as intestinal permeability, bile acid signaling, hepatic lipid metabolism, inflammation, and fibrogenesis.

What Is New: • This review provides current evidence for interventions targeting the gut microbiome and gut-liver axis in pediatric MASLD including dietary modulation, probiotics, and pharmacological interventions and highlights new approaches such as precision nutrition, engineered probiotics, bacteriophage therapy, and personalized treatment strategies.

title: Sustained Versus Minimal GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Exposure and Metabolic Outcomes in Older Adults Without Diabetes
abstract: Aims: To compare changes in body mass index (BMI) categories after sustained versus minimal glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) exposure in older adults with obesity and without diabetes. A secondary aim was to compare changes in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) categories among those with paired HbA1c measurements.

Materials And Methods: Retrospective cohort study within Clalit Health Services, Israel. Adults aged ≥ 65 years without diabetes, with baseline BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 and paired BMI measurements, were classified as minimal (1-2 dispensations) or sustained (≥ 3) exposure. The primary outcome was BMI category improvement. Secondary outcomes were relative BMI change, HbA1c category change in the paired-HbA1c subset, and incident diagnosed diabetes. BMI improvement was modelled by logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, socioeconomic status and comorbidity.

Results: Of 13 387 patients (69% female), 11 121 (83%) had sustained and 2266 (17%) minimal exposure. BMI category improved in 55% of the sustained versus 30% of the minimal group (p < 0.001; median change -8% vs. -2%). Among 7392 with paired HbA1c, HbA1c improved in 34% versus 20% (sustained vs. minimal; p < 0.001), and 65% versus 37% of those with prediabetes became normoglycaemic. Diabetes diagnosis was less frequent with sustained exposure (2.5% vs. 5.3%; p < 0.001). Adjusted for measured confounders, sustained exposure was associated with BMI improvement (OR: 2.77, 95% CI: 2.51-3.06).

Conclusions: Among older adults with obesity and without diabetes, sustained versus minimal GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with greater improvement in BMI and HbA1c categories and a lower incidence of diabetes. These findings describe observed changes after treatment initiation, not a proven causal treatment effect.

title: How Well Are We Measuring Nausea? A Narrative Review of Patient-Reported Outcome Gaps in GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Obesity Trials
abstract: Across the full spectrum of major clinical trials evaluating glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for obesity management, nausea consistently emerges as the most documented adverse effect, yet the methods used to capture it have received little scrutiny relative to their clinical importance. This narrative review traces how nausea was actually measured across the pivotal liraglutide (SCALE), semaglutide (STEP) and tirzepatide (SURMOUNT) obesity trial programmes, and situates those methods against the standards set out in the Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) and the United States Food and Drug Administration's Patient-Focused Drug Development guidance. Across all three drug classes, nausea was ascertained through investigator-recorded, spontaneously reported adverse events coded to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), a pharmacovigilance framework built for a different purpose than symptom characterization, rather than through any validated, symptom-specific patient-reported outcome instrument. This observation gains further importance when considered alongside a second, less widely recognized fact: these same trial programmes devoted substantial methodological effort to developing and implementing a rigorous, quality of life measure specifically for obesity, the Impact of Weight on Quality of Life-Lite Clinical Trials Version in addition to the Short Form-36 and EuroQol-5D. We argue that this asymmetry, more than any single mismeasurement, helps explain why real-world persistence with these agents falls so far short of what trial-reported tolerability figures would predict, and we outline what a fit-for-purpose metabolic nausea instrument would need to capture that adverse-event surveillance cannot.

title: Closing the Gap to Bariatric Surgery: Predictors of Non-Progression in Patients with Obesity Class IV and V at a Community-Based Bariatric Center
abstract: Introduction: Patients with obesity class IV and V benefit substantially from bariatric surgery, yet many do not complete the preoperative pathway. The contribution of system-level barriers and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) therapy to non-progression remains poorly understood, particularly in community settings.

Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective study of adults with obesity class IV and V evaluated for bariatric surgery (2024-2025). The primary outcome was progression to surgery. Variables included demographics, comorbidities, insurance, primary care physician (PCP) status, GLP-1 RA use, specialist consultation completion, prior authorization activity, and surgeon follow-up. Chi-square testing, stratified odds ratios, and multivariable logistic regression were performed.

Results: Among 73 patients, 38 (52.1%) did not progress to surgery. Demographics and comorbidities were similar between groups. Patients who did not progress had lower PCP establishment (44.7% versus 97.1%, P < .001), fewer completed specialist consultations (28.9% versus 71.4%, P = .001), fewer nutrition visits (P = .004), and fewer surgeon follow-up visits (P < .001). GLP-1 RA use at initial consultation was associated with lower progression to surgery (57.9% versus 11.4%, OR 0.12, P = .008), with consistent findings across insurance types but a weaker association among patients without an established PCP. Patients who did not progress also had higher emergency department utilization and more system-related scheduling barriers (both P < .001).

Conclusion: Non-progression to bariatric surgery was associated with modifiable system-level barriers, including limited PCP integration, incomplete specialist evaluation, and reduced surgical follow-up. GLP-1 RA use at presentation was also associated with non-progression, although this relationship may reflect differences in treatment pathways rather than a direct treatment effect. Structured patient navigation and integrated medical-surgical obesity care may improve pathway completion.
journal: Journal of laparoendoscopic & advanced surgical techniques. Part A

title: Modern antidiabetic therapy in older adults with type 2 diabetes: evidence, best practice and a clinical pharmacist's framework
abstract: Introduction: Older adults with type 2 diabetes require treatment that balances cardiovascular and kidney protection against hypoglycemia, treatment burden, undernutrition, and functional vulnerability.

Areas Covered: This narrative review considers PubMed-indexed literature and ClinicalTrials.gov records covering January 2010-October 2026, with targeted updating on 12 October 2026. It examines sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, tirzepatide, and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors. Age-stratified outcome evidence is distinguished from whole-trial results and the limited evidence in adults aged 80 years or older. Body-composition findings, neurodegenerative outcomes, kidney-protective treatment, and pharmacist-supported regimen modification are critically appraised.

Expert Opinion: Organ protection and glycemic simplification should be considered separately. Frailty is not synonymous with kidney impairment, and reductions in lean mass do not establish treatment-induced sarcopenia. Weight-neutral therapy remains useful when weight loss is undesirable. A structured medication review should integrate patient priorities, nutrition, physical performance, renal function, and hypoglycemia risk, followed by explicit monitoring and communication across care transitions. Prospective validation of this integrated framework in the oldest and most vulnerable populations is needed.

title: The Veterans Affairs Pentoxifylline in Diabetic Kidney Disease (VA PTXRx) Study: Baseline Characteristics
abstract: Introduction: Experimental and clinical data suggest that the non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor pentoxifylline (PTX) reduces proteinuria and may delay the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). However, no large-scale randomized clinical trial has determined whether PTX can reduce end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and mortality in DKD.

Design: VA PTXRx is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter clinical trial designed to test the hypothesis that PTX, when added to usual care, prolongs the time to kidney failure or death in type 2 diabetic (T2D) participants with DKD compared to usual care plus placebo. Enrolled participants at very high risk for ESKD and/or death were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either PTX 400 mg twice daily or matching placebo using randomly permuted blocks with stratification for site, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAAS) inhibitor use, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. The study is event-driven, requiring 646 primary events (ESKD (chronic dialysis or transplantation) or death) to achieve 80% power to detect a relative risk reduction of 19% with PTX.

Baseline Results: Between December 2019 and November 2025, 2376 participants at 34 VA sites in the USA were randomized. The mean age at randomization was 72.3 years (SD 7.7), with 97% being male. The mean baseline eGFR was 33.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 (SD 9.4). The median urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) was 401 mg/g (IQR 122-1076). At baseline, the usage of RAAS inhibitors was 80.0%, sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors 52.9%, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists 33.2%, and finerenone 3.0%. The majority (88%) of participants had stage 3B or 4 CKD (eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73m2).

Conclusions: The results, anticipated in 2027, are expected to determine whether PTX is a treatment option for patients with high-risk DKD. Because PTX is a generic medication, it is inexpensive in many health systems, which would facilitate access if it proves effective. Trial Registration: This study is registered with clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT03625648).
journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use before Total Knee Arthroplasty is Associated with Lower Postoperative MI, DVT, and VTE Rates
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly prescribed for glycemic control and weight management, but their association with postoperative thrombotic events after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains unclear. We performed a retrospective cohort study using de-identified data from the TriNetX United States Collaborative Network, including adults who underwent primary TKA between December 1, 2006, and June 1, 2025. Patients with prior myocardial infarction (MI), deep vein thrombosis (DVT), venous thromboembolism (VTE), or pulmonary embolism (PE) were excluded. Exposure was defined as a prescription for a GLP-1 RA within 1 year and 1 day before surgery. A 1:1 propensity score match was performed on demographics, relevant comorbidities, and medications, yielding 11,765 patients in each cohort. Outcomes were postoperative MI, DVT, VTE, and PE. Compared with matched controls, patients prescribed GLP-1 RAs had a significantly lower risk of MI (25/11,246 vs. 47/11,171; risk ratio [RR] 0.528; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.325-0.858). GLP-1 RAs use was also associated with a reduced risk of DVT (74/11,319 vs. 103/11,308; RR 0.718; 95% CI, 0.533-0.966) and VTE (133/11,040 vs. 172/11,027; RR 0.772; 95% CI, 0.617-0.967). In contrast, no statistically significant difference was observed in the incidence of PE between groups (49/11,352 vs. 58/11,382; RR 0.847; 95% CI, 0.580-1.238). Overall, preoperative GLP-1 RA use was associated with a significantly lower postoperative risk of MI, DVT, and VTE following TKA in this large, nationally representative cohort.

title: Pharmacogenetics of incretin-based therapies
abstract: Interindividual variability in the efficacy of various glucose-lowering drugs has been previously reported and partly explained by genetic variants. The aim of this review was to summarize currently available information on pharmacogenetic studies of the efficacy of incretin-based therapies such as glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP1RA) and dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4i) inhibitors. Several missense variants of the GLP1R gene have been associated with the effects of GLP1RA or DPP-4 inhibitors on glycaemic compensation or weight. Pharmacogenetic effects have also been reported for several type 2 diabetes-associated loci, such as TCF7L2, THADA, MTNR1B, CDKAL1, KCNQ1, KCNJ11, and PAM in candidate gene approach studies. Genome-wide pharmacogenetic studies have identified new genes with potentially relevant pharmacogenetic effects (CTRB1/2, ARRB1, PRKD1). Although none of these genetic associations are currently used in guiding the treatment choices in clinical practice, they offer valuable insights bringing us a little closer to precision medicine.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Cancer Risk in Obesity Treatment
abstract: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for numerous cancers, with body habitus, especially central adiposity, contributing to increased cancer incidence and worse prognosis. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), initially developed to treat Type 2 diabetes, have rapidly gained prominence as powerful anti-obesity agents due to their ability to induce significant weight loss and potential to improve metabolic health. These medications act by reducing appetite, enhancing insulin sensitivity, lowering systemic inflammation, and preferentially targeting fat mass for reduction. This review explores the growing body of evidence linking GLP-1 RA therapy to potential changes in cancer risk among individuals with obesity. To date, data suggest that GLP-1 RAs do not increase overall cancer risk and may reduce the risk of certain obesity-related cancers, likely by interrupting obesity-driven metabolic dysregulation. Still, questions remain about the beneficial effects of weight loss and the sustainability of health benefits if weight is regained after stopping treatment. We examine how GLP-1 RAs' anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects might mediate reductions in cancer risk, review emerging data regarding both protective signals and specific safety concerns (e.g., increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma), and emphasize the critical role of combining pharmacotherapy with lifestyle interventions to maintain muscle mass and long-term weight loss. Ultimately, given the strong link between obesity and cancer, GLP-1 RAs represent a promising new class of agents that may not only help to manage obesity but also serve as effective chemopreventive tools against obesity-associated cancers.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

title: The Impact of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists on Post-Anesthetic Pulmonary and Gastrointestinal Adverse Events: A Target Trial Emulation Using Multinational Database
abstract: Objective: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) delay gastric emptying, raising concerns about perioperative aspiration and postoperative complications. This target trial emulation aims to evaluate the association between the use of GLP-1 RAs and the risk of postoperative pulmonary and gastrointestinal adverse events in patients undergoing general anesthesia.

Methods: Data was utilized from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. The study analyzed data from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2023. Patients aged 20 years or older who underwent general anesthesia were included. These patients were divided into two groups: those using GLP-1 RA and those who were not. Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics. The primary outcome measures were the incidence of pulmonary and gastrointestinal adverse events within one-month post-anesthesia. Hazard ratios were calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression models to estimate the risk of these adverse events associated with GLP-1 RA use.

Results: A total of 21,948 patients were included after matching. Patients who used GLP-1 RAs demonstrated a significantly lower risk of pulmonary adverse events (HR 0.682 [0.496-0.938]). Secondary outcomes further revealed a reduction in the risk of postoperative respiratory failure, as well as postoperative hospitalization and emergency department revisits. However, there was a marginally increased risk of gastrointestinal adverse events in the GLP-1 RA group (HR, 1.034 [1.003-1.067]).

Conclusions: The use of GLP-1 RAs prior to general anesthesia was not associated with higher risk of pulmonary adverse events. A slight elevation in gastrointestinal risks was observed, although the signal remained modest.

title: Outcomes after Posterior Cervical Spine Surgery: A Matched Cohort Analysis and Comparison of GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use and Bariatric Surgery in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: Background Context: Obesity and diabetes can increase perioperative risk, especially in posterior cervical spine surgery. Bariatric surgery provides durable weight loss but carries surgical and nutritional risks, while glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are non-surgical alternatives that may optimize weight and metabolic status preoperatively. Evidence evaluating GLP-1 therapy in spine surgery is limited.

Purpose: To evaluate associations between preoperative GLP-1 RA use and perioperative, short-term, and long-term complications following posterior cervical spine surgery in patients with type 2 diabetes, including comparisons to matched controls and patients with prior bariatric surgery.
Study Design: Retrospective database analysis.

Patient Sample: Patients with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin undergoing posterior cervical spine surgery between 2010 and 2023 were identified in the PearlDiver Mariner database. Patients were stratified into GLP-1 users, non-GLP-1 controls, and patients with prior bariatric surgery.

Outcome Measures: Physiologic measures included perioperative outcomes and postoperative complications assessed at 90 days and 2 years, including pneumonitis, surgical site infection, revision surgery, readmission, nutritional deficiency, and other medical and surgical complications.

Methods: The PearlDiver Mariner database was queried for eligible patients. Propensity-score matching adjusted for baseline cohort differences. Outcomes included perioperative, 90-day, and 2-year complications, with BMI-stratified analyses conducted within the matched GLP-1 and control cohort. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied for multiple comparisons.

Results: GLP-1 users demonstrated lower odds of perioperative complications, including pneumonitis (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.43-0.75; p <0.001). At 90 days, GLP-1 users experienced reduced odds of surgical site infection (OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.65-0.80; p <0.001), revision surgery (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.29-0.36; p <0.001), readmission (OR 0.82; 95% CI 0.76-0.90; p <0.001), and other complications. At 2 years, GLP-1 users had lower odds of revision surgery (OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.28-0.34; p <0.001), nutritional deficiency (OR 0.62; 95% CI 0.59-0.66; p <0.001), and other complications. Exploratory BMI-stratified analyses suggested similar directional trends across overweight and obese patients. Comparisons to prior bariatric surgery patients showed no significant differences.

Conclusions: Preoperative GLP-1 RA use was associated with reduced perioperative, short-term, and long-term complications following posterior cervical spine surgery in patients with type 2 diabetes. When compared with a matched bariatric surgery cohort, no significant differences in postoperative outcomes were observed. These findings should be interpreted in the context of potential residual confounding and support further prospective investigation of GLP-1 therapy as a strategy for preoperative metabolic optimization in posterior cervical spine surgery.
Classifications: Cervical Spine, Outcomes Research, Risk Factors, Perioperative Complications.
journal: The spine journal : official journal of the North American Spine Society

title: Decoding the Safety Profile of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Facts, Myths, and Ongoing Controversies
abstract: Purpose Of Review: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) represent one of the most significant therapeutic advances in the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. As their indications have expanded to include cardiovascular and kidney disease, safety concerns involving multiple organ systems have received increasing attention. This narrative review examines the spectrum of adverse effects linked to GLP-1RAs and provides a clinically relevant platform for assessing their safe prescription.

Recent Findings: Gastrointestinal intolerance, modest increases in heart rate, and a modest but reproducible increase in the risk of gallbladder and biliary disease represent the most consistently supported adverse effects of GLP-1RAs. A risk of pancreatitis is also considered to exist, although some studies have challenged this association. Conversely, correlations with neuropsychiatric and dermatological disorders, diabetic retinopathy, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, perioperative aspiration, sexual and reproductive disturbances, sarcopenia, and malignancy remain controversial. Most available evidence derives from pharmacovigilance databases, retrospective observational studies, and secondary analyses of randomized trials, which are limited by reporting bias, residual confounding, and inability to establish causality. Heterogeneity in study design, statistical methodology, outcome definitions, and patient populations further complicates interpretation. Although several proposed adverse effects have biologically plausible mechanisms, prospective clinical validation remains limited. Notably, recent regulatory decisions, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)'s removal of the suicidality warning from GLP-1RA prescribing information, reflect the evolving nature of these safety assessments. The overall benefit-risk profile of GLP-1RAs is favorable. Most emerging safety concerns should currently be regarded as hypothesis-generating signals rather than established toxicities. Individualized risk assessment and appropriate clinical monitoring remain important as ongoing and future prospective studies further define the long-term safety of this rapidly expanding therapeutic class.

title: Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist versus selective GLP-1 receptor agonist in patients undergoing primary total knee or hip arthroplasty
abstract: Purpose: Tirzepatide is a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, whereas semaglutide is selective for the GLP-1 receptor. We compared post-operative outcomes after primary total knee or hip arthroplasty (TKA/THA) between patients prescribed tirzepatide and those prescribed semaglutide.

Methods: A retrospective cohort study was performed using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults undergoing primary TKA or THA with at least two coded prescription fills for tirzepatide or semaglutide within six months of surgery were identified, and patients taking both agents were excluded. Cohorts were propensity score matched 1:1 (2,858 per group, all standardized differences below 0.05). Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated at 90 days, 1 year, and 2 years.

Results: Of 669,698 patients who underwent primary TKA or THA, 8,797 (1.3%) had ≥ 2 tirzepatide or semaglutide prescriptions. At 90 days and 1 year, no surgical, medical, or implant-related outcome differed significantly. At 2 years, tirzepatide exposure was associated with lower odds of mechanical complications (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.96) and periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.99; P = .048). Reoperation did not differ significantly (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.08).

Conclusion: Tirzepatide and semaglutide prescriptions were associated with similar 90 day and 1 year outcomes, while tirzepatide was associated with lower mechanical complications and PJI at 2-years. These preliminary associations warrant further investigation in larger cohorts to improve precision and clarify their clinical relevance.
journal: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie

title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
abstract: Background: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).

Methods: In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results.

Results: A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal.

Conclusions: In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).
journal: The New England journal of medicine

title: Semaglutide modulates explore/exploit decision-making in major depressive disorder: A randomized clinical trial
abstract: Background: Explore/exploit decision-making is a crucial component of motivated behavior. Explore/exploit behaviors are related to disparate cognitive and reward-related functions and have been implicated in multiple neuropsychiatric conditions, including major depressive disorder (MDD). Several mediators of explore/exploit decision-making have been proposed; metabolic mechanisms have been theorized to potentially affect its underlying processes. Here, we examined the effects of a GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), semaglutide, on explore/exploit behavior in patients with MDD, using a four-armed restless bandit task.

Methods: In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, 72 participants with MDD were randomized either to oral semaglutide (n = 35) or placebo (n = 37), and completed the bandit task at baseline and following 16 weeks of treatment. Explore/exploit decision-making was assessed using computational modeling of choice behavior, with a trial-by-trial reinforcement-learning model.

Results: Treatment with semaglutide resulted in increased exploitation (i.e. choosing the option with the highest expected reward) (Average Treatment Effect [ATE] = 0.0242, p < 0.001), directed exploration (i.e. exploring a choice with higher uncertainty) (ATE = 0.0619, p = 0.013), and perseveration (i.e. the value-independent tendency to repeat the previous action) (ATE = 0.3017, p = 0.013). These effects were moderated by, but ultimately independent of, baseline characteristics and weight loss during the trial.

Conclusions: Treatment with semaglutide modulated explore/exploit behaviors in patients with MDD. These results highlight the role of metabolic mechanisms in decision-making processes in MDD and expand knowledge of the potential neuropsychiatric effects of GLP-1RAs.

title: 2026 International Society of Hypertension Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines
abstract: Guideline reviewers: Claudio Borghi (Italy), Fadi Charchar (Malaysia), Alfred Doku (Ghana), Maria Dorobantu (Romania), Joseph Flynn (USA), Nadia Khan (Canada), Anastasios Kollias (Greece), Reinhold Kreutz (Germany), Azra Mahmud (Pakistan), Giuseppe Mancia (Italy), Gianfranco Parati (Italy), Neil Poulter (UK), Jane Reckelhoff (USA), Nicolas Renna (Argentina), Abdulla Shehab (UAE), Markus Schlaich (Australia), Aletta Schutte (Australia), Boon Wee Teo (Singapore), Maciej Tomaszewski (UK), Rhian Touyz (Canada), Jiguang Wang (China), Thomas Weber (Austria), Paul Whelton (USA) and Yuqing Zhang (China).

title: Oral Versus Injectable Incretin-Based Anti-Obesity Therapies: An Integrated Computational and Evidence-Based Comparison of Orforglipron, Semaglutide, and Tirzepatide
abstract: Incretin-based agents are transforming obesity pharmacotherapy, and orforglipron, the first oral non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist to complete phase 3 testing, invites direct comparison with the injectable agents semaglutide and tirzepatide. We integrated clinical trial evidence, including the direct head-to-head SURMOUNT-5 trial, independently verified molecular descriptors, a fully specified drug-target-disease network with permutation-tested hub significance, hypergeometric pathway enrichment, and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) across four weighting schemes with formal sensitivity analysis.
