Tirzepatide produced significantly greater weight loss than semaglutide under randomized, head-to-head conditions (20.2% vs. 13.7% at week 72) and ranked highest under balanced, efficacy-, and safety-dominant MCDA models once a composite ADMET score misapplied to two large peptides was removed. Orforglipron's lipophilicity exceeds the Lipinski ceiling, showing that its oral absorption reflects deliberate chemistry rather than default small-molecule developability; it nonetheless ranked highest under an accessibility-dominant model driven by oral feasibility and manufacturing scalability. These rankings were stable under Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis for three of four weighting schemes, with the balanced model comparatively fragile. Tirzepatide's cardiovascular evidence has also advanced, with SURPASS-CVOT reporting non-inferiority to dulaglutide. No single agent dominates every criterion; treatment selection should match the clinical priority the individual patient weights most heavily.
journal: Omics : a journal of integrative biology

title: Periocular surgery risk after glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy for type 2 diabetes
abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the association between GLP-1RA therapy and the hazard of involutional periocular surgical procedures among patients with type 2 diabetes.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX electronic health record database. Adults aged 45 years and older with type 2 diabetes were included. A GLP-1RA cohort was created with evidence of continued therapy defined by a second prescription at least 1 year after initiation. The comparison cohort included patients prescribed other antidiabetic medications, excluding GLP-1RAs. Propensity score matching balanced demographics, comorbidities, and insulin use. The primary outcomes were the hazards of periocular surgery during four nonoverlapping 9-month intervals (0-9, 9-18, 18-27, and 27-36 months) and cumulatively over 0-36 months.

Results: GLP-1RA use was associated with a higher hazard of upper eyelid blepharoplasty (HR range: 1.988-2.788), blepharoptosis repair (HR range: 1.322-1.813), and brow ptosis repair (HR range: 1.683-2.393) compared with other antidiabetic medications (all p ≤ 0.028). Elevated hazard occurred within 0-9 months of treatment and generally increased through 18-27 months.

Conclusions: GLP-1RA therapy was associated with an increased hazard of involutional periocular surgical procedures compared with other antidiabetic medications, suggesting a potential association between GLP-1RA use and periocular soft tissue changes.

title: Adverse oral effects of GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists: a scoping review protocol
abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual incretin receptor agonists such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are increasingly being prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity due to their efficacy in glycaemic control, weight loss and cardiovascular risk reduction. Emerging pharmacovigilance data suggest potential oral adverse effects, including xerostomia, dysgeusia, oral hypoesthesia and throat discomfort. Therefore, alterations in salivary function may compromise oral homeostasis and increase susceptibility to dental caries, periodontal inflammation and mucosal irritation. Additionally, metabolic and inflammatory changes mediated by GLP-1 and GIP may indirectly affect oral tissues. However, current evidence remains limited and inconsistently reported. Further research is needed to investigate the prevalence, underlying mechanisms and clinical significance of oral manifestations associated with GLP-1RA and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist medications, as well as to explore the need for individualised management strategies and more frequent monitoring for patients receiving these therapies.

Methods And Analysis: This protocol describes the methodology for a future scoping review to be conducted in accordance with the JBI reporting guidelines. Studies addressing incretin-based medications and their implications for oral health will be eligible for inclusion in the review, with no restrictions on language or publication date. The following databases will be searched: Cochrane, LILACS, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science. Additional literature will be identified through Google Scholar and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global. The snowballing technique and consultation with experts in the field will be used to identify additional relevant studies. The findings will be presented through a narrative synthesis, supported by tables, graphs and maps. When data are available, exploratory comparisons will be performed according to therapeutic indication (type 2 diabetes or obesity) and pharmacological class (GLP-1RAs and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonists), with particular attention to tirzepatide and other incretin-based agents, to explore potential differences in reported oral manifestations. In particular, studies involving different GLP-1RA and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonists agents (eg, semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide) may be compared to explore potential differences in reported oral manifestations. These comparisons will be conducted descriptively, considering variations in dosage, treatment duration and pharmacological class when such information is reported.
Registration Details: This protocol has been registered prospectively on the Open Science Framework (DOI:10.17605/OSF.IO/NWTCS).

Ethics And Dissemination: This scoping review protocol does not require ethics approval, as it only describes the methodological aspects of a future scoping review and uses secondary data from previously published studies. The findings of the review will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presentations at scientific conferences. As this study is a protocol for a scoping review and does not involve human participants or identifiable data, ethics committee approval was not required.
authors: Maria de Fátima De Magalhães Gonzaga

title: Exploring heterogeneous treatment effects for GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with type 2 diabetes
abstract: Understanding treatment effect heterogeneity (TEH) is essential to improve care for patients living with chronic diseases like type 2 diabetes. Individual responses to treatment can vary substantially, and identifying the factors that drive TEH may enable increased personalization of treatment and follow-up. In this study, we conduct an exploratory analysis of TEH for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists used to treat type 2 diabetes. Endpoints are defined using hemoglobin A1c measurements, body mass index, and blood pressure. We use causal forests to conduct global tests for TEH, estimate variable importances to rank candidate effect modifiers, and estimate the magnitude of heterogeneity. Data from three clinical trials are analyzed: SUSTAIN 6 (subcutaneous semaglutide versus placebo, n=3297), PIONEER 6 (oral semaglutide versus placebo, n=3183), and LEADER (subcutaneous liraglutide versus placebo, n=9340), pooled to 13,670 patients after exclusions. Baseline hemoglobin A1c ranks highest among candidate effect modifiers across methods, and kidney function ranks next in the relative risk causal forest; we discuss their clinical implications. The magnitude estimates, however, show that the variation these covariates jointly explain is small. As such, large covariate-driven heterogeneity can be ruled out in these trials, and the average treatment effect provides a reasonable summary for most patients.

title: Dose-Response Profiles in Incretin and Multi-Agonist Obesity Pharmacotherapy
abstract: Incretin and multi-agonist therapies have transformed obesity pharmacotherapy, but dose selection remains less mature than efficacy assessment. This critical narrative review examines nonlinear relationships among administered dose, systemic exposure, weight and cardiometabolic benefit, gastrointestinal tolerability, treatment persistence, and maintenance. Across established and newer programs, average efficacy generally increases with dose, yet incremental gains may narrow at higher exposure while adverse-event burden and discontinuation can increase. The maturity of evidence is heterogeneous, and later-stage programs should not be interpreted as clinically equivalent to agents supported mainly by earlier-phase dose-ranging data. Moreover, an "optimal dose" is not an endpoint-independent quantity: the exposure most appropriate for weight loss may differ from that relevant to glycemic control, cardiovascular benefit, body composition, tolerability, or maintenance. We therefore distinguish nominal dose from exposure and present response-guided titration as a hypothesis-generating framework for prospective testing, not as an evidence-based dosing algorithm. Existing continuation and withdrawal studies support the importance of ongoing pharmacological treatment after successful weight loss but do not establish a minimum or optimal de-intensified maintenance dose. Future trials should jointly model efficacy, safety, body composition, patient-reported outcomes, pharmacokinetics, and discontinuation to test objective-specific, patient-level dosing strategies.
journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology

title: Gut-derived glucagon-like peptides attenuate T cell-induced intestinal injury
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) are produced in enteroendocrine L cells and control energy homeostasis. GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activation improves glucose homeostasis and induces satiety and weight loss, whereas GLP-2 receptor (GLP-2R) signaling promotes intestinal growth and nutrient absorption. GLP-1R and GLP-2R agonism also reduce intestinal damage in preclinical studies. Here, we demonstrate that endogenous GLP-1R and GLP-2R signaling are essential for protecting the intestine from T cell-mediated enteropathy. Gut injury induced by T cell activation is increased in Glp1r-/- and Glp2r-/- mice, as well as in mice with selective loss of intestinal proglucagon gene expression (GcgGut-/-). Conversely, the GLP-2R agonist teduglutide and the GLP-1R agonist semaglutide, administered separately or together, attenuate αCD3-induced intestinal damage in GcgGut-/- mice. Collectively, these findings demonstrate distinct biological roles for endogenous GLP-1R/GLP-2R activity in immune-mediated intestinal injury and highlight the therapeutic potential of glucagon-like peptides, alone or together, for ameliorating T cell-mediated mucosal injury.

title: Tirzepatide for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Trial Evidence, Cardiometabolic Effects, and Implications for Cardiovascular Practice
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea affects approximately one billion adults worldwide and is associated with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and stroke. Obesity is its dominant reversible cause, yet positive airway pressure therapy splints the pharyngeal airway without addressing the adiposity that narrows it, and randomized trials have not shown that it reduces cardiovascular events. In December 2024, the United States Food and Drug Administration approved tirzepatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, as the first drug for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. We summarize the pharmacology of tirzepatide and the anatomic basis by which weight reduction improves upper airway patency, notably reduction of tongue and parapharyngeal fat. We then review the SURMOUNT-OSA program: two parallel 52-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials enrolling 469 adults with obesity and an apnea-hypopnea index of at least 15 events per hour, one conducted without positive airway pressure and one during established positive airway pressure use. Tirzepatide reduced the apnea-hypopnea index by an estimated 20.0 and 23.8 events per hour relative to placebo, with concurrent reductions in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, systolic blood pressure, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Incident Cardiovascular Events and Death in Treated Serious Mental Illness, Type 2 Diabetes, and Obesity
abstract: Background: Adults with serious mental illness (SMI), type 2 diabetes, and obesity have elevated cardiovascular risk. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have established cardiometabolic benefits in the general population, but their effects in SMI are unclear. We evaluated whether GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risks of incident myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), and all-cause death.

Methods: This was a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study of 218 043 adults with SMI, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and active antipsychotic or antidepressant medications in the TriNetX database (73 health care organizations). Outcomes were incident MI, HF, and all-cause death at 1 and 3 years. The primary exposure was GLP-1RA use versus nonuse; secondary analyses examined semaglutide or tirzepatide. Exploratory analyses evaluated sex, race, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor use.

Results: GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risks of incident MI, HF, and all-cause death. Risk differences at 1 and 3 years were -0.007 and -0.010 for MI, -0.011 and -0.018 for HF, and -0.039 and -0.065 for death (all P<0.001). Semaglutide or tirzepatide use was also associated with lower risks of MI, HF, and death (all P<0.001). Findings were directionally consistent after accounting for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor use.

Conclusions: Adults with treated SMI, type 2 diabetes, and obesity using GLP-1RAs, particularly semaglutide or tirzepatide, had significantly reduced 1- and 3-year risks of incident MI, HF, and all-cause death versus nonusers. These pooled associations should be interpreted in the context of SMI's clinical heterogeneity and the limitations of administrative case ascertainment.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

title: GLP-1 Ads Are Everywhere. What Are They Doing to Our Body Image?
abstract: GLP-1 medications are incredibly accessible-while this may be a net positive for eligible patients, their widespread marketing may not be. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Anna Zucker reports on concerns being raised about the potential impact of GLP-1 marketing practices on body image and well-being.

title: Beyond neuroprotection: Context-dependent effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on seizure susceptibility
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used in type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity and are increasingly considered to exert neuroprotective effects. Recent large-scale clinical and real-world studies report a predominantly neutral to protective association between GLP-1 RA use and seizure- or epilepsy-related diagnoses. However, how these agents affect neuronal excitability in patients with established epileptogenic networks remains insufficiently understood. This narrative review critically examines the experimental and clinical evidence from GLP-1 RA effects on neuronal excitability and seizure susceptibility, with a focus on possible discrepancies between population-level outcomes and individual network-level vulnerability. Preclinical studies demonstrate heterogeneous, network-dependent effects of GLP-1 RAs. Although anticonvulsant and neuroprotective properties are observed in chemically induced seizure models, paradoxical pro-seizure effects occur in genetic absence epilepsy models. In contrast, population-level analyses report neutral to reduced rates of incident epilepsy or seizure-related outcomes under GLP-1 RA therapy. However, these findings are based largely on administrative diagnostic codes, lack epileptological phenotyping, and are not designed to capture transient, exposure-dependent alterations in neuronal excitability or short-term seizure dynamics. Additional factors, including delayed gastric emptying affecting anti-seizure medication absorption, rapid metabolic shifts during titration, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and agent-specific pharmacokinetics, may further modulate individual susceptibility. We propose that GLP-1 RA effects on neuronal excitability are context dependent, shaped by epilepsy subtype, network vulnerability, exposure dynamics, and treatment phase. Targeted prospective studies incorporating clinical phenotyping, therapeutic drug monitoring, and temporal seizure assessment are required to ensure neurological safety in patients with epilepsy.

title: Real-world observational study evaluating metabolic and kidney outcomes in patients living with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus with obesity prescribed tirzepatide
abstract: Background: Obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) accelerate chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression. Tirzepatide, a dual glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist, has demonstrated metabolic and potential renoprotective benefits in clinical trials. There have been limited reports of the implications of prescribing tirzepatide in a real-world cohort of patients with advanced CKD.

Methods: This observational study includes a multi-ethnic cohort of 62 adults with CKD stages 1-5 who initiated tirzepatide indicated for T2DM with concurrent obesity in a general nephrology clinic between June 2024 and October 2025. Patients were followed for a median of 21.4 weeks. Clinical outcomes including weight, glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR), blood pressure, lipid profile and insulin requirements were collected.

Results: Tirzepatide significantly reduced median weight (103-100 kg; p < 0.0001), HbA1c (63 [7.9%] to 54 [7.1%] mmol/mol; p = 0.002) and uACR (111-44 mg/mmol; p = 0.008), while eGFR remained stable. Significant improvements were also observed in triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and total daily insulin dose. Gastrointestinal symptoms and decreased serum bicarbonate were the most common adverse events.

Conclusions: In this real-world, multi-ethnic cohort, including patients with advanced CKD, tirzepatide was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in weight, glycaemic control, albuminuria, lipid profile and insulin requirements without adversely affecting kidney function. The introduction of tirzepatide to patients with CKD should be guided by a multidisciplinary team.
journal: Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association

title: Influence of GLP-1-Based Pharmacotherapies on Eating Behavior, Appetite, and Energy Intake in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Although GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies achieve clinically significant weight loss, their influence on eating behavior is unknown.

Methods: This systematic review examined the effects of GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies on eating behavior, appetite, and energy intake in adults (≥ 18 years) with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2) without major comorbidities. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, EMBASE and Web of Science were searched on 4th November 2025. Risk of bias was assessed, and meta-analyses were conducted for energy intake and overall appetite suppression, with other outcomes synthesized qualitatively.

Results: Twenty-five articles involving 4060 participants were included (64% female, mean age = 44 years, mean BMI = 36.7 kg/m2). Four studies were deemed low risk of bias. A reduction in energy intake was observed (SMD = -0.775, 95% CI = -1.21 to -0.34, p = 0.002), although heterogeneity was high (I2 = 82.7%) and the prediction interval included no effect. A small increase in appetite suppression was also observed (MD = 7.800, 95% CI = 3.74 to 11.86, p = 0.001). Qualitative findings suggested reductions in food craving and some measures of food reward. Nausea was more frequent with active treatment and may have influenced the observed effects or increased awareness of treatment allocation.

Conclusion: GLP-1-based pharmacotherapies may reduce short-term energy intake and appetite. However, the magnitude and consistency of these effects remain uncertain because of substantial heterogeneity, imputation of variance data, and variability in outcome assessment. Evidence relating to food craving, food preferences and other eating behaviors requires further investigation.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

title: Real-World Semaglutide Initiation Behaviours in the United States: Impact on Early Treatment Discontinuation and on 1-Year Persistence
abstract: Aims: Little is known about how glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are initiated in real-world settings and whether prescribing behaviours in routine care contribute to the high discontinuation rates seen in practice. We examined prescribing behaviours for injectable semaglutide at treatment initiation and evaluated their impact on early medication discontinuation and on 1-year persistence among US adults.

Materials And Methods: Using MarketScan data (2018-2021), this retrospective cohort study identified US adults with diabetes and/or obesity on no prior incretin therapy starting injectable semaglutide. Initiating dose was categorized as low or high (≤ 0.5 and ≥ 1.0 mg/week, respectively); treatment status was followed for 12 months. Medication persistence was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Piecewise Cox proportional hazards regression assessed early discontinuation risk, logistic regression assessed the odds of high-dose initiation.

Results: Among this cohort of 48 658 adults, 14.5% were started on semaglutide using high doses. The off-label high-dose regimen was associated with decreased 1-year persistence (p = 0.01), and a 25% increase in early discontinuation risk (HR: 1.25, 95% CI: 1.17-1.34, p < 0.001) independently of age, obesity status, co-morbidity measures and cost. Odds of high-dose initiation were increased in the West and South (p < 0.001), for endocrinologists (p = 0.02), for patients who were male (p < 0.001), younger (p = 0.02), with obesity versus overweight (p = 0.002), and for treatment initiation in 2018 compared with 2019-2021 (p < 0.001).

Conclusion: Initiation of injectable semaglutide therapy using high doses is common in real-world settings. High-dose initiation represents a modifiable risk factor for early medication discontinuation and decreased 1-year persistence.

title: Patient-Reported Outcomes Following Initiation or Simplification of Treatment With iGlarLixi in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Narrative Review
abstract: Introduction: Given the significant burden that diabetes self-management poses, it is important to assess patient-reported outcomes (PROs) for Type 2 diabetes (T2D) treatments in clinical trials and real-world studies. Complex insulin regimens are associated with increased risk of hypoglycaemia and body weight gain, which could negatively impact treatment adherence and, therefore, achievement of glycaemic targets. iGlarLixi is a once-daily fixed-ratio combination of insulin glargine 100 U/mL and the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), lixisenatide. iGlarLixi is an effective treatment alternative to complex insulin regimens, with a favourable between-group difference in body weight and reduced risk of hypoglycaemia.

Methods: This is the first review to summarise data from multiple validated PRO measures for recent iGlarLixi studies (Soli-CGM, SoliMix, Soli-SWITCH, IDEAL, SUCCESS and SIMPLIFY JP), including: Global Treatment Effectiveness Evaluation, Audit of Diabetes Dependent Quality of Life, Diabetes Medication Satisfaction Tool, Diabetes Therapy-Related Quality of Life, Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, Hypoglycaemic Attitudes and Behaviour Scale and Treatment-Related Impact Measure Diabetes.

Results: In clinical studies, once-daily iGlarLixi was associated with numerical improvements in selected treatment satisfaction measures in those who switched from: complex insulin regimens (once- or twice-daily premixed insulin and basal-bolus insulin), basal insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications. Additionally, in real-world studies, iGlarLixi was generally associated with improvements in treatment satisfaction and quality of life outcomes in adults with T2D who previously received basal-bolus insulin or oral glucose-lowering medications ± basal insulin or GLP-1 RAs.
Conclusions: In conclusion, a once-daily injection of iGlarLixi may offer a clinically beneficial, simplified treatment option for adults with T2D compared with complex insulin-based regimens.

title: Weight Regain After Incretin Treatment: The Lean Mass Deficit Hypothesis and a Role for Testosterone Combination Therapy in Men
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1RA and triple (GIP)/GLP-1RA/glucagon agonists achieve placebo-subtracted weight loss of 15% to 22%. Their long-term value depends on how well the weight loss is maintained and on the composition of weight loss, not only amount of weight loss. Part of incretin-induced weight loss is lean tissue. It is unknown whether the proportion of lean mass, and especially, muscle mass loss is greater than with other weight-loss interventions, and whether it may cause clinically meaningful harm. Men with obesity commonly have low or low-normal testosterone, which is associated with reduced muscle mass, increased visceral adiposity, impaired insulin sensitivity, and increased cardiovascular risk.

Hypothesis: We propose, as an exploratory hypothesis, that in men with obesity and low testosterone, combining incretin therapy with testosterone therapy may preserve muscle mass, increase the proportion of weight lost as fat mass, and reduce fat-predominant weight regain after incretin discontinuation.

Rationale: Resistance exercise and adequate protein intake are first-line measures for preserving muscle mass during weight loss. No lifestyle measure reliably prevents the fat-predominant weight regain that follows diet discontinuation, and long-term adherence to lifestyle interventions is poor. We position testosterone therapy as a pharmacological adjunct for weight loss maintenance in men with obesity and low testosterone, to be evaluated in clinical trials.

Conclusions: The only direct human data come from a small, non-randomized pilot study and are hypothesis-generating. The clinical consequences of incretin-associated loss of lean mass, and particularly muscle mass, should be investigated in future studies. The hypothesis requires evaluation in randomized controlled trials that properly assess changes in lean mass and muscle mass, along with safety monitoring, before it can inform clinical practice.

title: Phase 1, open-label, randomized study of the elecoglipron pharmacokinetic profile in healthy participants under fed and fasted conditions
abstract: Aims: Elecoglipron (AZD5004/ECC5004) is an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) in development for weight management in people living with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes. This study aimed to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK) profiles of two formulations of elecoglipron under fed and fasted conditions.

Methods: We assessed the PK profiles, safety and tolerability of two formulations of elecoglipron, 50 mg, under fed and fasted conditions in healthy participants in a phase 1, open-label, randomized, single-dose, fixed-sequence, crossover study.

Results: Of 23 participants screened, 14 were randomized to elecoglipron and 13 (92.9%) completed the study. The half-life for both formulations under fasted and fed conditions ranged between 20.7 and 21.2 h. Between the fed (reference) and fasted groups, geometric mean ratios (GMR) and 90% confidence intervals (CI) for the F1 formulation: area under the plasma-concentration curve (AUC) from time zero to the last measurement (AUC0-last) was 0.96 (0.82, 1.12), AUC from time zero extrapolated to infinity (AUC0-inf) was 0.95 (0.82, 1.11), and maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) was 1.15 (0.90, 1.46). Similar results were observed for F2 in the fed and fasted groups. Safety and tolerability were comparable for the two formulations. The most common AEs were gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort) and mostly mild in severity.

Conclusions: Elecoglipron demonstrated a PK profile supportive of once-daily dosing and may be administered under fed or fasted conditions. These findings support the continuing clinical development of elecoglipron. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06268145). The trial was first registered on 20 February 2024.

title: The development of obesity pharmacotherapy: from early challenges and setbacks to recognition by WHO
abstract: Obesity is a chronic, progressive disease associated with disability, increased morbidity, and reduced life expectancy. Global prevalence has risen sharply in recent decades, yet obesity and its treatment-particularly pharmacotherapy -have been highly stigmatised. A legacy of early medications withdrawn over safety concerns, together with poor efficacy, and widespread lack of recognition of obesity as a chronic disease contributed to persistent underuse of obesity pharmacotherapy. This underuse changed in the 2020s with GLP-1 receptor agonists and, later, multiagonist therapies, with their substantially greater efficacy, safety, and disease-modifying benefits compared with older agents. Reflecting this paradigm shift, WHO issued global guidelines and included GLP-1 receptor agonists in the Essential Medicines List, albeit for a narrowly defined population. We take a critical historical perspective, charting the highs and lows of obesity medication development and examining the scientific, regulatory, and societal factors that have slowed or impeded the translation of pharmacological advances into safe, effective, and widely accepted treatments for obesity.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Multi-hormone Receptor Modulators for Kidney Protection in Nondiabetic Kidney Disease
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), together with newer multi-hormone receptor modulators that target glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), glucagon and amylin, have emerged as promising therapies for chronic kidney disease. This review examines the mechanisms through which these agents may protect the kidney and summarizes the emerging clinical evidence in populations without diabetes. Kidney protection appears to arise through complementary direct and indirect routes. Direct effects include natriuresis through inhibition of the sodium-hydrogen exchanger (NHE)-3, modulation of glomerular hemodynamics through effects on afferent arteriolar tone and vasoconstrictor pathways, and attenuation of renal inflammation; mechanisms that are largely independent of glucose lowering. Indirect mechanisms include reductions in the metabolic, hemodynamic and cardiac burden on the kidney through weight loss, blood pressure lowering, and improvement of heart failure. Beyond selective GLP-1R-agonism, the added hormonal components of multi-hormone receptor modulators engage distinct physiological pathways whose interactions may be additive, synergistic or counteracting, but remain incompletely understood. The efficacy of GLP-1 RAs and multi-hormone receptor modulators in people without diabetes is currently supported by results from secondary kidney endpoints in phase-3 obesity and cardiovascular outcome trials, including reductions in albuminuria and preservation of estimated glomerular filtration rate. Several dedicated outcome studies of GLP-1 RAs and multi-hormone receptor modulators are now underway and will determine whether these therapies become a new pillar of care in nondiabetic kidney disease.
journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN

title: Antidiabetic medications in the pipeline
abstract: There is an extensive pipeline of therapies for diabetes mellitus. It has been known for the past three decades that obesity is a key pathophysiological player, involving inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction leading to type 2 diabetes and to significant cardiovascular, renal and hepatic complications, all central to the metabolic syndrome. On the basis of this knowledge and the disposition of drugs with multiple effects on different disease components, the diabetes therapeutic paradigm has shifted from merely glucocentric to multitargeted against these interconnected pathways.Much more recently, incretin-based multi-agonists have been developed that deliver unprecedented glycemic and weight benefits as well as weekly insulins and oral GLP-1 agonists that are able to reduce the burden of injectable therapies. An antibody-peptide conjugate that acts as a dual GLP-1/GIP receptor modulator has also shown promising results. Today, novel insulin sensitizers are modulating metabolic pathways towards higher energy expenditure with fewer side effects. Adjunctive agents for type 1 diabetes are improving glucose control while reducing hypoglycemia risk. Finally, drugs designed to restrain the inevitable muscle mass loss caused by antiobesity treatments are being tested. The diabetes pipeline is rich and there is hope that in the next few years, the therapeutic landscape will be further transformed with even more efficacious and individualized treatments.

title: Peptide profiling of casein peptide reveals its anti-diabetic effects via DPP-IV inhibition and IRS1/PI3K/AKT signaling
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a growing global health burden, increasing demand for safe food-derived strategies for glycemic control. Casein-derived peptides have potential metabolic benefits, but their antidiabetic mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, casein peptide (CNP), enriched in low-molecular-weight peptides (<3 kDa), was investigated as the principal bioactive intervention for T2DM regulation. LC-MS/MS identified 880 peptides; among the 50 most abundant, all were predicted to inhibit DPP-IV, 26 to inhibit α-glucosidase, and one to inhibit α-amylase. CNP inhibited DPP-IV in vitro in a concentration-dependent manner (IC50 = 5.06 ± 0.41 mg mL-1) and crossed Caco-2 monolayers partly through endocytosis and PepT1-mediated transport. In HFD/STZ-induced T2DM mice, CNP improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, ameliorated dyslipidemia, attenuated tissue injury and systemic inflammation, and restored GLP-1/DPP-IV balance and IRS1/PI3K/AKT signaling. These findings identify CNP as a key food-derived bioactive peptide system that modulates T2DM through complementary effects on intestinal transport, incretin regulation, glucose-lipid homeostasis, inflammation, and insulin signaling, supporting its potential for development as a functional food ingredient for T2DM management.

title: Targeting the Gut Microbiota-Metabolism Axis: Novel Pharmacological Mechanisms and Translational Application Strategies for Oral Antidiabetic Drugs
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a highly prevalent chronic metabolic disease worldwide, and the clinical prevention and control situation is severe. Although the various antidiabetic drugs currently in clinical use can lower blood glucose levels through different mechanisms, there are significant differences in efficacy among individuals. Existing evidence suggests that differences in gut microbiota (GM) composition and metabolic function may be one of the key factors contributing to the heterogeneity in drug efficacy. Based on this, this review describes the physiological and pathological mechanisms of the GM-metabolism axis and systematically reviews the modulatory effects of different classes of antidiabetic drugs on this axis and their underlying mechanisms. Available studies suggest that metformin, α-glucosidase inhibitors, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), thiazolidinediones (TZDs), and oral glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) may differentially affect GM composition and/or microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), and bile acids. These alterations may be associated with glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance through pathways involving GPR41/43, HDACs, AMPK, mTORC1/S6K1, FXR-FGF15/19, and TGR5-GLP-1 signaling. By integrating clinical and mechanistic evidence, this review highlights the potential contribution of the GM-metabolism axis to the glucose-lowering effects of antidiabetic drugs. However, the quantity and confidence of evidence vary substantially across drug classes, and causal and clinical relevance requires further validation. These findings provide a basis for future research on personalized interventions for T2DM characterized by SCFA-producing bacterial deficiency, BCAA overload, or dysregulated bile acid metabolism.

title: The Impact of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists on Risk of Retinal Vascular Occlusions
abstract: Purpose: To investigate whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are protective against retinal vascular occlusions. Methods: Using a large aggregated, de-identified electronic health records data platform in the United States, patients with type 2 diabetes ages ≥18 years prescribed glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists or non-glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (controls) and having ophthalmology follow-up of at least 1, 3, or 5 years were included. The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist and control cohorts were propensity score matched (1:1) on demographics and risk factors, and outcomes were compared at 1, 3, and 5 years. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were reported, with significance defined as P < .05. Results: After matching, each cohort comprised 53 413 patients after 1 year, 25 738 patients after 3 years, and 14 695 patients after 5 years. Significantly reduced risk of all vascular occlusions was observed in the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist cohort at 1 year (HR, 0.66, 95% CI, 0.54-0.80), 3 years (HR, 0.71, 95% CI, 0.59-0.86), and 5 years (HR, 0.79, 95% CI, 0.64-0.97). Retinal vein occlusion risk was significantly reduced in the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist cohort up to 3 years (HR, 0.75, 95% CI, 0.60-0.94), but not after 5 years (HR, 0.83, 95% CI, 0.64-1.08). While there was no reduction in retinal artery occlusion risk at 1 year (HR, 0.69, 95% CI, 0.48-1.00), there were significant reductions at later time points. Conclusions: Results suggest that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists may reduce the risk of retinal vascular occlusions. Additional prospective trials and analysis of long-term outcomes are needed to further investigate this association.

title: Glucose-Lowering Therapies in Type 2 Diabetes-Associated Sarcopenia: Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence and a Muscle-Centred Framework
abstract: Sarcopenia is increasingly recognised as a clinically important comorbidity in diabetes mellitus, particularly in older adults and individuals with long-standing type 2 diabetes. Because skeletal muscle is the principal site of insulin-stimulated glucose disposal, declines in muscle mass, quality, strength and physical performance may exacerbate insulin resistance and glycaemic instability and increase the risks of frailty, disability, falls, fractures, cardiovascular events and mortality. Contemporary glucose-lowering therapies have transformed diabetes care through established cardiorenal benefits and weight reduction, yet skeletal muscle outcomes are rarely prespecified or systematically assessed in pivotal trials. This evidence gap is especially relevant for weight-reducing agents such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, which are often associated with reductions in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived or bioelectrical impedance analysis-derived lean-mass estimates. However, these changes should be interpreted cautiously, as they often occur in the context of overall weight loss and may be influenced by alterations in body water. In addition, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry- or dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived lean-mass estimates do not directly quantify contractile skeletal muscle. Accordingly, reductions in lean-mass estimates alone are insufficient to infer clinically meaningful muscle loss without concurrent assessment of muscle strength or physical performance. This narrative review summarises the bidirectional mechanisms linking diabetes and sarcopenia and appraises major glucose-lowering drug classes from a muscle-centred perspective. It integrates mechanistic insights with human evidence on muscle-relevant outcomes, including body composition, strength and physical performance, and addresses practical safety and monitoring considerations in sarcopenia-prone phenotypes, including sarcopenic obesity. We also propose a pragmatic, hypothesis-generating Cardiorenal-Muscle Quadrant Framework that considers glycaemic efficacy and cardiorenal benefit alongside muscle reserve, functional status and treatment-related risks, with emphasis on functional monitoring, resistance exercise, nutritional optimisation and individualised glycaemic targets in older or frail adults.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy and incident atrial fibrillation in non-diabetic adults with obesity and chronic kidney disease: a propensity matched cohort study
abstract: Background: Obesity and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are potent risk factors for atrial fibrillation (AF), yet whether GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) prevent incident AF in non-diabetic adults with obesity and CKD is unexamined. We assessed whether GLP-1RA therapy reduces 1-year AF incidence in this cardiorenal phenotype.

Methods: Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network (66 healthcare organizations), we conducted a retrospective target trial emulation of non-diabetic adults aged 18 or older with obesity and CKD stages 3-5 diagnosed 2021-2024. Patients receiving semaglutide, liraglutide, or tirzepatide (n = 10,985) were compared with unexposed patients (n = 94,527). After propensity score matching, 7326 patients remained per cohort. The primary outcome was incident AF at 1 year; secondary outcomes included AF subtypes, ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and all-cause hospitalization. Cox models generated hazard ratios (HRs); sensitivity analyses extended follow-up to 2-3 years with landmark analyses.

Results: At 1 year, GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower incident AF (1.63% vs. 2.62%; HR 0.655, 95% CI 0.508-0.844; p = 0.001), a 34.5% relative risk reduction. Reductions were consistent for paroxysmal (HR 0.586), persistent (HR 0.482), and longstanding persistent AF (HR 0.527; all p < 0.05); permanent AF was non-significant at 1 year. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias (HR 0.556; p = 0.002) and hospitalization (HR 0.668; p < 0.001) were also significantly reduced. Benefits persisted across 2- and 3-year follow-up and remained consistent in landmark analyses.

Conclusions: In non-diabetic adults with obesity and CKD, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significant, durable reductions in incident AF, ventricular arrhythmias, and hospitalization. These findings are consistent with a possible cardiorenal benefit and support prioritizing this phenotype for dedicated randomized trials.

title: Associations between positive body image, embodiment, and GLP-1 consideration for weight loss among women in the United Kingdom
abstract: Interest in glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications has increased rapidly among the general population in the Global North, yet little is known about the psychological factors that influence consideration of GLP-1 use for weight loss. While recent research suggests that body appreciation may be negatively associated with interest in GLP-1 use, other dimensions of positive body image remain largely unexplored. This study examined associations between body appreciation, functionality appreciation, experiences of embodiment (attuned self-care, positive body connection and comfort, resisting objectification), and GLP-1 consideration among women residing in the United Kingdom (N = 327). Hierarchical multiple regression analyses examined the unique contributions of body appreciation, functionality appreciation, and embodiment subscales on GLP-1 consideration, while controlling for age and body mass index (BMI). Body appreciation, functionality appreciation, and all embodiment variables were negatively associated with GLP-1 consideration, while BMI was positively associated with GLP-1 consideration. When examined simultaneously (controlling for age and BMI), only resisting objectification emerged as a significant and negative correlate of consideration of GLP-1 medications for weight loss, while BMI emerged as a significant and positive correlate. BMI did not moderate the association between resisting objectification and GLP-1 consideration. Findings suggest that resisting objectification may be uniquely associated with lower GLP-1 consideration, independent of other dimensions of positive body image and BMI. These findings extend emerging literature by highlighting the potential importance of embodiment, particularly resisting objectification, in understanding consideration of GLP-1 use for weight loss.

title: Modulating neuroinflammation with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists: a scoping review exploring their therapeutic potential in schizophrenia
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a key contributor to the pathophysiology and symptomatology of schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), clinically approved anti-diabetic and -obesity medication, have been associated with anti-inflammatory properties. It remains unclear whether GLP-1RA treatment can improve neuroinflammation within psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia. This scoping review synthesizes evidence from clinical and preclinical studies on the anti-inflammatory effects of GLP-1RAs in psychiatric, neurodegenerative and neurological disease models, identifying crucial research gaps and providing future recommendations to guide potential clinical translation. The literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO and included outcomes of cytokine levels within blood and brain samples. Within the 40 included studies, two were clinical (schizophrenia and alcohol-use disorder) and 38 were preclinical models of psychiatric diseases, Alzheimer's -, Parkinson's Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, Epilepsy and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies showed anti-(neuro)inflammatory effects of GLP-1RAs, whereas the two available clinical studies found no significant changes in peripheral inflammatory markers. As these trials were not primarily designed or powered to test neuroinflammatory effects, the clinical findings remain inconclusive. Differences in study design, inflammatory measurements, pharmacokinetics and dosing may have contributed to the discrepancy between preclinical and clinical findings. Future research should prioritize early-phase dose-finding trials in non-diabetic, or -overweight patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, evaluating the effects of alternative GLP-1RA regimens on neuroinflammatory markers, safety and clinical symptomatology. This is an essential step to determine their potential mental health-enhancing effects through the modulation of neuroinflammation within schizophrenia spectrum disorders.

title: Cardiovascular safety of orforglipron versus insulin glargine in adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk (ACHIEVE-4): a phase 3, event-driven, randomised, open-label, non-inferiority, active comparator trial
abstract: Background: Orforglipron is an oral, non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist. While some peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists have established cardiovascular benefit, the cardiovascular safety of non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists has not been studied. This study aimed to compare the effect of orforglipron with insulin glargine on the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in individuals with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight who are at increased risk for cardiovascular events.

Methods: This event-driven, phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label, active comparator, parallel-group study was conducted in 317 sites across 16 countries and territories. Adults with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) concentrations between 7·0% and 10·5% (53-91 mmol/mol) and a BMI of 25 kg/m2 or more, treated with up to three glucose-lowering medications (metformin, a sulfonylurea, and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor), were randomly assigned (1:1) to oral orforglipron maximum tolerated dose (up to 36 mg capsule [equivalent to 17·2 mg tablet]) or injectable titrated insulin glargine, each administered once daily. All participants had established cardiovascular or chronic kidney disease. The primary outcome was time to occurrence of four-component major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE-4), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or hospitalisation for unstable angina. Non-inferiority of orforglipron to insulin glargine was declared if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the hazard ratio (HR; orforglipron vs insulin glargine) was less than 1·8. The primary endpoint and other safety endpoints were assessed in all participants who took at least one dose of assigned treatment using all datapoints from baseline until withdrawal or study completion, regardless of treatment adherence. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05803421) and is completed.

Findings: Between May 1, 2023, and Sept 5, 2024, 2749 participants were randomly assigned (1371 to orforglipron and 1378 to insulin glargine). 1032 (38%) participants were female and 1717 (62·5%) male. 2362 (85·9%) participants had established cardiovascular disease and 1033 (37·6%) had chronic kidney disease. Mean baseline age, HbA1c, and BMI were 63·1 years (SD 9·9), 8·2% (1·0), and 33 kg/m2 (6·2), respectively. Over a median follow-up of 2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 57 (4·2%) of 1358 orforglipron participants and 67 (5·0%) of 1343 insulin glargine participants, showing non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4 (HR 0·84; 95% CI 0·59-1·20; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 851 (62·1%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 193 (14·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants; clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia (glucose <3 mmol/L [54 mg/dL]) occurred in 93 (6·8%) of 1371 orforglipron participants and 260 (19·2%) of 1355 insulin glargine participants. 62 deaths were reported during the study: 19 (1·4%) of 1371 participants receiving orforglipron and 43 (3·2%) of 1355 participants receiving insulin glargine; all deaths except one (in the insulin glargine group) were deemed unrelated to treatment.

Interpretation: In people with type 2 diabetes at increased cardiovascular risk, the cardiovascular safety of orforglipron was confirmed by demonstrating non-inferiority to insulin glargine for MACE-4. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent adverse event and most common reason for orforglipron treatment discontinuation with orforglipron, while clinically significant hypoglycaemia occurred less frequently with orforglipron than with insulin glargine. These findings support orforglipron as a potential once-daily, oral treatment option with established cardiovascular safety in people with type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk.
Funding: Eli Lilly and Company.

title: Novel variant and enteroendocrine hormone deficiency in a patient with proline and glutamate-rich protein with a coiled coil domain 1 (PERCC1) associated enteropathy: New diagnostic and therapeutic insights
abstract: Proline and glutamate-rich protein with a coiled coil domain 1 (PERCC1)-associated enteropathy is a rare monogenic congenital diarrhea due to defective enteroendocrine cells (EECs). We describe a 6-year-old female with intestinal failure since birth. Biopsies demonstrated normal appearing gastric mucosa on hematoxylin and eosin stains. Commercial whole-exome sequencing did not reveal clinically relevant variants. Subsequent testing, prompted by undetectable serum Gastrin, identified compound heterozygous variants in PERCC1: c.390 C > G (Y130X) and a novel c.492del (S164RfsX33) variant. Hormonal profiling showed low endogenous glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1 and -2 levels, pre and postprandial. Immunohistochemistry showed a markedly reduced density of Gastrin containing G-cells and preserved EEC. At 5.5 years, endogenous GLP-2 deficiency supported off-label Teduglutide therapy. Baseline Parenteral Nutrition Dependency Index (PNDI) was 67%; after 16 months, PNDI decreased to 35%, with improved stool output and appetite. Congenital diarrhea with low serum levels of Gastrin, GLP-1, and -2 and abnormal G-cell staining should prompt targeted genetic analysis for PERCC1 with whole genome sequencing. Timely diagnosis enables Teduglutide therapy and parenteral nutrition weaning.

title: Qualitative Exit Interviews to Characterize the Positive Treatment Experiences of Patients in the Phase III Trial of Orforglipron Versus Oral Semaglutide for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: Background And Objective: There is an unmet need for effective and well-tolerated oral formulations of glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists for the management of type 2 diabetes. Orforglipron and oral semaglutide are two oral glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists evaluated in the ACHIEVE-3 clinical trial (NCT06045221). These novel treatments have the means to achieve clinically meaningful glycemic control and weight reduction, which may result in substantial positive changes in patients' daily lives. The objective of this study was to conduct exit interviews following the ACHIEVE-3 trial to characterize positive treatment experiences and outcomes, beyond glycated hemoglobin and weight reduction, reported by patients living with type 2 diabetes who received oral glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist-based treatments.

Methods: Qualitative interviews were conducted across ten clinical sites within the USA with patients who had enrolled in ACHIEVE-3 and completed at least 3 months of treatment. Interviews were conducted in English or Spanish, audio-recorded, and transcribed. Transcripts were analyzed to identify and categorize positive treatment benefits reported during the interviews. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize the sample.

Results: Sixty patients completed the qualitative exit interviews. Patients had a mean age of 59.1 years (standard deviation [SD] = 10.3), and almost half were female (n = 28, 46.7%). Patients had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes for a mean of 8.5 years (SD = 5.7). By the end of the study, patients reduced their glycated hemoglobin by 1.6% (SD = 1.3) from a baseline of 8.3% and lost a mean of 4.7 kg (SD = 6.8) from a baseline of 96.0 kg. All patients reported being satisfied with the trial medication (n = 59/59), were likely to recommend the treatment to other patients, and all but one were willing to continue taking the medication. As expected, the two most important and most frequently reported positive changes were controlled glycated hemoglobin (n = 53, 88.3%) and weight reduction (n = 50, 83.3%). Other common spontaneously reported positive concepts included increased perceived energy (n = 28, 46.7%), reduced appetite and cravings (n = 23, 38.3%), improved exercise/movement (n = 18, 30.0%), and psychological improvements (n = 18, 30.0%). Additional positive changes included increased confidence/self-esteem, improved diet and eating habits, improved sleep, and improved or a lack of deterioration in vision. All reported positive changes were considered meaningful by patients.

Conclusions: The current study explored the positive experiences of patients taking an oral glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist in the ACHIEVE-3 trial beyond traditional clinical benefits, such as glycemic control and weight reduction. The positive changes identified may be suitable targets for future clinical trial clinical outcome assessment endpoint strategies to help differentiate treatments and in clinical practices to classify patients' experiences.

title: Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P < 0.001), representing 15.5% of baseline weight; 83.1% achieved ≥10% and 22.4% achieved ≥20% weight loss, with consistent responses across age, baseline weight and socioeconomic strata. Among participants with paired biomarker data, mean glycated hemoglobin decreased by 3.3 mmol mol-1 (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P < 0.001), normalizing in 84.5% of those with baseline diabetes-range values and 96.3% with prediabetes, and lipid parameters improved significantly (reductions in total cholesterol of 0.77 mmol l-1, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l-1 and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l-1). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment and cardiovascular outcomes following aortic valve replacement: a nationwide observational study
abstract: Background: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce major adverse cardiovascular events among patients with diabetes, overweight, and obesity. Whether these benefits extend to patients undergoing aortic valve replacement (AVR) for severe aortic stenosis (AS) remains unknown. Thus, we investigated the association between GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment and cardiovascular outcomes after AVR.

Methods: Nationwide population-based cohort study including consecutive patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI or SAVR in Western Denmark between January, 2016 and April, 2022. Patients were followed until death, emigration, crossover, or end of follow up on May 12, 2026. Propensity score-matching was performed to balance confounding. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, or aortic valve reoperation. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, aortic valve reoperation, with analyses accounting for the competing risk of death.

Results: Among 5259 eligible patients undergoing AVR, 292 propensity score-matched patients were included in the final analyses. During a mean follow up of 4.8±2.4 years, GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment was associated with a lower risk of the primary composite outcome compared with controls (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.50-0.96, p=0.029). GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment was also associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality (HR 0.66, 95%CI 0.46-0.95, p=0.025). In competing risk analyses accounting for death, lower risks were observed for heart failure hospitalization (HR 0.67, 95%CI 0.48-0.93, p=0.018), and aortic valve reoperation (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.49-0.98, p=0.037).
Conclusion: Treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists was associated with lower risk of cardiovascular outcomes including mortality following AVR among patients with severe AS.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist use and contrast-associated acute kidney injury after contrast-enhanced CT and CT angiography in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease: a propensity score-matched cohort study
abstract: Aims: To examine whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use is associated with contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) after contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT) or computed tomographic angiography (CTA) in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD).

Methods: We conducted a TriNetX retrospective cohort study of adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD who underwent CE-CT or CTA from January 2020 to January 2025. GLP-1 RA use was defined by a prescription within six months before imaging. The primary outcome was a new acute kidney injury diagnosis within three days. Separate 1:1 propensity score-matched analyses were conducted for CE-CT and CTA, with eGFR-stratified and sensitivity analyses.

Results: After matching, the CE-CT and CTA cohorts included 6,995 and 3,285 pairs, respectively. CA-AKI occurred in 3.8% of GLP-1 RA users versus 4.5% of non-users after CE-CT (odds ratio [OR] 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71-0.99) and in 4.5% versus 6.1% after CTA (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59-0.92). The absolute risk differences were 0.7% points and 1.5% points, respectively. HbA1c remained imbalanced after matching. Negative-control outcomes were null, and eGFR-stratified associations were inconsistent between cohorts.

Conclusions: GLP-1 RA use was associated with a lower observed risk of CA-AKI after CE-CT and CTA in adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD. Residual HbA1c imbalance and the observational design limit causal interpretation; prospective studies using creatinine-based outcomes are needed.

title: Evolving phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a 15-year population-based comparison
abstract: Aims/Hypothesis: Our aim was to describe the phenotype at diagnosis and the early therapeutic profile of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes across two periods spanning approximately 15 years within the same integrated healthcare system.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used electronic health record data from Clalit Health Services (Haifa & Western Galilee, Israel). Adults with incident type 2 diabetes in 2005-2008 (period 1: n=80,201) were compared with those diagnosed in 2020-2023 (period 2: n=101,392). Between-period differences are presented as crude estimates, with an age-stratified sensitivity analysis, and quantified using standardised mean differences (SMDs; values ≥0.20 indicate at least a small effect) alongside non-parametric and χ2 tests.

Results: The median age at diagnosis increased from 63.0 to 66.7 years between the two periods; the proportion aged ≥85 years nearly doubled (from 3.5% to 6.6%). The score for the Charlson comorbidity index increased from 4 to 6 (SMD 0.48); metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) increased from 4.4% to 18.6%. HbA1c at diagnosis decreased from 56 to 53 mmol/mol (7.3% to 7.0%); pre-diagnosis LDL-cholesterol decreased from 2.90 to 2.21 mmol/l (SMD 0.65). Within 31-90 days of diagnosis, use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors increased from 0.07% to 15.0%, use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) increased from 0% to 11.1%, and sulfonylurea use decreased more than fourfold (20.8% to 4.5%).

Conclusions/Interpretation: The phenotype of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes has been fundamentally restructured since 2008: patients are older with a higher comorbidity burden but present with better glycaemic and lipid management, with the latter reflecting statin therapy already established before diagnosis. MASLD has emerged as a major but largely ascertainment-driven comorbidity. The shift to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs alongside declining sulfonylurea use indicates displacement of glucose-centric strategies by a cardiorenal- and weight-driven paradigm. These findings indicate a need for age-appropriate management and trials enrolling very elderly patients.

title: Altered glucagon and GIP responses in South Asian versus Nordic women after gestational diabetes mellitus
abstract: Aims/Hypothesis: We aimed to compare ethnic differences in levels of glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) following a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and to assess whether the higher insulin levels observed in South Asian compared with Nordic women could be explained by differences in the hormone secretory responses.

Methods: We measured glucagon, GIP and GLP-1 in 178 South Asian and 107 Nordic women during an OGTT, and stratified participants by glycaemic status. Glucagon and total GLP-1 and GIP responses when fasting and post-OGTT were assessed by linear mixed models. Ethnic differences in incretin and glucagon levels were evaluated by linear regression analyses. Pre-hepatic insulin levels were estimated using deconvolution of C-peptide kinetics.

Results: Ethnic differences in glucagon and incretin levels varied by glycaemic status. In the normoglycaemic South Asian group, early (0-15 min) glucagon suppression post-OGTT was significantly attenuated compared with the Nordic group (p=0.002). Fasting glucagon levels did not differ (p=0.139), but total glucagon exposure (including fasting levels) was higher in South Asian women (p=0.013). No differences in GIP and GLP responses to the OGTT were observed (p=0.490 and p=0.802). In women with prediabetes or diabetes, fasting glucagon was higher in the South Asian group (p=0.010), but there were no significant differences in early glucagon suppression post-OGTT (p=0.986). GIP responses to the OGTT were lower among South Asian women (p<0.001), despite higher insulin responses compared with the Nordic women. GLP-1 responses did not differ between the ethnic groups (p=0.661). The higher pre-hepatic insulin levels in South Asian vs Nordic normoglycaemic women were not associated with differences in incretin levels, but were associated with lower insulin sensitivity in the regression analyses (p<0.001).

Conclusions/Interpretation: When examined 1-3 years post-GDM, normoglycaemic South Asian women had less early glucagon suppression and higher total glucagon exposure post-OGTT compared with Nordic women. The higher pre-hepatic insulin levels were not associated with higher incretin levels, but were associated with lower insulin sensitivity.

title: An Incretin-Dependent Modulation of Periprandial Neutrophilia
abstract: We determine how innate immunity adapts to transitions between fasting and feeding. Feeding rapidly induced periprandial neutrophilia. HFD accelerated this reponse. We therefore sought to examine whether periprandial states regulate neutrophil dynamics. We identified that the glucagon-like peptide 1 and insulin axis modulates the neutrophil surge, which is critical during endotoxin challenges. The periprandial state prepares the host for endotoxemia. We bridge nutrient intake and incretin-sensitive immunity to inflammatory tone, redefining postprandial inflammation, insulin resistance, and cardiometabolic risk in diabetes.

title: Obesity: oral therapy for those afraid of needles
abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) pharmacotherapy has transformed obesity management, yet subcutaneous administration remains a barrier for patients with needle phobia. This review examines needle phobia and agoraphobia as contributors to treatment non-adherence and evaluates the evidence for oral GLP-1 RA alternatives.

Areas Covered: We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology of needle phobia (trypanophobia) and agoraphobia, their mechanisms and psychiatric comorbidities, real-world discontinuation rates of injectable GLP-1 RAs, and clinical efficacy data for oral semaglutide and emerging oral agents. A brief overview of the literature search methodology (PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov; searched to June 2026) is provided in the Introduction. A structured clinical decision algorithm is proposed.

Expert Opinion: Oral semaglutide 25 mg/day (the currently approved dose for weight management) demonstrates weight loss of similar magnitude to subcutaneous formulations across separate trials and should be considered preferentially in patients with moderate-to-severe needle phobia. Systematic needle phobia screening at obesity clinic entry, combined with a severity-based treatment algorithm integrating pharmacological and psychological approaches, is recommended to maximize equitable access to obesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Metabolic reprogramming in diabetic panvascular disease: Molecular mechanism and therapeutic strategies
abstract: Diabetes mellitus substantially increases the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal, retinal and peripheral vascular complications. These are collectively referred to as diabetic panvascular disease. A traditional approach that treats each complication separately is no longer sufficient. An emerging framework places metabolic reprogramming at its center. This review examines how the diabetic environment, including hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia, rewires core metabolic pathways in vascular cells. Major changes include the diversion of glucose through the polyol, hexosamine and AGE-PKC axes, lipotoxicity resulting from excessive fatty acids, disruption of amino acid networks such as BCAA and one-carbon metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction with increased mtROS production, and epigenetic modifications that drive metabolic memory. These interconnected abnormalities promote oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, which in turn lead to endothelial dysfunction, atherosclerosis, microvascular rarefaction, and end-organ damage in the heart, brain, kidney, retina, and peripheral nerves. We also describe the current therapeutic landscape, ranging from established agents such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, RAAS blockers, and anti-VEGF therapies to emerging mechanism-based strategies including aldose reductase inhibitors, glucokinase activators, PKC, RAGE, NOX, and NLRP3 inhibitors, miRNA modulators, and exosome therapy. Finally, we highlight unmet needs and future directions. These may include multi-omics guided precision phenotyping, cross-organ causal inference, single-cell metabolic flux technologies, and adaptive clinical trial designs. By shifting from a glucose-centric to a metabolic reprogramming-centric paradigm, this review aims to provide a roadmap for developing more targeted therapies for diabetic panvascular disease.

title: Medical treatments for obesity: what does the future have in store?
abstract: Context: Obesity is a chronic relapsing disease associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and health care costs. Contemporary obesity pharmacotherapies extend beyond weight reduction, with evidence for improvements across multiple obesity-related complications, supporting a shift toward phenotype-guided, complication-centric care.

Evidence Acquisition: A systematic literature search of the Medline database using MeSH terms and keywords related to new-generation obesity pharmacotherapy was conducted to identify articles published between 2021 and 2026. Reference lists of relevant reviews were screened to identify additional eligible studies. Phase 2 and 3 clinical trials evaluating emerging obesity pharmacotherapies in adults and reporting outcomes, including weight loss and obesity-related complications, were included.

Evidence Synthesis: Entero-pancreatic hormone-based therapies targeting glucagon-Like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, amylin, and glucagon pathways demonstrate substantial efficacy beyond weight reduction. These hormones act through complementary mechanisms regulating appetite, energy balance, and metabolic homeostasis. GLP-1 based agents achieve approximately 10-15% weight loss, whereas agents targeting multiple pathways demonstrate greater efficacy. Tirzepatide, CagriSema, and amycretin achieved weight reductions exceeding 20% and the triple agonist retatrutide produced reductions exceeding 25%. Beyond weight loss, these agents improve glycemia, support diabetes prevention, and produce organ-specific benefits, including reduced cardiovascular events, improved heart failure symptoms, decreased obstructive sleep apnea severity, improvement of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, slowing chronic kidney disease progression, and reduced osteoarthritis-related pain.

Conclusion: Next-generation obesity pharmacotherapies represent a major advance in obesity management and support a treat-to-target approach prioritizing improvement in obesity-related complications and metabolic health. Effective implementation will require individualized therapy and attention to long-term safety, access, and equitable delivery of care.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist exposure and malignancy risk in patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome
abstract: Context: Patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome (CS) have increased malignancy risk. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are increasingly used for diabetes and obesity, yet their oncologic outcomes in CS remains limited.
Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the association between GLP-1RA exposure and incident malignancy in patients with CS.

Methods: This was a nationwide cohort study using the Clalit Health Services database in Israel, including patients with endogenous CS diagnosed between 2000 and 2023. Patients with adrenal carcinoma or ectopic CS were excluded. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist exposure was defined as ≥3 prescription dispensations and modeled as a time-varying variable. The main outcome was incident malignancy following a CS diagnosis in GLP-1RA-exposed vs nonexposed patients. Sensitivity analyses included a 12-month lag-period approach and stratification by remission.

Results: The cohort included 609 patients with CS (mean age ± SD, 48.05 ± 17.17 years; 65.02% women). During a mean follow-up of 14.7 ± 6.4 years, 116 patients developed cancer and 141 died. Overall, 137 patients (22.5%) received GLP-1RA therapy. A total of 8159.69 nonexposed and 795.88 exposed person-years were accrued, with cancer incidence rates of 12.50 and 17.59 per 1000 person-years, respectively. In time-varying competing risk analysis, GLP-1RA exposure was not associated with increased malignancy risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.65; 95% CI, 0.94-2.90), with consistent results after adjustment (adjusted HR 1.22; 95% CI, 0.45-3.29). Findings were similar in lag-period and remission-stratified analyses.

Conclusion: In this nationwide cohort of patients with CS, GLP-1RA exposure was not associated with altered malignancy risk. These findings provide reassuring evidence regarding the oncologic safety of GLP-1RAs in this high-risk population.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT for insulinoma localization in patients with negative or inconclusive conventional imaging
abstract: Context: Insulinomas are the main cause of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (EHH) in adults, with surgery as the only cure. Pancreas-preserving surgery is preferred, making precise preoperative localization crucial. GLP-1R-targeted imaging, such as [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT, outperforms other imaging procedures for insulinoma localization.

Objective: To investigate the performance and clinical impact of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT for the detection of insulinomas in patients with EHH and prior negative or inconclusive conventional imaging.

Methods: In this retrospective, real-world, dual-center imaging study, 101 patients with biochemically proven EHH and/or a positive Whipple's triad underwent [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT at two tertiary centers between April 2017 and March 2024. Among these, 58 patients with prior negative or inconclusive conventional imaging constituted the primary analysis cohort. Endpoints: Insulinoma detection rate and sensitivity by [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT after negative or inconclusive conventional imaging and impact on clinical management.

Results: Among the 58 patients with prior negative or inconclusive conventional imaging, [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT was positive in 42 patients, corresponding to a detection rate of 72% (95% CI, 59-83%). Thirty patients subsequently underwent PET/CT-guided surgery. Overall, 32 patients had histological verification (including two PET/CT-negative cases), corresponding to a sensitivity of 93.8% (95% CI, 79-99%).

Conclusion: In real-world clinical practice, [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT provides a high detection rate of 72% for localizing insulinomas, including one case of diffuse nesidioblastosis in patients with EHH and prior negative or inconclusive conventional imaging, thereby enabling PET/CT-guided surgical approaches. These findings underscore the substantial clinical impact of GLP-1R-targeted PET/CT on patient management and prognosis.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: The effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists versus metformin on pregnancy rates in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
abstract: Background: PCOS-related infertility is closely linked to metabolic dysfunction. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve insulin resistance and promote weight loss in women with PCOS, but their direct effect on reproductive outcomes remains uncertain.
Objectives: To evaluate whether GLP-1RA-based therapy improves pregnancy outcomes in women with PCOS.
Search Strategy: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 2026.
Selection Criteria: Randomized controlled trials comparing GLP-1RA-based therapy, alone or combined with metformin, with metformin monotherapy in women with PCOS.

Data Collection And Analysis: Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2. Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals using a random-effects model. Certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE, and trial sequential analysis was performed.

Main Results: Four reports from three randomized trials (252 participants) were included. GLP-1RA-based treatment did not significantly improve overall pregnancy (OR 1.41, 95% CI 0.81-2.45), but was associated with an increase in natural pregnancy (OR 3.10, 95% CI 1.74-5.49), with no significant effect on IVF pregnancy (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.36-2.85).
