TSA supported the finding for natural pregnancy, while evidence for overall pregnancy remained underpowered. Certainty of evidence was moderate for natural pregnancy and low for the other outcomes.

Conclusions: GLP-1 receptor agonists show promising preliminary signals for improving spontaneous conception in women with PCOS, but the available evidence remains limited. Current evidence is insufficient to draw conclusions regarding IVF outcomes. Larger trials with standardized endpoints, including live birth, are needed.
journal: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in Alzheimer's disease and MCI: a meta-analysis
abstract: Introduction: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in older individuals and remains a major clinical and socioeconomic burden. Despite the success of anti-amyloid therapies in reducing biomarker burden, more effective and safer treatments are still needed. Given the emerging evidence of a role for metabolic dysfunction and brain insulin resistance in AD pathophysiology, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have been proposed as potential disease-modifying therapies.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to April 22, 2026 to evaluate the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 RAs in AD and mild cognitive impairment. Randomized controlled trials comparing GLP-1 RAs with placebo, standard care, or non-intervention across the Alzheimer's continuum were eligible; abstracts and studies with unavailable results were excluded. Random-effects models were used. Risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for binary outcomes, and mean or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool.

Results: Seven studies comprising 4132 participants met the inclusion criteria. The mean age of the pooled studies was 72.1 years, while the mean baseline Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) varied from 2.71 to 3.8. GLP-1 RAs were not associated with significant improvement in cognition (Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale: standard mean difference -0.05; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.12 to 0.02; p = 0.1928) or disease progression (CDR-SB: mean difference: 0.09; 95% CI: -0.10 to 0.28; p = 0.362). They were associated with a higher frequency of adverse events (RR 1.07; 95% CI: 1.04 to 1.10; p < 0.0001) and weight loss (RR 5.01; 95% CI: 3.99 to 6.27; p < 0.0001). Biomarker and neuroimaging findings were inconsistent and failed to translate to clinical benefit.

Discussion: GLP-1 RAs did not improve cognitive or functional outcomes in AD and were associated with adverse events. Their role may be better explored in biomarker-enriched, metabolically selected populations or assessment of GLP-1 RAs with greater brain penetrance.

title: Treatment of hyperphagia and obesity in Prader-Willi syndrome
abstract: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare, neurodevelopmental, multisystemic syndrome caused by lack of expression of paternal genes on chromosome 15q11.2-13. PWS is characterized by muscular hypotonia, abnormal body composition, hormone deficiencies, cognitive dysfunction and behavioural issues, including hyperphagia, increasing the risk of severe obesity. A single causative gene for hyperphagia has not been identified, and regulation of hunger and satiety is complex and multifactorial, making it difficult to identify a specific neuropeptide or hormone as the most important. Cornerstone treatments are a strict, controlled diet and regular physical activity. Several clinical trials with different pharmacological agents have been performed attempting to reduce or treat hyperphagia and obesity. However, many drug programmes have been discontinued due to adverse events or not reaching endpoints. In this review, we have focused on phenomenology and management of hyperphagia, treatment with oxytocin (OT), glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and diazoxide choline. We conclude that controlled food access is crucial; managing expectations about food mitigates food-related behaviour; OT treatment of infants with PWS results in less severe hyperphagia at ages 3 and 4 years old; and that the effects of GLP-1RA on body weight seem modest. Studies of diazoxide choline extended-release (DCCR), the first approved treatment of hyperphagia in PWS, have shown promising results, particularly in managing severe hyperphagia, reducing fat mass and improving behavioural issues. Thus, although progress is being made in targeted pharmacological therapies to control hyperphagia, controlled food access remains crucial to prevent obesity but is not sufficient for management of food and behaviour.

title: A Retrospective Chart Review of Tirzepatide and Semaglutide Use in Prediabetes Management and Cardiometabolic Outcomes in a Rural Primary Care Setting
abstract: Background: Prediabetes and obesity are highly prevalent conditions associated with increased risk of progression to type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and cardiovascular disease. While clinical trials demonstrate the efficacy of glucagon-like peptide-1 and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, limited evidence exists in routine primary care, particularly in rural populations. Objective: This review aimed to examine associations between tirzepatide and semaglutide use and changes in glycemic status and cardiometabolic risk factors among rural-dwelling adults with prediabetes treated in a single rural primary care clinic. Methods: A retrospective chart review was conducted among 40 adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity treated for 3-24 months with semaglutide or tirzepatide. Primary outcomes included body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin (A1c). Secondary variables included blood pressure (BP), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and triglycerides. Results: Significant improvements were observed in A1c, BMI, systolic and diastolic BP, LDL, and triglycerides (p < .001). All participants achieved normoglycemic A1c levels. No significant changes were observed in HDL levels. Conclusions: In this rural primary care setting, treatment with tirzepatide or semaglutide was associated with improvements in glycemic control and cardiometabolic risk factors. Findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the observational design and potential confounding factors. Implications for Nursing: Nurse practitioners are positioned to advocate for and implement pharmacological therapies for early management of prediabetes. Providers can drive meaningful changes in T2DM prevention and cardiometabolic health optimization.

title: Type 2 diabetes medications and their implications for cancer treatment: A comprehensive review
abstract: The increasing prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a significant public health challenge with serious implications for cancer incidence and treatment. Currently affecting over 400 million individuals worldwide, T2DM is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance, which contribute to a pro-tumorigenic environment. This review seeks to elucidate the complex relationship between diabetes medications and cancer treatment, emphasizing how various agents, including metformin, sulfonylureas, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, thiazolidinediones (TZDs), and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, interact with critical signaling pathways involved in cancer progression. Evidence suggests that these medications can modulate oncogenic pathways such as AMPK/mTOR, insulin/IGF signaling, and Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), leading to either inhibition or stimulation of tumor growth and survival depending on the drug class and biological context. For instance, metformin activates AMPK, inhibiting mTOR and promoting apoptosis, while TZDs exert anti-inflammatory effects that may reduce obesity-related cancer risks. Conversely, some DPP-4 inhibitors have been associated with pro-tumorigenic effects under certain conditions. Given the intricate interplay among diabetes, obesity, and cancer, understanding the effects of antidiabetic therapies on tumor biology is crucial for refining treatment strategies. This review consolidates current findings on the cellular and molecular impacts of major T2DM drug classes on cancer, highlighting their potential benefits and limitations. In conclusion, the findings presented in this analysis are intended to enhance treatment strategies and shape future research initiatives aimed at effectively addressing the complexities of managing patients who are concurrently affected by diabetes and cancer.

title: Beyond Hemodynamics: Uremic Toxins, Post-Translational Modifications, and Inflammatory-Metabolic Remodeling in Uremic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Uremic cardiomyopathy has traditionally been attributed to pressure overload, volume overload, hypertension, and neurohormonal activation in chronic kidney disease. However, growing experimental and clinical evidence indicates that nonhemodynamic mechanisms also contribute to myocardial remodeling in uremia. These mechanisms include retention of uremic toxins and protein-bound solutes, mediators of mineral metabolism, gut-derived metabolites, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and post-translational protein modifications. In this review, we discuss uremic cardiomyopathy as a systemic inflammatory-metabolic disorder in which kidney failure reshapes myocardial structure and function through interacting biochemical and interorgan pathways. We first define the major classes of uremic toxins, including small water-soluble solutes, middle molecules, protein-bound uremic toxins, and reactive chemical intermediates. We then focus on post-translational modifications, particularly urea-derived cyanate-mediated carbamylation, a well-characterized uremia-associated mechanism that can alter collagen, extracellular matrix turnover, plasma proteins, lipoproteins, and potentially long-lived cardiac proteins. Additional injury pathways, including oxidative modifications, ferroptosis, fibroblast growth factor 23/Klotho imbalance, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation by indoxyl sulfate, gut-derived adrenergic metabolites, endotoxemia, and inflammasome signaling, are discussed as complementary and partially overlapping mechanisms. Because much of the current mechanistic evidence comes from preclinical models, circulating biomarkers, or associative human studies, we distinguish established evidence from plausible mechanistic hypotheses throughout the review. Finally, we discuss therapeutic implications, including enhanced toxin removal, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, and future strategies targeting uremic toxins, proteostasis, ferroptosis, inflammasome activation, and toxin-induced post-translational modifications.

title: Impact of GLP-1 Agonists on Post-Operative Outcomes in Aesthetic & Body Contouring Surgery: A Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have rapidly expanded in use for weight loss, resulting in a growing population of patients presenting for aesthetic and body-contouring procedures. Despite their increasing prevalence, the effects of GLP-1 RAs on postoperative wound healing and surgical outcomes remain poorly defined.

Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from database inception through May 2026. Studies comparing postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing aesthetic and/or body-contouring surgery with and without GLP-1 RA exposure were included. Primary outcomes included infection, wound dehiscence, delayed wound healing, hypertrophic scarring, seroma, hematoma, and venous thromboembolism (VTE). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results: Twelve studies comprising 29,357 patients met inclusion criteria, with 10 studies included in quantitative synthesis. In pooled observational analyses, GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with increased risk of delayed wound healing and hypertrophic scarring. Subgroup analysis comparing GLP-1 RA users with patients who had previously undergone bariatric surgery demonstrated decreased seroma rates in the GLP-1 RA group.

Conclusions: GLP-1 RA use in patients undergoing aesthetic and body-contouring surgery was associated in pooled observational analyses with increased risks of delayed wound healing and hypertrophic scarring, while GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower seroma rates in comparison with patients who have undergone bariatric surgery. As GLP-1 RA use become increasingly prevalent, further prospective studies are needed to clarify their perioperative effects and optimize patient selection and surgical outcomes.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Lipoprotein (a): Insights, Gaps and Clinical Implications in Cardiovascular Diseases
abstract: Purpose Of Review: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], a predominantly genetically determined biomarker that remains relatively stable throughout life, is a well-established and independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated broad cardiometabolic benefits, yet their potential influence on Lp(a) remains unclear. This review synthesizes the most recent evidence at the intersection of GLP-1RAs, Lp(a), and cardiovascular disease, with particular emphasis on underlying mechanistic pathways and their potential implications for cardiovascular risk stratification and clinical outcomes.

Recent Findings: Beyond glycemic control, the multisystem effects of GLP-1RAs suggest a plausible influence on Lp(a) metabolism through multiple mechanistic pathways, including modulation of hepatic and intestinal lipoprotein synthesis and secretion, anti-inflammatory and endothelial-protective actions, attenuation of adipokine signaling, and broader metabolic outcomes. Preclinical and early clinical studies suggest modest but significant reductions in Lp(a) with GLP-1RA therapy, and ongoing large-scale studies aim to clarify the magnitude and clinical relevance of this effect. GLP-1RAs may offer a novel approach to addressing residual cardiovascular risk in patients with elevated Lp(a), although their direct effects on Lp(a) remain uncertain and warrant further investigation. Emerging evidence suggests a promising link between GLP-1RA therapy and Lp(a)-related pathways.

title: Advances in disease management and treatment outcomes for obesity and knee osteoarthritis in primary care practice
abstract: The lifetime risk of developing knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is approximately doubled in people with obesity compared with those without obesity. Many patients with KOA are treated by primary care physicians in the community setting. We performed a targeted literature search on PubMed to identify relevant literature describing the impact of weight loss in patients with obesity and KOA. A strong body of evidence supports the use of weight loss through lifestyle interventions, including caloric restriction in combination with exercise, as a primary intervention in patients with KOA and obesity. Studies show that these interventions are associated with improvements in pain, physical function, and quality of life; however, adherence to lifestyle interventions can be challenging, even with individually tailored programs. Obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, are emerging as a new addition to weight management approaches in KOA, with a recent phase 3 clinical study demonstrating the benefits of semaglutide for weight loss in adults with KOA and high body mass index. Although initial data are promising, further clinical evidence is required, and perceived barriers to use need to be addressed before obesity medications can be widely adopted into clinical practice for patients with KOA. Specifically, further data are required to guide decisions regarding optimal treatment duration with obesity medications and to establish their tolerability profile associated with longer-term use. The importance of preserving functional muscle mass in patients with KOA and mitigation of weight regain after obesity medication treatment withdrawal are also identified as areas warranting further research. In this narrative review, we provide practical recommendations to primary care physicians on integrating obesity medications into weight-loss programs, including patient screening, risk stratification, communication, use of guidelines, and the benefits of a multidisciplinary approach.

title: Changes in Gait Speed During a 12-Month Multidisciplinary Obesity Management Program Including Semaglutide: A Real-World Observational Study in Japanese Adults With Musculoskeletal Disorders
abstract: Background Obesity is associated with musculoskeletal disorders, impaired mobility, and frailty. While semaglutide induces substantial weight loss, its effects on objectively measured physical function in routine clinical practice are unclear. We investigated the changes in gait speed and physical function during a multidisciplinary obesity management program that included semaglutide.Methods This retrospective observational study included 22 adults with obesity and musculoskeletal disorders who completed a 12-month multidisciplinary obesity management program. The program included nutritional counseling every two months, physical therapist-guided exercise intervention, and semaglutide treatment. The primary outcome was the usual gait speed. The secondary outcomes included body weight, pain score, step count, muscle function, and body composition.Results Body weight decreased significantly from 89.2±18.6 kg to 81.5±17.3 kg (p<0.001). Usual gait speed improved significantly from 0.77±0.20 m/s to 0.91±0.19 m/s (p<0.001). Pain scores also significantly improved (p<0.001). Improvements in gait speed were not associated with weight loss (r=0.22, p=0.32) or pain reduction (r=-0.04, p=0.84). Baseline gait speed was inversely associated with gait speed improvement (r=-0.44, p=0.043), indicating greater gains in participants with poorer baseline mobility.Conclusions A 12-month multidisciplinary obesity management program, including semaglutide, significantly improved gait speed in patients with obesity and musculoskeletal disorders. Greater improvements were observed in participants with impaired baseline mobility. These findings support the evaluation of obesity treatment not only by weight loss, but also by recovery of mobility.

title: Akkermansia muciniphila HHAKKα Prevents High-Fat Diet-Induced Obesity in Mice via Gut Microbiota Modulation and Regulation of Hepatic Lipid Metabolism
abstract: Obesity and its associated metabolic disorders pose significant global health challenges. This study investigated the anti-obesity effects of Akkermansia muciniphila HHAKKα in high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obese mice. C57BL/6J mice were administered HHAKKα orally for 8 weeks while maintained on HFD. Results demonstrated that HHAKKα significantly inhibited weight gain (5.76 g vs. 10.79 g in HFD group), with efficacy comparable to orlistat. HHAKKα intervention effectively maintained glucose homeostasis, decreased serum triglycerides and LDL-cholesterol levels, and elevated adiponectin and GLP-1 levels. Furthermore, HHAKKα significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, MCP-1) and alleviated hepatic steatosis and adipocyte hypertrophy. Mechanistically, HHAKKα modulated gut microbiota composition, increasing beneficial bacteria (Akkermansia, Roseburia, Eubacterium) while decreasing the Bacillota/Bacteroidota ratio by 55.35%. Notably, the HHAKKα intervention significantly enhanced fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production-particularly butyrate, which was restored to approximately 1.5 times its normal level-and this effect correlated negatively with serum lipid levels and inflammatory markers. Molecular analysis revealed that HHAKKα regulated hepatic lipid metabolism by inhibiting FASN expression and upregulating PGC-1α. These findings suggest that A. muciniphila HHAKKα ameliorates HFD-induced obesity through a multi-faceted mechanism involving gut microbiota modulation, SCFA production enhancement, inflammation suppression, and hepatic lipid metabolism regulation, highlighting its therapeutic potential for obesity management.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

title: Deoxycalyxin A exerts hypoglycemic effects through activating TGR5-induced GLP-1 secretion via TGR5/PKA/MEK/ERK pathway
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and progressive β cell dysfunction. Deoxycalyxin A (DCA), a unique diarylheptanoid-chalcone hybrid isolated from Alpinia katsumadai, was identified as a novel stimulator of GLP 1 secretion in both STC-1 (EC50: 10.7 μM) and NCI-H716 (EC50: 13.4 μM) cells. Oral administration of DCA (40 and 80 mg/kg) in db/db mice significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, ameliorated glucose intolerance and insulin resistance by enhancing endogenous GLP-1 secretion, and lowered the total serum cholesterol levels. Mechanistic study demonstrated that DCA identify the TGR5 receptor, which induces a significant increase in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels, which activates PKA with subsequent sequential phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK activation, ultimately enhancing GLP-1 secretion. Our findings identify DCA as a novel TGR5 agonist to stimulate GLP-1 secretion via the TGR5/PKA/MEK/ERK pathway, which has the potential to be developed as a promising antidiabetic lead with a distinct mechanism of action.

title: Association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and ischemic stroke severity
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) reduce stroke incidence, but their impact on the severity of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) when events occur remains unclear. The aim of this study is to evaluate whether pre-stroke GLP-1RA use is associated with reduced ischemic stroke severity and improved post-stroke outcomes.

Method: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2016-2024 data from the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Patients were categorized based on documented use of GLP-1RAs for at least six months prior to the index stroke event. After, propensity score matching, primary outcome was measured by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), with secondary outcomes including rates of severe stroke (NIHSS ≥10), intensive care unit admission, neurological symptoms, in-hospital complications, and 30-day mortality.

Results: A total of 209,180 first-time AIS patients were identified, of whom 4773 (2.3%) were GLP-1RA users. After PSM, 4769 patients remained in each group. GLP-1RA users had lower median NIHSS (3 vs 4, p < 0.001). GLP-1RA users also had lower rates of severe stroke (18.4% vs 25.5%, p < 0.001), dysphagia/dysarthria (43.5% vs 48.0%, p < 0.001), aphasia (25.2% vs 28.7%, p < 0.001), hemiplegia/hemiparesis (37.6% vs 43.3%, p < 0.001), intracranial hemorrhage (13.2% vs 14.7%, p = 0.031), and 30-day mortality (6.3% vs 7.6%, p = 0.016).

Conclusions: Among adult patients who suffered a first-time AIS, pre-stroke use of GLP-1RA was associated with reduced stroke severity, lower rates of symptoms and complications, and lower mortality. These findings suggest that the benefits GLP-1RA may extend beyond preventing the occurrence of cerebrovascular events.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Incretin-Based Therapies for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Narrative Review of Available Clinical Evidence
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major global health burden, but pharmacological treatment options are limited, and there is an urgent need for novel molecular targets for the treatment of AUD. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been used for more than 2 decades to treat type 2 diabetes and subsequently overweight and obesity. Unexpected effects, including reduced alcohol intake, have been reported by patients as well as by clinicians, and these (often anecdotal) reports have been supported by a growing body of data from large registry studies; target trial emulation analyses; preclinical experiments with mice, rats, and nonhuman primates; and randomized clinical trials associating the use of GLP-1RAs with reduced alcohol consumption. This convergence has sparked growing interest in GLP-1RAs as a novel therapeutic strategy for AUD. In this narrative review, we synthesize current evidence on the effects of GLP-1RAs in individuals with AUD. To date, only 3 randomized controlled trials have examined GLP-1RAs in AUD, showing reductions in alcohol cue brain reactivity and alcohol consumption, particularly among individuals with overweight or obesity. We also report on observational data, including large registry studies, target trial emulation analyses, and real-world data, which have consistently associated GLP-1RA use with reduced alcohol consumption. Case reports and social media analyses further corroborate reductions in alcohol craving and consumption. Mechanistically, emerging evidence points to modulation of reward circuitry, incentive salience, gastric emptying, and metabolic signaling. Overall, GLP-1RAs represent a promising and mechanistically novel approach to AUD treatment, warranting confirmation in larger, long-term randomized trials.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists as a Candidate Treatment for Opioid Use Disorder: From Rats to Humans
abstract: Despite recent progress and at least 3 medications approved for the treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD), the number of deaths due to opioid overdose remains unacceptably high. Therefore, there is a need for new treatments. To this end, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dual GLP-1RA+glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists (e.g., tirzepatide), and triple agonists (e.g., GLP-1RA+neuropeptideY1/Y2 receptor agonists) show promise. Here, we review preclinical and clinical data. In the preclinical studies, acute administration of exendin-4 and the longer-acting liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, and other dual and triple agonists reduced opioid taking and/or opioid seeking when elicited by exposure to drug-related cues, the drug itself, or by stress. Chronic treatment with GLP-1RAs also reduced responding for opioids, but tolerance occurred with chronic administration of higher doses of GLP-1RAs. In the human studies, 1 small clinical trial found a 40% reduction in opioid craving following treatment with the GLP-1RA liraglutide. Three other clinical trials are ongoing, with 2 testing the efficacy of semaglutide and 1 testing the efficacy of tirzepatide as adjunctive treatments to buprenorphine or methadone. Pending completion of these clinical trials, recent studies used data from electronic health records, the TriNetX database, and Medicare claims and found a 40% reduction in opioid overdose and in hospital admissions for OUD in patients treated with a GLP-1RA or a GLP-1RA/GIP agonist for type 2 diabetes and/or for obesity. Thus, while additional clinical trials are needed, these data suggest that GLP-1RAs hold promise as a novel treatment for OUD in humans.

title: GLP-1 and Alcohol-Related Behaviors: Insights From Preclinical Studies
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) has gained attention for its broad physiological effects, and both short-acting (exenatide/exendin-4 [Ex4]) and long-acting (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide) GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists have been approved for type 2 diabetes and/or obesity. Initial preclinical research has highlighted the role of GLP-1 and its receptor in the pathophysiology of alcohol use disorder (AUD) and their potential use in the treatment of AUD. Specifically, systemic treatment of Ex4 reduces alcohol intake, the motivation to consume alcohol, and relapse-like behavior in male animals. Similarly, alcohol consummatory behaviors are reduced in male or female animals treated with either of the long-acting GLP-1R agonists. Moreover, both short- and long-acting GLP-1R agonists consistently attenuate the rewarding properties of alcohol, as measured by locomotor stimulation, dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, and conditioned place preference in male mice. Because alcohol consumption is largely driven by alcohol-induced reward, it is hypothesized that GLP-1R agonists attenuate the rewarding effects of alcohol, thereby decreasing alcohol intake. However, it should be emphasized that other factors, including altered gastric emptying, nausea, and enhanced stress, may also contribute to these effects. Taken together, these preclinical studies offer insight into the potential use of GLP-1R agonists in the treatment of AUD.

title: From evidence to practice: Identifying candidates for semaglutide in chronic atherosclerotic disease
abstract: Background And Aim: Randomised clinical trials (SELECT and SOUL) demonstrated that semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, reduces the combined outcome measure of atherothrombotic events or cardiovascular mortality in patients with coronary artery disease, both with and without diabetes. Because real-world populations may differ from trial cohorts, we assessed the proportion of patients potentially eligible for semaglutide using the criteria set out by the regulatory authorities based on the SELECT and SOUL results.

Methods And Results: Patients whose clinical characteristics were comparable to those of patients enrolled in the SELECT and SOUL trials were identified within the START and BRING-UP prevention registries. Among 12,430 patients, 623 were excluded because of severe renal impairment or ongoing GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy. The final population included 11,807 patients: 8682 without diabetes and 3125 with diabetes. Among non-diabetic patients, 3689 (42.5%) were SELECT-like, defined as overweight or obese individuals with established coronary disease. Among diabetic patients, 3059 (97.9%) were SOUL-like, defined as individuals aged ≥50 years with cardiovascular disease. Overall, 6748 of 12,430 patients (54.3%) theoretically fulfilled eligibility criteria for semaglutide treatment in real-world cardiology practice.

Conclusions: According to the criteria set out by the regulatory authorities based on the SELECT and SOUL trial results, a large proportion of patients with coronary artery disease managed by cardiologists may be potentially eligible for semaglutide therapy. Identifying the target population for this therapeutic strategy may help clinicians and healthcare authorities estimate unmet clinical needs and evaluate the sustainability of innovative approaches for secondary cardiovascular prevention.

title: From Satiety to Substance Use: Neural Mechanisms of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Signaling in Appetite and Reward
abstract: The central glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) system encompasses homeostatic and hedonic neural circuits. GLP-1-producing neurons within the brainstem project broadly to GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R)-containing brainstem, hypothalamic, limbic, and mesolimbic nuclei. The diverse expression of the GLP-1R throughout metabolic and reward nuclei positions this system to integrate motivated behavior with physiological state. GLP-1 acts as a state-dependent behavior-ending signal that suppresses appetite, promotes satiety, and dampens hedonic and motivational reward value-effects that extend beyond palatable foods. GLP-1R agonists, which can partially cross the blood-brain barrier, engage central GLP-1Rs via circumventricular organs and adjacent nuclei leading to polysynaptic relays that suppress feeding and drug-seeking behaviors. An abundance of preclinical and clinical evidence highlights the efficacy of GLP-1R agonists for the treatment of obesity and other metabolic disorders. Emerging evidence also indicates that the therapeutic application may extend to other disorders characterized by reward-related maladaptive behaviors, including substance use disorders.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Signaling in Learning and Memory: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Implications
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is primarily known for its role in glucose homeostasis and food intake control, and GLP-1 analogs (either as monotherapy or dual agonists) are commonly used for type 2 diabetes and obesity treatment in humans. Beyond these functions, the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) is widely expressed throughout the brain, including in the hippocampus (HPC) and interconnected regions that contribute to learning and memory processes. Here we review emerging evidence supporting a role for GLP-1 signaling in promoting learning and memory function, particularly in dementia and other conditions that manifest with HPC dysfunction. Evidence is synthesized from preclinical rodent models revealing that GLP-1 analog treatment improves deficits in memory function and HPC neuronal signaling processes in various models of dementia, aging, and metabolic disruption. While findings from human clinical trials and meta-analyses also show promise for GLP-1 analog-based treatment for memory disorders, results thus far are mixed, with many studies underpowered and/or lacking comprehensive memory evaluation. We describe several distinct yet non-mutually exclusive neurobiological mechanisms by which GLP-1R signaling can enhance memory, including blood-brain barrier penetration and direct action on HPC GLP-1Rs, improved peripheral and central insulin sensitivity, vagus nerve GLP-1R activation, and peripheral metabolic and inflammatory improvements. We conclude by emphasizing important considerations for future clinical trials for GLP-1 analogs in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and other memory disorders, including focusing on metabolically vulnerable individuals, stratifying results by cardiovascular and metabolic status, and leveraging existing GLP-1 analogs and drug delivery approaches toward maximizing bioavailability and brain penetrance.

title: Do Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists Sabotage Fat Grafts?: A Scoping Review of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist Effects on Adipocyte Biology and Implications for Autologous Fat Transfer
abstract: The rapid adoption of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for weight management has created an unprecedented overlap with aesthetic surgery. Millions of patients experiencing GLP-1-mediated weight loss now present with facial volume depletion, soft tissue deflation, and contour irregularities; conditions for which autologous fat grafting remains the gold-standard solution. However, the fundamental biology of GLP-1 receptor agonism may be inherently antagonistic to the mechanisms upon which fat graft survival depends. This scoping review, conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), synthesizes current preclinical and clinical evidence on the effects of semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide, and the emerging triple agonist retatrutide on adipocyte metabolism, adipose-derived stem cell (ASC) function, and tissue revascularization, and maps these effects onto established models of fat graft take. We identify multiple potential interference points, including GLP-1-mediated adipocyte browning and thermogenic activation with upregulation of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) and mitochondrial uncoupling, enhanced lipolysis through adipose triglyceride lipase and hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) upregulation, suppression of white adipogenic differentiation in ASCs with preferential commitment toward thermogenic beige lineages, and modulation of inflammatory and angiogenic signaling during the critical revascularization window. The growing off-label use of retatrutide in bodybuilding communities introduces additional concerns through glucagon receptor-mediated lipolysis and thermogenesis. Despite the strong mechanistic rationale, no clinical or preclinical studies have directly examined fat graft outcomes in patients receiving incretin-based therapies. We propose a framework for future investigation and offer preliminary, mechanism-based clinical considerations regarding perioperative GLP-1 RA management in fat transfer patients. These recommendations should be understood as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence-based guidelines. Level of Evidence: 1 (Therapeutic) For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.

title: Preclinical and Emerging Clinical Evidence Supporting the Translational Potential of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists for Treating Psychostimulant and Nicotine Use Disorders
abstract: Psychostimulant use disorder (PSUD) and nicotine use disorder (NUD) affect tens of millions of people worldwide, yet no clinically approved medications exist for PSUD, and existing NUD treatments have limited long-term efficacy. Recent preclinical evidence suggests that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists could be repurposed for treating PSUD and NUD. This review summarizes the current literature investigating the efficacy of GLP-1R agonists to reduce psychostimulant and nicotine-mediated behaviors in animal models of PSUD and NUD, respectively. The neural mechanisms underlying the suppressive effects of GLP-1R agonists on drug-mediated behaviors as well as the role of central endogenous GLP-1 neural circuits in voluntary drug-taking and drug-seeking behaviors are also discussed. Overall, a growing preclinical literature and emerging clinical studies support the translational potential of GLP-1R agonists as novel pharmacotherapies for treating substance use disorders including PSUD and NUD.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists for Mood Disorders and Suicide Risk
abstract: Identifying innovative mechanisms that translate into improved therapeutics when compared to the extant options is a strategic imperative in mood disorders. More specifically, there is a need for treatments with greater efficacy, shorter time-to-peak efficacy, greater durability of effect, and improved tolerability profiles. Moreover, priority has also shifted toward identifying mood disorder therapeutics capable of targeting domains of psychopathology that are most pervasive, debilitating, and inadequately treated by conventional pharmacology (e.g., anhedonia and cognitive impairment). Available preclinical, translational, observational, and clinical data suggest that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) hold promise as potentially mechanistically informed therapeutics for people with mood disorders. Although metabolic effectors are implicated as a putative mechanism of action of GLP-1RAs, nonmutually exclusive targets also include direct effects on neuroplasticity, neurogenesis, neurodifferentiation, neuroprotection, antiapoptotic, and autophagy mechanisms. Available evidence supports the initiation of adequate and well-controlled clinical studies in both major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder as acute and/or maintenance treatments. Although associations between suicidality and GLP-1RAs have been reported, causality has not been established. Moreover, preliminary evidence suggests that GLP-1RAs may benefit aspects of mood disorder psychopathology (e.g., reward) that may be predictive of potential beneficial effects on aspects of suicidality.

title: From the Discovery of GLP-1 to Today's Diabetes/Obesity Therapy and Beyond
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) was discovered as an insulinotropic peptide from the gut during a search for candidates for the incretin effect. It was found to also inhibit glucagon secretion and is now considered an important regulator of glucose metabolism. In further investigations of its physiological effects, GLP-1 also inhibited gastrointestinal secretion and motility and inhibited appetite and food intake. Because of these effects, GLP-1 was eventually shown to be able to improve glucose control and beta cell function in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and was even associated with weight loss. Because of a very short half-life in the circulation due to renal clearance and enzymatic degradation, stable analogs were developed allowing long-term treatment. Analogs suitable for weekly administration proved highly effective in improving glycemic control in patients with T2DM, and the analogs showed efficacy with respect to weight loss. Moreover, in cardiovascular outcome trials, the agonists were protective against major cardiovascular events and showed renoprotection and neuroprotection. Several observational studies also indicated protection against psychiatric illnesses and dementia. Thus, GLP-1 receptor agonists seem to be an effective weapon against the obesity-associated cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome affecting millions of patients.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists for Smoking Cessation
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) therapies are under investigation for a growing number of neuropsychiatric conditions, including substance use disorders. Cigarette smoking accounts for the largest proportion of substance use-related morbidity and mortality, in part reflecting increased risk for cardiometabolic disease among people who smoke. Given modest quit rates with approved smoking cessation therapies, medications with novel mechanisms of action are needed to expand the available monotherapy and combination treatment options. Treatments that prevent postcessation weight gain could further reduce relapse and cardiometabolic risks following smoking cessation. Preclinical findings have shown that GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) modulate nicotine reward, reduce nicotine self-administration, and prevent withdrawal-related hyperphagia. Early clinical investigations suggest that GLP-1RAs prevent postcessation weight gain while potentially improving cessation or reducing craving. These findings, combined with the efficacy of GLP-1RAs for cardiometabolic risk reduction, position GLP-1 medicines as a promising therapeutic class for people who smoke. This review addresses the therapeutic potential of GLP-1-based therapies for smoking cessation, emphasizing emerging findings from randomized trials and other human investigations. Potential neural mechanisms for effects of GLP-1RAs on nicotine reward are reviewed, and priorities for future clinical and translational studies are discussed. Individuals with metabolic disorders or psychiatric disorders are proposed as clinical subgroups for which therapeutic benefits of GLP-1 medicines may prove important based on elevated risk for tobacco-related morbidity and mortality.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Psychiatry: A Pharmacoepidemiological Scoping Review
abstract: Pharmacoepidemiological studies have expanded the capacity to detect therapeutic benefits and adverse drug effects of medications. In the case of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), their fast uptake for treating diabetes and obesity has generated substantial real-world experience, facilitating exploration of benefits for additional indications. In the context of psychiatric disorders, studies based on pharmacovigilance data and large electronic health record (EHR) databases have shown that initial concerns regarding an association between suicidality and GLP-1RA use were not supported by the evidence. Emerging data also suggest potential therapeutic benefits, with the strongest evidence for substance use disorders, binge-eating disorder, and bulimia nervosa, as well as improved metabolic outcomes in patients with schizophrenia. However, randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether such beneficial associations represent mechanistic effects, and further surveillance is needed to assess potential risks for anorexia. Also, more comprehensive EHR databases using harmonized methodologies and integrated with multimodal data will expand pharmacoepidemiology capabilities, including the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence. In this scoping review, we summarize the pharmacoepidemiologic evidence regarding the potential psychiatric effects, both therapeutic and adverse, of GLP-1RAs and the methodological and translational gaps that need to be addressed to strengthen the robustness of pharmacoepidemiologic findings and accelerate therapeutic discovery.

title: Loss of Intestinal MSTN Promotes GLP-1 Secretion Through SGLT1 Palmitoylation
abstract: Intestinal glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is secreted by intestinal L cells in a glucose-dependent manner. The localization and surface abundance of glucose-sensing proteins on the cell membrane affect the response to glucose, but the regulatory mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we show that S-palmitoylation is required for stable plasma membrane enrichment of SGLT1 and for SGLT1-mediated GLP-1 secretion. Notably, myostatin (MSTN) was identified as a key upstream regulator of this modification. Intestinal MSTN deficiency markedly enhanced SGLT1 palmitoylation, increased its plasma membrane abundance, and thereby promoted glucose-stimulated GLP-1 secretion. Importantly, simvastatin induced intestinal MSTN upregulation and impaired glucose homeostasis, whereas MSTN deficiency largely alleviated these effects. Mechanistically, MSTN regulated the expression of the palmitoyl acyltransferase ZDHHC20, which catalyzed SGLT1 S-palmitoylation at Cys301. Blocking SGLT1 palmitoylation attenuated SGLT1 membrane enrichment and markedly suppressed the induction of GLP-1 secretion caused by MSTN deficiency. Collectively, our research results have revealed a new mechanism by which MSTN regulates intestinal endocrine function and S-palmitoylation modification promotes GLP-1 secretion, providing potential targets for regulating endogenous GLP-1 secretion in the intestine and treating metabolic diseases related to glucose imbalance.

title: Real-World Treatment Patterns and Weight Outcomes Before and After a Tirzepatide Price Increase in Over One Million Self-Paying UK Adults With Overweight or Obesity
abstract: Aims: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist-based medicines are highly effective treatments for overweight and obesity, but population-scale real-world evidence remains limited, particularly in self-funded settings where treatment choice may be influenced by relative price. We aimed to characterise provider reach and treatment patterns through a large United Kingdom (UK) telehealth provider, assess changes around the September 2025 tirzepatide list-price increase of up to 170%, and estimate longitudinal weight trajectories.

Materials And Methods: A retrospective cohort study of adults initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide through MedExpress from 1 May 2024 to 1 January 2026 was conducted. Treatment initiation and switching were analysed using segmented interrupted time-series models, with sensitivity analyses addressing anticipatory changes in August 2025. Weight trajectories were estimated using linear mixed-effects models.

Results: Among 1 033 522 adults, 932 659 (90.2%) initiated tirzepatide and 100 863 (9.8%) semaglutide; provider reach was higher among women than men. In September 2025, semaglutide initiation increased by 31.15 percentage points (95% CI: 26.07-36.24) relative to the projected pre-interruption trend. Tirzepatide-to-semaglutide switching increased by 9.26 percentage points (95% CI: 7.09-11.42) and subsequently attenuated. Sensitivity analyses supported anticipatory changes in August. At 12 months, estimated weight loss was 19.93% with tirzepatide (95% CI: 19.88-19.98; n = 30 763) and 16.40% with semaglutide (95% CI: 16.16-16.64; n = 979).

Conclusions: A single UK telehealth provider achieved substantial reach among adults with overweight or obesity. Treatment initiation and switching changed markedly around the tirzepatide price increase. Substantial longitudinal weight loss was observed among patients contributing follow-up in the context of limited adjunctive lifestyle support.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy Is Associated With Lower Risk of Lower Extremity Amputation in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes and Foot Ulcer Without Coded Peripheral Arterial Disease: A Hypothesis-Generating Real-World Cohort Study
abstract: Aims: To compare lower extremity amputation (LEA) risk in adults with Type 2 diabetes and diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) treated with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) versus other glucose-lowering therapy, and to test whether coded peripheral arterial disease (PAD) modifies this association and replicates across comparator classes.

Materials And Methods: This new-user, active-comparator retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (queried 11 July 2026). Adults with Type 2 diabetes and DFU were propensity-score matched 1:1 on 22 covariates, giving 21 325 pairs for the primary comparison. Effect modification by coded PAD (ICD-10 I70.2) was examined in independently matched subgroups. Six sensitivity analyses were pre-specified: 30- and 180-day landmarks, all-cause mortality, background-therapy balancing, limb-severity adjustment and a broadened PAD definition.

Results: GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower 5-year LEA risk than all non-GLP-1 RA therapy (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.54-0.67). The association was confined to the no-PAD stratum (HR: 0.21, 0.13-0.33) and absent where PAD was coded (HR: 0.97, 0.78-1.20); ratio of hazard ratios 0.21 (0.13-0.36; p < 0.001). All-cause mortality was also lower (HR: 0.48, 0.45-0.50). The insulin no-PAD estimate persisted under background-therapy balancing (0.14), limb-severity adjustment (0.16) and 30- and 180-day landmarks (0.28, 0.33). Broadening the PAD definition attenuated the no-PAD association without abolishing it (HR: 0.34, 0.17-0.65).

Conclusions: In Type 2 diabetes with DFU, GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower LEA risk, surviving six pre-specified sensitivity analyses. These observational findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective confirmation.

title: Efficacy and safety of HRS-7535, a novel oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, in participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled by metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase II trial
abstract: Aims/Hypothesis: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HRS-7535, an oral small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), in Chinese participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately managed by metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i).

Methods: This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase II study included participants aged 18-75 years with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 58-97 mmol/mol (7.5-11.0%) and BMI 20.0-35.0 kg/m2 and on stable-dose metformin and sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor therapy for ≥8 weeks prior to screening. Participants were assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive HRS-7535 30 mg, HRS-7535 60 mg or visually matching placebo tablets once daily using a stratified block randomisation method, with treatment assignments concealed until study completion. The primary endpoint was the change in HbA1c from baseline to week 16. Secondary efficacy outcomes included the proportions of participants achieving HbA1c targets of <53 mmol/mol (7.0%) and ≤48 mmol/mol (6.5%), and changes from baseline in fasting body weight to week 16.

Results: A total of 155 participants with a mean baseline HbA1c of 69 mmol/mol (8.5%) were randomly assigned to HRS-7535 30 mg (n=51), HRS-7535 60 mg (n=53) or placebo (n=51). At week 16, the least‑squares mean differences in HbA1c from baseline for the HRS-7535 30 mg, HRS-7535 60 mg and placebo groups were -16 mmol/mol (95% CI -19, -14) (-1.5% [95% CI -1.7, -1.3]), -20 mmol/mol (95% CI -22, -17) (-1.8% [95% CI -2.0, -1.6]) and -4 mmol/mol (95% CI -7, -2) (-0.4% [95% CI -0.6, -0.2]), respectively (p<0.0001 for both HRS-7535 doses vs placebo). The proportions of participants achieving HbA1c <53 mmol/mol (7.0%) were 51.0% in the HRS‑7535 30 mg group, 66.0% in the HRS‑7535 60 mg group, and 9.8% in the placebo group; the corresponding proportions for HbA1c ≤48 mmol/mol (6.5%) were 35.3%, 37.7% and 3.9%, respectively. Body weight loss was -2.4% in the HRS-7535 60 mg group vs -0.7% in the placebo group. Most treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild to moderate, and gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common. No severe hypoglycaemia was reported. The only TEAE that led to treatment discontinuation occurred in the placebo group.

Conclusions/Interpretation: Treatment with HRS-7535 resulted in significant improvements in glycaemic management in participants with type 2 diabetes, and the drug exhibited a favourable safety profile. To address a significant clinical data void, this research focused on the addition of HRS‑7535 to the background regimen of metformin and SGLT2i for glycaemic management in participants with type 2 diabetes. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06393348. Funding This study was funded by Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals.

title: Effects of sitagliptin combined with GTS-21 on improving glycemic control and diabetic nephropathy by anti-apoptosis in Leprdb/db mice
abstract: Objective: Activation of α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) by GTS-21 engages the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway (CAP). This study investigated adding GTS-21 to sitagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor used to increase endogenous GLP-1, confers additional benefit over sitagliptin monotherapy on glycemic control and diabetic nephropathy (DN) in Leprdb/db mice, focusing on anti-apoptotic mechanisms.

Methods: Leptin receptor-deficient (Leprdb/db, 8-week-old) mice were randomized into control (saline), sitagliptin (20 mg/kg), or combination (sitagliptin 20 mg/kg + GTS-21 4 mg/kg) groups for 4 weeks. Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), serum creatinine (Scr), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and IL-6 were measured. Renal histology was evaluated by H&E staining. Apoptosis was assessed by TUNEL staining and cleaved caspase-3 expression. In vitro, HK-2 cells exposed to high glucose (30 mM) were treated with liraglutide (100 nM) and/or GTS-21 (20 nM) to examine apoptosis.

Results: Combination therapy significantly improved glucose tolerance at weeks 1 and 4 (AUC reduction, P = 0.0366 and P = 0.0435 vs control), whereas sitagliptin alone showed no effect. Both treatments reduced Scr (P = 0.0002 for combination; P = 0.0101 for monotherapy), but only combination therapy attenuated renal histological injury (P = 0.002) and decreased IL-6 in serum and kidney (P = 0.0433 and P = 0.0041). Renal apoptosis was also suppressed, with reduced TUNEL-positive cells (P = 0.0043) and cleaved caspase-3 (P = 0.0122). In HK-2 cells, high glucose increased cleaved caspase-3 (P = 0.0324), which was attenuated by liraglutide plus GTS-21 (P = 0.0320).

Conclusions: Add-on GTS-21 to sitagliptin improved glycemic control and attenuated diabetic nephropathy beyond sitagliptin monotherapy in Leprdb/db mice, with reduced renal inflammation and suppressed apoptosis. These findings suggest that combined activation of GLP-1 receptor and α7nAChR signaling warrants further investigation as a renoprotective strategy in diabetic nephropathy.

title: Obesity-Related Asthma: Structure and Inflammation
abstract: Purpose Of Review: Asthma and obesity are affecting children and teenagers at higher rates than previous generations. Epidemiological data link obesity during childhood with the subsequent development of asthma. In this review we describe developmental and inflammatory factors that contribute to asthma severity in children with obesity.

Recent Findings: Asthma driven by obesity is likely due to both structural and inflammatory changes. Excess weight places mechanical stress on the airway thereby reducing lung volumes. In addition, obesity is linked to chronic inflammation. Adipose tissue releases pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α) which drives the airway towards hyperresponsiveness. This "obesity-related asthma" phenotype does not respond well to corticosteroids making these patients difficult to treat. In children and teenagers, treatment options are limited to currently approved asthma medications; however, improvement in asthma control has been observed in adults utilizing metformin and GLP-1 agonists. Children with obesity are more likely to develop asthma. Their asthma symptoms tend to be more frequent and harder to control. With the rate of obesity on the rise, it is paramount to identify the mechanisms underlying systemic inflammation in those with elevated BMIs. This will allow us to find better treatment options for "obesity-related asthma."

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and hair loss: adverse effect, epiphenomenon, or therapeutic paradox?
abstract: Objective: Incretin-based therapies, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual/triple agonists, have revolutionized the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes. However, hair loss has emerged as an adverse event in clinical practice. This review synthesizes the evidence on the prevalence, mechanistic pathways, and clinical course of hair loss associated with semaglutide, tirzepatide, and retatrutide.

Methods: A narrative review was conducted using the PubMed/MEDLINE database. Data were integrated from clinical trials, real-world observational studies, and pharmacovigilance databases to evaluate the oncological and dermatological implications of these therapies.

Results: There is a discrepancy in hair loss prevalence, ranging from 3 to 7% in controlled trials to over 70% in real-world cohorts. Telogen effluvium (TE) is the predominant phenotype, driven primarily by the magnitude and velocity of weight loss rather than drug toxicity. Newer agents like tirzepatide demonstrate stronger associations with hair shedding compared to older GLP-1 RAs. Pharmacovigilance data show inconsistent but significant signals for semaglutide and tirzepatide, with reporting odds ratios indicating a drug-associated risk. Conversely, paradoxical improvements in androgenetic alopecia and inflammatory scarring alopecias have been reported, likely mediated by metabolic normalization and anti-inflammatory effects. Female sex and significant weight reduction (> 10%) were the most robust predictors of hair loss.

Conclusion: Hair loss associated with incretin-based therapies is a biologically complex, threshold-dependent phenomenon reflecting systemic metabolic reprogramming. While predominantly transient and reversible, its psychological impact can compromise treatment adherence. Clinicians should provide proactive counseling, emphasizing the self-limiting nature of TE in this context while monitoring for diverse follicular responses.

title: Risk of recurrent acute pancreatitis with GLP-1 receptor agonists after prior pancreatitis: a systematic review
abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. However, their safety in patients with prior pancreatitis remains uncertain. This systematic review aims to evaluate the risk of recurrent acute pancreatitis (RAP) associated with GLP-1 RA therapy.

Methods: We systematically searched for studies evaluating the safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) or obesity and a history of acute pancreatitis. The primary outcome was recurrent acute pancreatitis. We included studies of adults with prior acute pancreatitis treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists for type 2 diabetes, obesity, or related metabolic conditions. Studies without recurrent acute pancreatitis outcomes, pediatric populations, overlapping cohorts, insufficient data, or non-original publications were excluded.

Results: We included four studies comprising 10,624 patients, of whom 5,427 (51.0%) received GLP-1 receptor agonists. Two studies provided comparative data (5,224 GLP-1 RA users; 5,197 controls). GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with lower odds of recurrent acute pancreatitis than placebo (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.05-1.32) and lower risk than SGLT2 inhibitor use (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.52-0.64). Two additional studies provided recurrence rates among GLP-1 RA users with prior pancreatitis, reporting rates of 9.9% (95% CI 5.8%-16.3%) and 11.9% (95% CI 5.1%-25.8%).

Conclusion: Across the four included studies, GLP-1 receptor agonist use was not associated with an increase in RAP among patients with a prior history of acute pancreatitis. However, comparative evidence was limited to two studies, warranting cautious interpretation of these findings.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Dentistry: Promise, Pitfalls, and Evidence Gaps
abstract: GLP-1RAs (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) have become one of the fastest-growing drug classes worldwide, with prescriptions for obesity treatment increasing by 587% from 2019 to 2024. While their metabolic and cardiovascular benefits are well established, the implications for oral health remain largely unexamined. Preclinical evidence consistently demonstrates anti-inflammatory and osteoprotective effects on periodontal and peri-implant tissues: GLP-1RAs promote osteogenic differentiation of periodontal ligament stem cells, reduce alveolar bone resorption in animal models of periodontitis, and enhance implant osseointegration in diabetic rats. However, these findings are based exclusively on in vitro and animal studies, with only a single retrospective cohort study providing limited clinical data. Conversely, several oral adverse effects have been reported based on pharmacovigilance analyses, including xerostomia, dysgeusia, and anosmia, particularly for semaglutide. Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly nausea (15% to 50%), vomiting (5% to 24%), and gastroesophageal reflux, pose a plausible but unquantified risk for tooth erosion and secondary caries. A bidirectional link between GLP-1 signaling and the oral microbiota, mediated by bacterial dipeptidyl peptidase (DPP)-4-like enzymes that degrade endogenous GLP-1, adds further complexity. Despite this breadth of potential interactions, no prospective study has used any dental outcome as an endpoint in patients receiving GLP-1RAs. This critical appraisal synthesizes the evidence across multiple dental disciplines, grades it in each domain, and identifies the gaps that demand urgent investigation.

title: Nutrient-specific combinatorial secretion of GLP-1 and neurotransmitters in the enteroendocrine L-cell line GLUTag
abstract: Enteroendocrine L cells function as chemosensors in the intestine, secreting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) to signal nutrient ingestion to the brain. Since GLP-1 secretion is induced by a variety of nutrients, including sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids, GLP-1 receptor-expressing neurons are also activated regardless of the nutrient identity, making it unclear how the brain discriminates between different nutrients. By examining vesicle dynamics and extracellular signals associated with GLP-1, glutamate, and ATP in GLUTag cells using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, a technique that selectively visualizes fluorescent molecules near the plasma membrane, we demonstrated that distinct nutrients evoke specific secretory patterns. D-glucose induced the co-secretion of GLP-1, glutamate, and ATP, whereas L-glutamine induced the secretion of GLP-1 and glutamate but not ATP. Butyrate and sucralose, which are also GLP-1 secretagogues, did not induce the secretion of glutamate or ATP. While Ca2+ acts as the trigger for exocytosis, additional regulatory mechanisms are required to generate these distinct secretory patterns. We therefore investigated the cAMP and cGMP pathways and found that neither their activation nor inhibition detectably affected glutamate and ATP secretion, suggesting the involvement of other nutrient-specific signaling pathways. Collectively, our findings suggest that L cells distinguish and encode nutrient identity as combinatorial secretion patterns of GLP-1 and neurotransmitters.

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist-Associated Facial Changes: A Comprehensive Review of Pathophysiology, Clinical Manifestations, Risk Factors, Prevention, and Management
abstract: Facial hollowing, skin laxity, and more prominent folds are increasingly reported during weight loss with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). The term 'Ozempic face' can imply a drug-specific adverse effect, although similar changes occur after other forms of substantial weight loss. This review examines the clinical evidence, proposed mechanisms, and implications for aesthetic care. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for January 2014 through August 2026. Selection was reported using PRISMA 2020 where applicable, followed by narrative synthesis. Of 958 records, 46 reports were included. Serial imaging in 20 patients showed a median 9% reduction in midfacial volume, with greater loss in superficial than deep compartments (11% vs 7%). Regression estimated approximately 7% total midfacial volume loss per 10 kg lost. A FACE-Q short-form has been validated, and a survey of 1,226 participants found more reports of facial volume loss and laxity with greater percentage weight loss. Post-bariatric studies also describe facial deflation and increased apparent age, particularly in older patients and after larger losses. Current evidence favors weight-loss-associated deflation superimposed on baseline anatomy and aging. The independent effect of weight-loss rate and the modifying roles of menopause and hormone therapy remain uncertain. Aesthetic treatment evidence is limited and largely uncontrolled.

title: Effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) mono-agonists on reward processing in animal models: a systematic review
abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), indicated in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, influences reward processing, integral to disparate mental disorders. Emerging evidence suggests that GLP-1 receptor mono-agonists (GLP-1RAs) are potential treatment strategies for select mental disorders. Herein, we systematically review preclinical research documenting how GLP-1 and GLP-1RAs may impact reward function.

Methods: Relevant studies were identified through Web of Science, OVID (MedLINE, Embase, PsycInfo), and PubMed from database inception to June 28, 2026. Preclinical research investigating the association between GLP-1 and select GLP-1RAs and reward function was included. Reward functions assessed were food-, drug-, and sexual-related reward.

Results: A total of 66 studies met inclusion and were synthesised herein. Taken together, results indicate that GLP-1 and GLP-1RAs affect measures of food-related, drug-associated, and sexual behaviours. GLP-1 administration was associated with a reduction in food intake and gross locomotor activity with respect to approaching and engaging in reward-seeking behaviours. When locally administered in selected brain regions of evaluated animal models, exenatide was associated with reduced substance use, food seeking, and sexual behaviours (p < 0.05). Similarly, liraglutide was observed to attenuate substance and food-related rewards (p < 0.05). In addition, semaglutide was demonstrated to reduce substance and sucrose intake, while dulaglutide is reported to reduce substance intake (p < 0.001).

Discussion: Extant preclinical findings demonstrate a trend toward reductions in reward-associated behaviours following GLP-1RA administration. Our findings can also provide rationale and impetus for evaluating GLP-1RAs in the treatment of psychiatric disorders characterised by disturbance in hedonic function and behaviours.

title: Liraglutide ameliorates obese type 2 diabetes by regulating macrophage cholesterol metabolism and H3K27ac modification to promote M2 polarization and adipocyte thermogenic activation
abstract: Obesity-related type 2 diabetes mellitus (O&T2DM) has become a major global public health issue. Chronic low-grade inflammation in adipose tissue is one of its core pathological features, among which excessive infiltration of M1-type macrophages and impaired function of M2-type macrophages are key drivers of inflammation. Liraglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, exhibits significant glucose-lowering, weight-reducing, and anti-inflammatory effects. However, the molecular mechanisms by which liraglutide regulates cholesterol metabolism and epigenetic modifications in adipose tissue macrophages remain to be fully elucidated. A high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin was used to establish an O&T2DM model in male C57BL/6 mice. After 8 weeks of intervention, metabolic phenotypes, adipose tissue macrophage polarization, and cholesterol metabolism-related indicators were assessed. Raw264.7 macrophages were cultured in vitro and stimulated with IFN-γ + LPS to induce M1 polarization. Following liraglutide pretreatment, cell polarization phenotypes, the expression of genes involved in cholesterol metabolic pathways, and histone modification levels were examined. Using shRNA gene silencing, p300 inhibitor intervention, and Acetyl-CoA supplementation experiments in combination with ChIP-qPCR, the central role of the cholesterol metabolism-epigenetic axis in macrophage polarization was elucidated. Finally, a Transwell co-culture system was employed to verify the regulatory effects of liraglutide-reprogrammed macrophages on adipocyte lipid accumulation and energy metabolism. Liraglutide significantly reduced body weight, fasting blood glucose, and HOMA-IR in O&T2DM mice, decreased visceral fat accumulation, and promoted adipose tissue browning. It also increased the proportion of M2 macrophages within adipose tissue and significantly activated the key cholesterol efflux pathway LXRα/ABCA1. In vitro experiments confirmed that liraglutide pretreatment suppressed IFN-γ + LPS-induced M1 polarization and promoted the expression of M2-type markers, upregulated the expression of ABCA1, ABCG1, PPARγ, and LXRα, and increased levels of histone H3K27ac. Mechanistic studies revealed that silencing ABCA1 or LXRα reversed the liraglutide-induced increase in H3K27ac and M2 polarization. Acetyl-CoA supplementation partially restored the macrophage polarization phenotype following ABCA1 silencing. ChIP-qPCR results showed that liraglutide significantly enhanced the enrichment of H3K27ac in the promoter regions of M2 polarization genes and cholesterol metabolism genes. Co-culture experiments demonstrated that liraglutide-reprogrammed macrophages significantly promoted adipocyte thermogenic gene expression, increased mitochondrial membrane potential-dependent staining intensity, and enhanced ATPase activity via paracrine signaling, an effect that was blocked by silencing ABCA1 or LXRα. This study demonstrates that liraglutide activates the ABCA1/LXRα-mediated cholesterol metabolism pathway, upregulates histone H3K27ac modification, and drives macrophage M2 polarization, which in turn induces adipocyte lipid accumulation and mitochondrial metabolic activation via paracrine signaling. These findings provide a new molecular mechanism for the anti-inflammatory and metabolic-improving effects of liraglutide, and also offers a potential epigenetic target for the treatment of O&T2DM.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists-a potential therapy for chronic kidney disease?
abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a significant health burden worldwide, characterized by a gradual decline in kidney function and increased risk of cardiovascular events. Current therapeutic strategies like inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system or sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), while beneficial, often fail to fully halt CKD progression, and a significant residual risk of disease progression persists. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), initially developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D), have emerged as promising agents with pleiotropic effects extending beyond glycemic control and weight loss. Evidence from major cardiovascular outcome trials and dedicated CKD studies demonstrates that GLP-1 RAs can confer significant cardiovascular and nephroprotective benefits in patients with T2D and CKD. These benefits include reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events, slowing of kidney disease progression (as measured by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline), and decreased albuminuria. The mechanisms underlying these effects are complex and involve multiple pathways, including anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and antioxidative actions, as well as improvements in hemodynamic parameters. We provide a comprehensive overview of the current clinical and preclinical evidence supporting the use of GLP-1 RAs in CKD. We discuss the proposed mechanisms of action by which GLP-1 RAs exert their nephroprotective effects and explore the potential for these agents to improve kidney outcomes across a broad spectrum of patients with CKD and critically evaluate the potential risks and safety profile associated with GLP-1 RA use.

title: How lipid ingestion is sensed: the mechanisms underlying intestinal hormone secretion
abstract: Dietary lipids are potent stimulators of intestinal hormone secretion, which plays a central role in the regulation of digestion, appetite, glucose homeostasis, and lipid metabolism. Following digestion in the intestinal lumen, lipid-derived molecules are detected through complementary mechanisms involving lipid transporters, nutrient-sensing receptors, intracellular metabolic pathways, and bile acid signaling. These pathways couple nutrient availability to the secretion of enteroendocrine hormones, including glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), peptide YY (PYY), cholecystokinin (CCK), ghrelin and serotonin, thereby coordinating local and systemic metabolic responses. In the small intestine, CD36 contributes to lipid uptake and sensing, while intracellular lipid processing and chylomicron formation influence hormone secretion. Bile acids facilitate lipid digestion and absorption and further regulate enteroendocrine function through receptor-mediated signaling pathways. This review examines the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying intestinal lipid sensing, with particular emphasis on the roles of CD36, chylomicron formation, bile acid signaling, and nutrient-sensing receptors in the regulation of enteroendocrine hormone secretion.

title: Targeted Gastrointestinal Delivery of mRNA Lipid Nanoparticles Enables Systemic Vaccination and Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Metabolic Therapy
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) administered parenterally often show poor localization to multiple tissue types, including the pancreas and gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Furthermore, patients typically prefer orally administered drugs to those that are given parenterally. We therefore investigated whether GI LNP administration to buccal, gastric, small intestinal, colonic, and rectal submucosal tissues could simultaneously circumvent parenteral administration while enhancing LNP delivery to previously inaccessible locations. We found that, in addition to local targeting, gastric LNP administration achieved an order of magnitude greater pancreas delivery in rodents than intravenous administration. Gastric dosing of glucagon-like peptide-1 mRNA also improved blood glucose regulation in mice compared with phosphate-buffered saline controls. Additionally, we found that buccal LNP administration targeted local and lymphatic tissues. Furthermore, dosing mice with ovalbumin mRNA resulted in equivalent immunoglobulin G blood titers to those of intramuscular delivery. These results suggest that GI administration can reprogram LNP biodistribution, expanding therapeutic opportunities for both local and systemic nucleic acid delivery.

title: Efsubaglutide Alfa: A Comprehensive Pharmacological Review
abstract: Efsubaglutide alfa (also known as supaglutide) is a long-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) engineered as a GLP-1 analogue fused to a human immunoglobulin G2 (IgG2) fragment crystallisable (Fc) domain. This narrative review summarises published and publicly available evidence on efsubaglutide alfa pharmacology, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, dose-exposure-response relationships, drug-drug interaction potential, and clinical efficacy and safety in type 2 diabetes (T2D) and overweight/obesity. Efsubaglutide alfa has prolonged exposure (terminal half-life approximately 182-215 h) and low steady-state fluctuation, but dosing-interval selection should not be inferred from half-life alone. Available population pharmacokinetic and exposure-response analyses indicate that steady-state trough concentration is most informative for glycaemic response, whereas average and peak concentrations contribute to interpretation of weight response and gastrointestinal tolerability. Across available studies, predominantly conducted in Chinese populations, efsubaglutide alfa shows class-consistent improvements in glycaemic control and body weight, with gastrointestinal adverse events as the main tolerability limitation. Exploratory every 2-week dosing and post-discontinuation glycaemic durability findings remain hypothesis-generating. No head-to-head comparative trials dedicated cardiovascular or renal outcome trials, or large globally diverse datasets are yet available; therefore, the current evidence should be interpreted as a clinical pharmacology synthesis rather than a comparative positioning claim.

title: Thyroid Disease in the Era of Obesity and Glucagon-Like-Peptide-1 Agonists
abstract: The thyroid gland plays a critical role in regulating metabolism. Dysfunctions in the thyroid gland are closely associated with alterations in body mass index. The relationship between thyroid disease and obesity is complex and bidirectional with hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism influencing body weight. In the last decade, there has been an increase in the incidence of thyroid cancer as well as the prevalence of obesity. Emerging weight loss therapies and their potential association with thyroid malignancy remains an active area of investigation. Additionally, important perioperative and surgical considerations must be addressed in patients undergoing thyroidectomy.

title: Efficacy of low-dose pioglitazone in combination with exenatide on glucose control in patients with T2DM
abstract: Introduction: Pioglitazone effectively reduces glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in patients with diabetes. The aim of the present study is to examine the safety and efficacy of lower doses of pioglitazone in combination with exenatide in EDICT and Qatar studies
