Research Design And Methods: Newly diagnosed, drug-naïve patients were started on combination therapy with metformin, plus pioglitazone plus exenatide in the EDICT study. Poorly controlled patients with long-standing diabetes on the maximal dose of metformin plus sulfonylurea were started on a combination of pioglitazone plus exenatide. Patients in both studies were followed for 3 years. Patients were stratified according to the pioglitazone dose used, and the efficacy of HbA1c lowering, change in body weight, and incidence of ankle edema were related to pioglitazone dose.

Results: The reduction in HbA1c was comparable in patients receiving 15, 30, and 45 mg of pioglitazone in both the EDICT and Qatar studies. However, the mean change in body weight was dose-dependent. Subjects receiving 15 mg of pioglitazone experienced a mean weight loss (~1.5 kg) in both studies compared with a mean weight gain in subjects receiving 30 and 45 mg doses (1–5 kg).

Conclusion: When combined with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, the lower doses of pioglitazone produce a comparable reduction in HbA1c with a lower risk of weight gain than the maximal approved pioglitazone dose (45 mg), especially in individuals with obesity.

title: Transgenerational effects of paternal in utero arsenic exposure on MASLD-like phenotypes
abstract: Previous study indicated that early-life arsenic (As) exposure caused adulthood metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)-like phenotypes. This study aimed to investigate the impacts of paternal in utero As exposure on MASLD-like phenotypes in offspring. Pregnant dams received NaAsO2 (15 mg/L) through drinking water. In utero As-exposed male pups were designated as F0 mice and mated with untreated females to produce F1 offspring. F1 males were subsequently mated with untreated females to generate F2 offspring, both without further As exposure. MASLD-like phenotypes were evaluated in F1 and F2 offspring. On PNW28, As-exposed F1 offspring exhibited hepatic steatosis, glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and obesity, accompanied by altered metabolic hormones, such as GLP-1, GIP, insulin, leptin, and ADPN. The core MASLD-like phenotypes, including hepatic steatosis, glucose intolerance and insulin resistance, exhibited transgenerational transmission from F1 to F2 generations. In F2 offspring, these metabolic abnormalities were detected at PNW45 but not at PNW28, predominantly in male offspring. In contrast, As-induced obesity and metabolic hormone alterations exhibited transgenerational attenuation. F2 offspring retained only adipocyte hypertrophy, with no significant changes in white or brown adipose tissue weight. Furthermore, hormonal alterations in F2 mice were limited to reduced GLP-1 levels in females and elevated insulin and ADPN levels in males, while other altered hormones normalized. This study is the first to confirm that paternal in utero As exposure causes MASLD-like phenotypes in F1 offspring and transgenerational transmission to F2 generation.

title: Previous bariatric surgery before knee arthroplasty: A cautious interpretation
abstract: We read with interest the nationwide register-based study by Aljuboori et al. examining previous bariatric surgery (BAS) and reintervention after knee arthroplasty. The authors appropriately state that their findings do not establish a benefit of BAS or negate the influence of residual obesity. We highlight several interpretive constraints. Matching on body mass index (BMI) at arthroplasty conditions on a post-exposure variable, while restriction to patients who ultimately underwent arthroplasty excludes those who improved sufficiently to avoid surgery. The 95% confidence interval for 2-year reintervention supports the absence of a statistically detectable difference, not equivalence or non-inferiority. Two-year follow-up may miss later mechanical failures, and exclusion of approximately 9% of screened records, including patients with missing BMI, may introduce additional selection bias. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists remain an important future perspective. Overall, the study provides useful short-term conditional observational evidence among selected arthroplasty recipients with comparable BMI, rather than an estimate of the overall causal effect of BAS before knee arthroplasty.
journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA

title: Audiovestibular adverse event reporting profiles of GLP-1 receptor agonists: A case-case pharmacovigilance study using FDA AEMS data
abstract: Purpose: To characterize and compare audiovestibular adverse-event reporting patterns among glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Monitoring System (AEMS).

Methods: We performed a retrospective case-level analysis of AEMS reports through 2026 Q1. Reports naming exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, lixisenatide, or semaglutide as the primary suspect and containing at least one prespecified audiovestibular MedDRA preferred term were deduplicated by case. Among adequately represented agents, phenotype composition was compared using chi-square testing, and case-case comparative reporting odds ratios (cRORs) were calculated for six common preferred terms with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Time to onset (TTO) was summarized descriptively.

Results: We identified 1,950 unique reports: exenatide 576, liraglutide 192, dulaglutide 622, lixisenatide 1, and semaglutide 559. Hypoacusis (46.9%), vertigo (27.7%), tinnitus (12.7%), and deafness (7.9%) were most frequent. Phenotype composition differed across the four adequately represented agents (chi-square = 78.12, P < 0.001; Cramer V = 0.142). Dulaglutide reports were enriched for hypoacusis (cROR 3.06, 95% CI 2.51-3.74), whereas liraglutide and semaglutide reports were enriched for vertigo and tinnitus. Median TTO was 3 days (IQR 0-35), but valid dates were available for only 19.3% of reports.
Conclusion: Individual GLP-1 RAs showed distinct audiovestibular reporting compositions. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish incidence, comparative safety, or causality.
journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery

title: Effects of tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist) on cardiorenal biomarkers and functional capacity in heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background: Tirzepatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, has demonstrated clinical benefits in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and obesity. However, its effects on cardiorenal biomarkers and functional capacity have not been comprehensively synthesized. We hypothesized that tirzepatide produces significant reductions in cardiorenal biomarkers and improvements in functional capacity compared to placebo or standard of care.

Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42026137255) searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to April 17, 2026, without restrictions. Randomized controlled trials and prospective observational studies reporting NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score (KCCQ-CSS), 6-minute walk test (6 MWT), or renal outcomes with tirzepatide vs placebo or standard of care were included. Data were pooled using random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment.

Results: Seven studies (5 RCTs, 2 observational; 5406 participants) were included. Tirzepatide significantly reduced hsCRP by 34.3% (95% CI: -38.4% to -30.1%; P < .0001; I2 = 0.0%; 6 studies) and NT-proBNP by 17.6% (95% CI: -26.7% to -8.5%; P = .0001; I2 = 58.1%; 3 studies). In the SUMMIT trial, KCCQ-CSS improved by 5.1 points (P < .001) and 6 MWT by 15.8 m (P = .004). Single-trial data demonstrated estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) preservation (+2.90 mL/min/1.73 m2/year; 95% CI: 0.94 to 4.86) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio reduction (-25.0%; 95% CI: -36.0% to -13.0%).

Conclusion: Tirzepatide produces consistent anti-inflammatory effects and significant natriuretic peptide reductions, supported by moderate Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation certainty. Evidence for functional and renal outcomes remains limited to single-trial analyses and should be considered hypothesis-generating pending larger dedicated heart failure trials.
Prospero Registration: CRD42026137255.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: Recovery from liraglutide-induced acute liver injury assessed for causality using the updated RUCAM as global gold standard: A case report and literature review
abstract: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) widely used for managing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity. Reports of liraglutide-associated hepatotoxicity are exceedingly rare. To our knowledge, this is the 9th case of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) caused by liraglutide to be reported. We present a case of a 40-year-old Chinese woman who developed acute liver injury with elevated liver enzymes following 2 weeks of liraglutide treatment for T2DM. Causality was assessed using the updated RUCAM scale, yielding a score of 7, indicating probable DILI, and the diagnosis was further confirmed by liver biopsy. Liver enzyme levels normalized after discontinuing the drug and administering liver-protective treatment within 3 weeks. Furthermore, this case report includes a comprehensive review of all published cases of liraglutide-associated DILI, emphasizing the necessity of regular hepatic-biochemistry monitoring in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists such as liraglutide and providing meaningful evidence regarding their hepatotoxic risk.
journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology and therapeutics

title: The Effects of GLP-1RA-Based and SGLT2 Inhibitor Therapy on Perirenal Adipose Tissue in CKD Patients
abstract: Aims: Perirenal adipose tissue (PRAT) surrounds the kidney and may contribute to chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression. SGLT2 inhibitors have been associated with reductions in this depot, but PRAT has not been quantified under GLP-1RA-based therapy in CKD. We assessed ultrasound-measured PRAT thickness under both treatments and whether changes tracked weight loss.

Materials And Methods: Adults with CKD Stages 1-4 in the prospective ADIPO-CKD inception cohort underwent ultrasound at baseline and at the 8-month visit. PRAT thickness was the mean of right and left measurements; epicardial adipose tissue and body composition were also assessed. Patients received neither drug class (reference), SGLT2i or GLP-1RA-based therapy. Follow-up PRAT was analysed by covariance analysis adjusted for baseline.

Results: Of 277 patients, 80 had paired studies (32 reference, 24 SGLT2i, 24 GLP-1RA-based; body weight 46-122 kg). PRAT was unchanged in the reference group (+0.035 cm, p = 0.376) and decreased with SGLT2i (-0.273 cm, -20.4%, p = 0.0006) and GLP-1RA-based therapy (-0.463 cm, -36.2%, p < 0.0001). Adjusted differences versus reference were -0.227 cm (95% CI -0.417 to -0.036) and -0.433 cm (-0.622 to -0.244); under multiple imputations, -0.218 cm (-0.482 to +0.046) and -0.421 cm (-0.693 to -0.149). GLP-1RA-based therapy reduced body weight, fat mass and visceral fat area; SGLT2i only body weight, modestly. PRAT change correlated with none.

Conclusions: In CKD, both drug classes were associated with lower follow-up PRAT, not explained by measured body-composition change. Under multiple imputations, both estimates were essentially unchanged, though the SGLT2i interval included no difference. PRAT may represent a candidate depot-specific target.
Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07309094 (ADIPO-CKD).

title: Nurse Practitioner-Led Integration of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients With Obesity-Related Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Prospective Clinical Effectiveness Study
abstract: Background: Obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by systemic inflammation and reduced functional capacity. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve symptoms and weight in randomized trials, but uptake in routine cardiovascular practice is inconsistent.
Objective: The purpose of this study was to evaluate a structured nurse practitioner-led program for GLP-1 RA initiation in obesity-related HFpEF.

Methods: Prospective 12-month, single-center pre-post effectiveness study at a U.S. urban academic outpatient cardiology clinic. Adults with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45%, body mass index ≥30 kg/m2, New York Heart Association class II-III symptoms, and at least 1 cardiometabolic comorbidity were enrolled. The intervention included registry-based identification, baseline assessment, patient education, protocolized titration, and longitudinal follow-up. Each participant's 12-month preenrollment period served as a comparator. The primary outcome was GLP-1 RA initiation and 12-month persistence.

Results: Of 156 enrolled, 128 (82.1%) completed follow-up. Mean age 67.4 ± 11.2 years; 61.7% female; 43.8% Black. GLP-1 RA use rose from 7.8% to 92.2% (87.5% at target dose). Mean weight decreased 6.2 ± 3.8 kg, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score improved 16.6 ± 11.3 points, and 6-minute walk distance rose 48.3 ± 36.2 m (all P < .001). Systolic blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c (diabetic subgroup), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide all decreased significantly. Heart failure hospitalization fell from 18.2% to 4.7% (P = .002). Gastrointestinal symptoms were most common; 4.7% discontinued for intolerance.

Conclusions: A structured nurse practitioner-led cardiometabolic program was associated with high GLP-1 RA initiation and persistence and with clinically meaningful improvements in symptoms, function, and hospitalization in obesity-related HFpEF.

title: The therapeutic potential of GLP-1 receptor agonists in central nervous system diseases: immune cell modulation and neuroinflammation
abstract: Introduction: Central nervous system (CNS) diseases impose a substantial global burden; however, effective treatments remain limited. Neuroinflammation contributes to the development and progression of various CNS diseases. Preclinical evidence suggests that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) may alleviate neuroinflammation by modulating immune cell-related processes, showing therapeutic potential in CNS diseases.

Areas Covered: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science for literature published between 2016 and 2026. We summarize preclinical evidence that various GLP-1RAs alleviate neuroinflammation across different CNS diseases through modulation of peripheral and central immune cells, focusing on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, T lymphocytes, microglia, astrocytes, and their crosstalk, and discuss related clinical translation and challenges.

Expert Opinion: Repurposing GLP-1RAs, including exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, and dulaglutide, may provide a therapeutic option for CNS diseases. However, most mechanistic evidence remains preclinical, and clinical efficacy has not been established. Future studies should integrate neuroimmune biomarkers with clinical outcomes to determine whether immunomodulatory effects translate into clinical benefit. Future research should also distinguish direct CNS effects from peripheral metabolic effects across different GLP-1RAs and identify appropriate patient populations. The effects of age, sex, comorbidities, and concomitant medications on efficacy and safety, as well as potential adverse effects of long-term use, also warrant attention.

title: Body composition changes in patients on GLP-1 receptor agonists undergoing an intensive cardiac rehabilitation program
abstract: Aims: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for type 2 diabetes and obesity and produce significant weight loss. However, concerns have emerged about potential loss of skeletal muscle mass (SMM) with pharmacologic weight reduction, particularly in older adults at risk for sarcopaenia. The effects of GLP-1 RA therapy on SMM among patients participating in intensive cardiac rehabilitation (ICR) remain incompletely characterized.

Methods And Results: A retrospective cohort study of 468 patients enrolled in a structured Pritikin ICR programme at UC San Diego Health between 2017 and 2024 was performed. At programme initiation, 67 patients were taking GLP-1 RAs with a median duration of 231 days (IQR 144-400). Body composition was assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis at baseline and programme completion. Outcomes included SMM and fat mass (FM). Multivariable regression models adjusted for age, sex, baseline body mass index (BMI), diabetes status, and baseline fitness (measured in metabolic equivalents of tasks [METs]). Both groups improved in METs with ICR (P < 0.001). At baseline, patients on GLP-1 RAs had higher BMI and percent FM compared with non-users, but no differences were observed in SMM. In adjusted analyses, GLP-1 RA use was not associated with significantly different per cent change in SMM from baseline to ICR programme completion compared with no GLP-1 RA use (β = 0.62%, 95% CI -0.62 to 1.86; P = 0.326). Similarly, there was no significant between-group difference in per cent change in FM (β = 3.01%, 95% CI -1.64 to 7.66; P = 0.204).

Conclusion: GLP-1 RA use during ICR was not associated with significantly different SMM changes after adjustment for measured covariates. These findings support the integration of GLP-1 based pharmacotherapy with structured exercise programmes.

title: The evolving role of metabolic and bariatric surgery in contemporary clinical practice
abstract: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) has long been considered the most effective long-term treatment for severe obesity and its associated comorbidities, including type-2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome, and cardiovascular disease. Beyond weight loss, MBS has been associated with improved glycaemic and metabolic control, lower apnoea burden, reduced risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, and improved overall survival. In the last few years, the use of safe and effective weight-loss medications has revolutionized the management of patients with obesity, and may in the future influence referral patterns for MBS. Future research is therefore warranted to clarify the integration between MBS and these novel pharmacological opportunities, with the aim of optimizing patient selection and therapeutic pathways. The aim of this narrative review is therefore to describe the role of MBS in contemporary clinical practice, considering the evolving landscape of pharmacological approaches to treat patients with obesity.

title: Extracellular vesicle signature is associated with cardio-metabolic improvement after bariatric surgery
abstract: Aims: Bariatric surgery (BS) reduces obesity-associated systemic inflammation leading to multiple cardiovascular (CV) and metabolic benefits. Here, we tested whether measuring vaso-inflammatory cytokines, gut hormones, and circulating extracellular vesicles (EV) provide vaso-inflammatory-metabolic signatures that better correlate to CV-metabolic outcomes after BS, compared to a standard clinical assessment including body weight (BW) loss and traditional CV risk factors.

Methods And Results: In 111 patients with severe obesity, conventional clinical-biochemical parameters and non-conventional vaso-inflammatory-metabolic markers were analysed at baseline, after 1- (T12) and 3-years (T36) post-BS and were associated to post-surgical BW loss and improvement of patients' CV-metabolic profile. Body weight decreased from a median of 111 to 77 Kg at T36 (30 Kg and 32.8% BMI cumulative reduction), and all traditional CV risk factors improved after BS. However, the baseline evaluation of these parameters was unable to discriminate patients according to their CV-metabolic outcome, after BS. This objective was achieved combining the decrease in circulating serum amyloid associated protein, IL-6, TNF-α, and insulin after BS, together with the increase of GLP-1, ghrelin, PYY and bile acids, and changes in EV profiling. Of note, a specific signature given by the reduced expression of several surface antigens carried by EVs and specific single EV markers (i.e. derived from endothelium, platelets, inflammatory cells), successfully discriminated patients at baseline according to their CV-metabolic post-surgical outcome.

Conclusion: Non-conventionally measured vaso-inflammatory-metabolic signatures, and in particular EV profiling, are associated with CV-metabolic outcome after BS and may be integrated to conventional parameters to improve the management and risk stratification of these patients.

title: Energy-Based Devices for GLP-1 Receptor Agonist-Associated Facial Aging: A Tissue-Specific Safety Framework
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA)-associated rapid weight loss may be accompanied by facial changes resembling accelerated aging, colloquially termed "Ozempic face". In this review, this proposed phenotype is termed GLP-1RA-associated facial accelerated aging (GLP-1RA-FAA) and is characterized primarily by facial volume loss and skin laxity, with possible but incompletely characterized alterations in dermal-adipose support, adipose-derived stem-cell biology, fibroblast-extracellular-matrix homeostasis, and facial muscle. Demand for energy-based device (EBD) treatment in this population is increasing; however, whether conventional EBD parameters are effective or safe in medication-associated facial volume depletion is unknown. A narrative review was informed by structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from January 2000 through August 31, 2026. Evidence was selected for clinical directness and relevance to radiofrequency, high-intensity focused ultrasound, broadband light, microwave, extracorporeal shock wave therapy, diode laser, and synchronized radiofrequency with high-intensity facial electrical stimulation. Available modalities differ in their intended tissue depth and in the potential relevance of three conceptual targets: preservation of adipose tissue, dermal fibroblast-extracellular-matrix remodeling, and facial muscle-SMAS support. Preclinical body-contouring studies suggest that sustained subcutaneous heating in the approximate 43-45°C range can be associated with adipocyte injury or apoptosis; however, no facial thermal dose threshold has been established, particularly in GLP-1RA-treated patients. No individual EBD modality has demonstrated simultaneous restoration of adipose, dermal, and muscle-related targets in prospective GLP-1RA-specific studies. Conservative control of treatment depth, careful avoidance of unnecessary deep energy deposition in volume-depleted regions, investigation of low-intensity dermal remodeling strategies, and evaluation of muscle-targeting approaches are proposed as research considerations. These concepts are hypothesis generating and do not constitute clinical recommendations or standards of care. Prospective controlled studies in well-characterized GLP-1RA-treated populations are required before device-specific protocols can be adopted.

title: Adherence and Persistence to Injectable versus Oral GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Comparative Systematic Review and Analysis
abstract: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) requires sustained glycemic control to prevent long-term complications. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are effective therapies, traditionally administered via injection. The introduction of oral formulations, such as oral semaglutide, may improve patient adherence and persistence.

Methods: A systematic review with descriptive pooled synthesis was conducted using studies identified from PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and relevant real-world observational data sources. Adherence and persistence outcomes were summarized and compared descriptively between injectable and oral GLP-1 RAs.

Results: Across the included total of 13 studies and medical records, data from 1348 patients were summarized. Oral GLP-1 RAs were associated with higher reported adherence (70.8% vs 62.4%) and persistence (62.1% vs 47.8%) compared with injectable formulations. A chi-square test of independence showed that the difference in adherence between oral and injectable GLP-1 was significant; (χ 2 = 10.8, p < 0.01). Similarly, chi-square test showed that the observed variation in persistence between Oral-GLP vs injectable GLP-1 was also significant (χ 2 = 37.9, p < 0.001). Injectable therapies were associated with higher rates of adverse events, particularly injection-site reactions.

Conclusion: Oral GLP-1 RAs may be associated with improved adherence and persistence in patients with T2DM. These findings suggest that formulation choice may influence long-term diabetes treatment continuation, although further study-level meta-analytic research is needed.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy

title: Semaglutide Use and Risk of Diabetic Retinopathy and Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy in Type 2 Diabetes: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), including semaglutide, are increasingly adopted for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) due to improvements in glycemic control and weight loss. Although concerns have been raised about a potential association with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), this relationship remains uncertain.

Objective And Method: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, we reviewed patients with T2DM treated with semaglutide at Rajavithi Hospital. A Kaplan-Meier time-to-event analysis was conducted to estimate the incidence of NAION and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) progression.

Results: Among 100 patients with T2DM treated with semaglutide, no cases of NAION were observed over 299 person-years of follow-up (crude incidence rate: 0 per 1,000 person-years; 95% CI: 0-6.17). PDR and diabetic macular edema (DME) were the main findings, accounting for 10.00% and 3.00%, respectively. Ophthalmic complications group (13 patients) demonstrated higher body mass index (23.72 ± 1.38 vs 21.18 ± 2.51 kg/m2; p < 0.001), higher fasting plasma glucose (197.77 ± 48.28 vs 148.70 ± 27.84 mg/dL; p < 0.001), and worse baseline best-corrected visual acuity ([BCVA]; 1.71 ± 0.74 vs 0.45 ± 0.39 logarithm of the Minimum Angle of Resolution [logMAR]; p < 0.001). Final BCVA remained significantly worse in the complication group (p < 0.001). Ophthalmic complication remained stable over the 60-month follow-up; longer diabetes duration (>60 months) was modestly associated with better survival (log-rank p = 0.049). By contrast, other demographic, optic disc characteristics, and concomitant systemic vascular diseases were not significantly linked to ophthalmic complication.

Conclusions: No NAION events were observed over 299 person-years; however, the limited sample size precludes definitive conclusions about NAION risk. A modest trend toward higher proliferative diabetic retinopathy rates suggests that ophthalmic monitoring may be warranted in at-risk patients. Larger prospective studies are needed to confirm these preliminary findings.

title: Tirzepatide use in adolescents with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD): A case series
abstract: Pediatric obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) prevalence has risen markedly over the past decade. Due to transition delays and workforce shortages, pediatric specialists often manage patients into young adulthood, and thus familiarity with adult pharmacotherapies for MASLD is essential. Currently, Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, is approved for adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and F2-F3 fibrosis; however, dual and triple agonists are being evaluated. Tirzepatide, a dual agonist that targets gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) and the GLP-1 receptor, has demonstrated superior weight reduction to Semaglutide (-20.2% vs. -13.7%) with a more favorable gastrointestinal adverse effect profile. Adult literature has demonstrated its effectiveness in MASH resolution, and pediatric data suggest it is safe in younger populations. Currently, there are no pediatric/adolescent studies exploring the use of Tirzepatide in MASLD. We present our experience using Tirzepatide in two adolescent patients with obesity and MASLD.

title: Beyond Weight Loss: Facial Remodeling Associated with GLP-1 Receptor Agonists-A Systematic Review and Therapeutic Framework
abstract: Background: Facial volume depletion and skin laxity have increasingly been reported during weight loss associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) treatment. However, these changes are not recognized as a distinct clinical entity and may overlap with those occurring after other forms of rapid or massive weight loss. Evidence regarding their treatment remains limited.

Methods: This systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261415797). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception to June 5, 2026. Clinical studies evaluating interventions for facial changes associated with GLP-1RA-related weight loss were included. Study characteristics, interventions, outcomes, safety, and methodological limitations were synthesized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools.

Results: Four uncontrolled observational studies involving 98 treated participants met the eligibility criteria. Two studies enrolled exclusively patients receiving GLP-1RAs or related incretin-based medications, whereas two included mixed weight-loss etiologies. Investigated interventions included injectable biostimulators and fillers, endotissutal bipolar radiofrequency, and a topical formulation. All studies reported favorable within-group findings; however, heterogeneous populations, weight-loss trajectories, interventions, outcomes, and follow-up durations, together with the absence of comparator groups, precluded conclusions regarding treatment effectiveness or superiority.

Conclusions: The available evidence is preliminary and insufficient to support a validated therapeutic algorithm. The proposed framework is hypothesis-generating and integrates limited review findings with established principles of post-weight-loss facial rejuvenation. Comparative studies evaluating surgical and nonsurgical interventions are required.

Level Of Evidence V: This journal requires that authors assign a level of evidence to each article. For a full description of these Evidence-Based Medicine ratings, please refer to the Table of Contents or the online Instructions to Authors www.springer.com/00266 . Trial registration number PROSPERO Registration CRD420261415797.

title: Acute Effects of Acarbose and Canagliflozin, Alone and in Combination, on Postprandial GLP-1 and Glycaemic Responses in Post-Bariatric Hypoglycaemia: A Randomised Crossover Study
abstract: Aim: To evaluate the acute effects of acarbose and canagliflozin, alone and in combination, on postprandial total GLP-1 and glycaemic responses during a mixed meal test in adults with post-bariatric hypoglycaemia (PBH).

Materials And Methods: This single-centre, randomised, four-period crossover physiological study included 12 adults with PBH after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Participants underwent meal tests after placebo, acarbose 100 mg, canagliflozin 300 mg or combination treatment. Co-primary outcomes were total GLP-1 area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) from 0 to 240 min and peak total GLP-1 concentration. Secondary outcomes included glucose, insulin, C-peptide, GIP and glucagon.

Results: Eleven participants completed all four visits and all 12 were analysed. During the placebo mixed meal test, 3/12 participants reached glucose < 3.0 mmol/L, while 10/12 reached < 3.5 mmol/L and 10/12 reported postprandial symptoms suggestive of hypoglycaemia. All active treatments reduced peak glucose and glucose excursion versus placebo, without changing glucose nadir or glucose AUC 0-240 min. Peak insulin, insulin AUC 0-240 min, peak C-peptide and C-peptide AUC 0-240 min were lower with both acarbose-containing regimens than with placebo. Total GLP-1 AUC 0-240 min did not differ between treatments, while peak total GLP-1 was higher with canagliflozin than with the other treatments. Peak GIP was lower with acarbose-containing regimens than with placebo, and GIP AUC 0-240 min was lower with combination treatment than with placebo. Peak glucagon was higher with combination treatment than with placebo.

Conclusions: Acarbose-containing regimens attenuated postprandial beta-cell responses, but adding canagliflozin did not provide clear additive benefit over acarbose alone on the prespecified GLP-1 outcomes or glucose nadir. Changes in glycaemic and beta-cell responses without a parallel reduction in total GLP-1 suggest that mechanisms beyond GLP-1 secretion contribute to the acute postprandial phenotype in PBH.

title: The Metabolic-Dermatologic Axis: GLP-1/GIP Agonists as Emerging Immunometabolic Therapies for Obesity-Associated Skin Disease
abstract: Obesity is increasingly recognized as a systemic determinant of dermatologic disease rather than merely a comorbidity accompanying skin disorders. Excess adiposity promotes insulin resistance, adipose-tissue dysfunction, chronic low-grade inflammation, altered immune responses, vascular abnormalities, mechanical stress, and impaired tissue repair, thereby influencing the development and severity of inflammatory and metabolic dermatoses. Psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), acanthosis nigricans, intertriginous disease, and impaired wound healing exemplify conditions in which metabolic and cutaneous pathways are closely interconnected. This relationship provides the biological basis for the concept of a metabolic-dermatologic axis, in which adipose tissue, systemic metabolism, immune activation, and cutaneous inflammation interact bidirectionally.

title: Cutaneous Effects and Aesthetic Management of Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists: A Narrative Review
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are among the most widely prescribed medications in the United States, with expanding indications beyond type-2 diabetes mellitus to include obesity, cardiovascular risk reduction, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. As their utilization increases, the dermatologic effects of these agents become increasingly relevant to clinical practice. This narrative review examines the cutaneous effects of GLP-1RAs across six domains: facial volume loss and accelerated skin aging, changes in hair density, wound healing, striae distensae and body skin laxity, cutaneous adverse events, and emerging therapeutic benefits in inflammatory skin disease. Herein, we review proposed mechanisms and evidence-based management strategies for each domain, including biostimulatory fillers, energy-based devices, nutritional optimization, and pharmacologic interventions. Prospective, large-scale clinical studies are needed to clarify mechanisms of GLP-1RA modulation in skin and to guide management of these AEs as next-generation agents enter clinical practice.

title: Characterizing the adverse event profile of semaglutide: A comprehensive U.S. food and drug administration adverse event reporting system-based pharmacovigilance study
abstract: Background: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, is increasingly used for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. Given its expanding clinical use, a comprehensive evaluation of its safety profile using real-world data is warranted. This study aimed to characterize adverse event signals associated with semaglutide using the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).

Methods: Adverse event reports associated with semaglutide were extracted from the FAERS database from 2004 Q1 to 2025 Q3. After data extraction and screening, cases in which semaglutide was recorded as the primary suspected drug were included. Adverse events were classified according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) at the preferred term (PT) and system organ class (SOC) levels. Signal detection was performed using disproportionality methods, including reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), relative reporting ratio (RRR), and empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM).

Results: A total of 43,754 reports were identified. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequently reported system organ class, with nausea (n = 5637; 12.88%), vomiting (n = 4097; 9.36%), diarrhoea (n = 3276; 7.49%) and constipation (n = 2257; 5.16%) being the most frequently reported adverse events. Impaired gastric emptying (n = 2200; 5.03%) showed a markedly elevated reporting signal. Significant signals were also observed for metabolic and nutritional events, including decreased appetite (n = 2221; 5.08%), dehydration (n = 1231; 2.81%) and diabetic ketoacidosis. Notably, high disproportionality signals were detected for weight loss poor and optic ischaemic neuropathy. Additional signals involved psychiatric, renal and hepatobiliary systems. The consistency of findings across multiple statistical methods, including empirical Bayes geometric mean, supports the robustness of the detected signals.

Conclusion: Semaglutide is primarily associated with gastrointestinal and metabolic adverse events consistent with its pharmacological effects; however, several less common but potentially important safety signals were identified. These findings highlight the need for continued pharmacovigilance and careful clinical monitoring in real-world use.

title: Cardiorenal Protective Glucose-Lowering Treatment Patterns in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Based on a Real-World Study: A Clinical Phenotype Cluster Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Cardiorenal protective glucose-lowering treatments (CPT), consisting of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), are widely applied in clinical management of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This study aimed to identify distinct clinical phenotypes linked to CPT prescribing patterns and construct a multilevel correlation framework for standardized CPT clinical application.

Methods: Data were extracted from the baseline dataset of an observational registry cohort study across 61 medical centers between 2023 and 2024. Based on multiple factors, clinical phenotypes of patients were identified via the Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) clustering algorithm, CPT utilization was compared across different phenotypes.

Results: A total of 9000 patients with T2DM were enrolled [median age 55 (46, 63) years, 60.8% male and 39.2% female, median diabetes duration 5.37 (0.85, 11.44) years]. Three clinically distinct phenotypes were identified: Cluster 1 [older patients with high atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk], Cluster 2 (metabolically stable patients without cardiorenal risk), and Cluster 3 (younger patients with obesity, high metabolic risk and short diabetes duration). The CPT utilization rates of the three clusters were 49.0%, 44.1% and 51.1%, respectively (P < 0.001), with Cluster 3 having the highest rate. Cluster 2 was dominated by SGLT2is monotherapy (73.1%). Cluster 3 showed a marked preference for GLP-1RAs-based regimens (43.6% in total), whereas Cluster 1 had an intermediate proportion of GLP-1RAs-related regimens (31.5%).

Conclusion: Three clinical phenotypes were identified via cluster analysis. The younger obese group with high metabolic risk had the highest CPT utilization rate and preferred GLP-1RAs, while the older group with high ASCVD risk was predominantly treated with SGLT2is alone.
Trial Registration: The trial was registered with https://www.chictr.org.cn/ under registration number ChiCTR230007376 on 20 July 2023.

title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Multiple Sclerosis: A Topical Narrative Review
abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) are a relatively new class of drugs that were initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and, subsequently, weight reduction in patients with obesity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is commonly associated with comorbidities for which GLP-1RAs are indicated. An increasing prevalence of comorbid chronic diseases has increased the number of people living with MS (pwMS) who are prescribed a GLP-1RA, for indications of obesity, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, and/or chronic kidney disease. This review addresses the following key considerations: (1) the use of GLP-1RAs for weight loss in pwMS and obesity, including considerations related to drug tolerability and safety; (2) the efficacy of the GLP-1RAs for their approved non-MS indications in pwMS; and (3) the potentially pleiotropic effects of the GLP-1RAs on the MS disease course beyond their approved indications.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

title: Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Impairment: Pathophysiology and Emerging Therapies
abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive impairment (DACI) is a common yet underrecognized condition, manifesting along a spectrum from mild cognitive impairment to dementia. DACI encompasses patients who develop vascular dementia (VaD) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) with diabetes as a risk factor; however, in certain patients, particularly those lacking clear VaD or AD features, diabetes may act as a primary driver of neurodegeneration. Mechanistically, DACI can be conceptualized as a neurovascular-metabolic disorder characterized by disruption of the neurovascular unit, impaired cerebral glucose metabolism, brain insulin resistance, and chronic neuroinflammation, contributing to small vessel disease, regional brain atrophy, and accelerated brain aging. In this narrative review, we synthesize current evidence on the clinical and imaging features of DACI, outline key mechanistic pathways linking diabetes to neurodegeneration, and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies, including GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors, with potential neuroprotective effects. Greater recognition of DACI as a neurovascular-metabolic entity may facilitate earlier identification, inform biomarker development, and guide future trials aimed at preserving cognitive function in individuals with diabetes.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

title: The Power of Two: Harnessing Dual Glucagon and Incretin Signaling for Treatment of Obesity and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis-A Narrative Review with a Translational Focus
abstract: A resurgence in glucagon research has repositioned this pancreatic hormone as a promising target in the treatment of obesity and related metabolic disorders. Glucagon is classically known for contributing to glucose homeostasis, but emerging evidence points to a much wider role in metabolism, including energy balance and liver health. These findings are fueling attempts to understand how to leverage glucagon signaling to treat obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Due to potential hyperglycemic effects of glucagon signaling, most investigational compounds are dual agonists of both the glucagon and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors to harness the antihyperglycemic and anorectic effects of the latter hormone, analogs of which such as semaglutide are already proven to be potent obesity medications. Glucagon receptor/GLP-1 receptor dual agonists reduce food intake, decrease hepatic fat, and increase energy expenditure in animal models of obesity and MASH. In early clinical trials, some dual agonists substantially reduced body weight, hepatic steatosis, and hepatic fibrosis. Whether they are more effective than GLP-1 receptor mono-agonists remains to be established in definitive head-to-head studies. The precise balance between glucagon and GLP-1 signaling within individual compounds appears important for overall therapeutic effects-including glycemic control, which worsened with some dual agonists. However, the two most clinically advanced compounds-mazdutide (approved for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes in China) and survodutide (ongoing global phase 3 trials)-had potent weight-loss and antihyperglycemic effects in people with obesity, with survodutide also improving liver health in people with MASH. Therefore, the research into glucagon physiology that led to glucagon receptor/GLP-1 receptor dual agonists is translating to advantageous new therapies for the highly prevalent diseases of obesity and MASH.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity

title: GLP-1-based therapies in lung diseases
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), initially developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, are increasingly recognised as multi-system agents with cardiovascular, renal and anti-inflammatory benefits. Emerging evidence suggests that their pleiotropic metabolic and immunomodulatory effects may have therapeutic relevance in chronic lung diseases. The lung is a metabolically active organ in which obesity, insulin resistance and systemic inflammation contribute to disease susceptibility, progression and treatment response. Chronic lung diseases such as asthma, COPD, pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung disease share overlapping inflammatory, vascular and fibrotic pathways that may be modifiable through GLP-1 RA-based therapies. Preclinical studies demonstrate that GLP-1R signalling influences airway inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial function and fibroblast activation. Observational and early clinical data suggest potential benefits in asthma control, exacerbation reduction in COPD, vascular remodelling in pulmonary hypertension and a reduction in all-cause mortality in interstitial lung disease. In addition to weight loss and glycaemic improvement, GLP-1 RAs exert direct anti-inflammatory and immune-regulatory effects that may act independently of metabolic change. Despite promising mechanistic and translational signals, high-quality randomised controlled trials with GLP-1 RAs in pulmonary populations remain limited. Key questions include patient selection, interaction with established anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic therapies, and the relative contribution of metabolic versus direct pulmonary effects. This review aims to synthesise current mechanistic, experimental and clinical evidence supporting GLP-1 RA use in chronic lung disease and outlines future research priorities within a precision-medicine framework.

title: Development and validation of a multiplexed LC-HRMS method for nine GLP-1 receptor agonists and its pharmaceutical application
abstract: A rapid, sensitive, and selective multiplexed liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) method was developed and validated for the identification and quantitation of nine structurally diverse peptide-based glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs): bofanglutide, ecnoglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, mazdutide, retatrutide, semaglutide, survodutide, and tirzepatide. These peptides represent single, dual, and triple receptor agonists, including four globally approved medications, two recently approved by China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), and three investigational drugs in Phase III clinical trials. Chromatographic separation was achieved on an ACQUITY Premier BEH C18 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.7 µm) at 50 °C using a multistep linear gradient with water and acetonitrile containing 0.1% difluoroacetic acid (DFA) and 0.5% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as mobile phases (flow rate 0.3 mL/min). The optimised method provided excellent resolution with baseline separation for most peptides within a 20-minute runtime. A key advantage of this work is the implementation of a dual strategy that combines high-resolution full-scan MS (HRMS) for accurate mass measurement with data-dependent HRMS/MS fragmentation for structural confirmation. Peptide identification adopted a top-down approach, achieving mass accuracy of 0.0-0.5 ppm and fragment ion coverage of 76-100%. The method showed good linearity (r² ≥ 0.995) over 4-235 ng/mL, with LODs of 0.44-2.06 ng/mL and LOQs of 8.29-11.74 ng/mL. It was successfully applied to marketed formulations of liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide using a simple dilute-and-shoot procedure, yielding mean recoveries of 113.7-118.4%. This LC-HRMS method offers superior selectivity and flexibility for analysing current and next-generation GLP-1 RAs.

title: Exploring semaglutide for alcohol use disorder: A review of clinical efficacy and neurobiological mechanisms
abstract: Aims: To examine emerging clinical evidence, real-world data, and neurobiological mechanisms supporting the repurposing of semaglutide as a novel treatment for alcohol use disorder (AUD) METHODS: Of records identified, articles were selected based on clinical relevance to AUD outcomes and mechanisms of action. Included studies ranged from hypothesis-generating designs to confirmatory randomized controlled trials in non-treatment-seeking individuals and patients diagnosed with AUD, with several cohorts enriched for comorbid obesity.

Results: Randomized controlled trials demonstrated that once-weekly semaglutide significantly reduced alcohol cravings and drinks per drinking day, even in non-treatment-seeking populations. Large-scale cohort studies showed a reduction in AUD-related hospitalizations for patients on semaglutide compared to non-users. Dual agonists like tirzepatide also showed significant reductions in binge drinking odds and AUDIT scores, with reductions in alcohol craving and consumption appearing most pronounced among individuals with comorbid obesity or metabolic disease. Mechanistically, preclinical and early human data indicate GLP-1 receptor activity in the VTA and nucleus accumbens modulates mesolimbic reward circuitry to attenuate dopamine-mediated reinforcement, alongside indirect behavioral and satiety effects.

Conclusions: GLP-1 receptor agonists show early promise in reducing alcohol craving and consumption, particularly in individuals with comorbid metabolic disease. No GLP-1 receptor agonist currently carries FDA approval for alcohol use disorder, and all discussed clinical applications still remain investigational. Definitive randomized trials in AUD-only populations are still needed. Current evidence remains limited by small sample sizes, brief follow-up periods, self-reported outcomes, and potential confounding from weight loss.

title: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) class of drugs is on the market to treat diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 drugs have also shown neuroprotective effects in animal models and clinical trials in PD patients. Apelin (APJ) is an adipokine peptide hormone with neuroprotective actions in preclinical studies. Here, we test the effects of a rationally designed bifunctional peptide, namely ELA (exendin-4-linker-apelin), in the MPTP mouse model of PD. The single GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide was used as a comparator. Motor activity was improved by both drugs (open field, pole test, Rotarod), and the inflammation response was reduced (activation of microglia and astrocytes, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels). In addition, synapse numbers were improved in the striatum (Golgi strain, TEM), expression of synapse-associated proteins was enhanced, alongside reduced expression of genes that increase mitochondrial fission. Mitochondrial fusion gene expressions (Opa1, Mfn2, Drp1) and mitochondrial morphology were also normalized (TEM). ELA was superior to liraglutide in some, but not all, parameters measured. The results suggest that the rational design of bifunctional peptides targeting both GLP-1 and APJ pathways-with optimized pharmacokinetics and enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability-merits further investigation as a strategy for developing more effective treatments for PD.

title: "Ozempic Face" and Facial Aging
abstract: The widespread adoption of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists has introduced a growing clinical challenge for dermatologists and cosmetic practitioners: managing the facial changes associated with rapid weight loss. The term "Ozempic face" has entered popular vocabulary to describe the appearance of accelerated facial aging in patients on these medications, characterized by volume deflation, skin laxity, and loss of structural support. This review examines the anatomical and histological basis of these changes, with attention to the roles of dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT), skeletal remodeling, and sarcopenia. We discuss the clinical presentation of weight-loss-associated facial change and outline a practical framework for patient assessment and counseling. The timing and sequencing of interventions across the weight loss journey are addressed, with emphasis on a health-first approach that prioritizes tissue preservation. As GLP-1 receptor agonists expand into new therapeutic indications, including inflammatory skin diseases, dermatology clinicians are uniquely positioned to counsel and manage patients experiencing these changes.

title: Preconception incretin therapy reduces pregnancy and cardiometabolic outcomes in polycystic ovary syndrome
abstract: Background: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), now polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), is associated with reproductive and cardiometabolic complications. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) receptor agonists (RAs) improve obesity-related outcomes, but their impact on pregnancy outcomes in PMOS remains unclear.

Methods: We conducted a target trial emulation using the TriNetX global federated health research network. Women ≥18 years with PCOS/PMOS receiving pre-conception GLP-1/dual GLP-1/GIP RA therapy (liraglutide, semaglutide or tirzepatide) were compared with metformin. Propensity score matching (1:1) accounted for demographics, anthropometrics, comorbidities and medications. The primary outcome was a composite of adverse pregnancy outcomes (hypertensive, glycaemic, placental, delivery, labour, foetal growth, preterm and early pregnancy complications) over two years. Individual pregnancy endpoints, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) were exploratory secondary outcomes. Cox regression generated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results: After matching, 48,126 patients were included per group. Pre-conception GLP-1/GIP RA use was associated with lower risk of the composite pregnancy outcome (HR 0.38; 95% CI 0.34-0.41). Exploratory analyses also demonstrated lower risks of individual pregnancy endpoints, MACE (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.81-0.95) and T2D (HR 0.31; 95% CI 0.30-0.33). Associations varied across some sensitivity analyses.

Conclusion: Pre-conception GLP-1/GIP RA use in women with PCOS/PMOS was associated with lower risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes and cardiometabolic disease compared with metformin, consistent with potential benefits of pre-conception metabolic optimisation. This study cannot evaluate in-pregnancy safety or efficacy, and these findings do not support GLP-1/GIP RA use during gestation.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

title: Tirzepatide-induced pneumatosis intestinalis: a rare but clinically significant gastrointestinal adverse effect
abstract: Objectives: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists such as tirzepatide are increasingly prescribed to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity because they improve glycemic control and promote weight loss. Although gastrointestinal adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and delayed gastric emptying are well recognized, very rare cases of pneumatosis intestinalis have also been reported in association with this class of medications. We report the first documented histologic diagnosis of a possible tirzepatide-associated pneumatosis intestinalis.

Methods: A 55-year-old man with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea underwent colonoscopy for evaluation of abdominal pain, constipation, and anal fissures. He had been receiving tirzepatide therapy for approximately 1 year and experienced a 49-pound weight loss. Colonoscopy demonstrated mucosal edema of the cecum and ascending colon.

Results: Biopsy specimens of the colon revealed mucosal and submucosal air-filled spaces associated with foreign body-type giant cell reactions and mixed inflammatory infiltrates, including eosinophils and neutrophils, consistent with pneumatosis intestinalis. The patient lacked other recognized risk factors for pneumatosis intestinalis, and his symptoms improved following discontinuation of tirzepatide.

Conclusions: As the use of tirzepatide and related glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists continues to increase, awareness of this rare side effect and its characteristic histologic features should facilitate prompt recognition and accurate diagnosis. Reporting these rare events remains essential to refine the safety profile of these increasingly used medications and improve our understanding of their long-term gastrointestinal effects in broader patient populations.

title: Implications of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Signaling for Hemophilic Arthropathy, Joint Inflammation, and Cartilage Degeneration: A Narrative Review
abstract: Introduction: Hemophilic arthropathy (HA) is a progressive, inflammatory joint disease that develops despite effective control of bleeding in people with hemophilia (PWH). Increasing evidence suggests that HA is initiated and then maintained by a complex cycle of synovial macrophage activation, angiogenesis, and cartilage catabolism-pathways shared with osteoarthritis (OA) and inflammatory arthritis. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RA), initially developed for diabetes and obesity, have emerged as pleiotropic immunometabolic modulators with potent anti-inflammatory, chondroprotective, anti-angiogenic, and analgesic properties.
Methods: A narrative review was undertaken to examine the potential role of GLP-1RA in HA.

Results: Although GLP-1RA have not yet been studied directly in hemophilia, a large and growing preclinical and clinical literature in OA and inflammatory arthritis provides strong mechanistic justification for their relevance in HA.

Conclusion: This review integrates experimental, translational, and epidemiologic data on GLP-1 signaling in joint biology and proposes a stage-specific framework for how GLP-1 pathways might modify HA downstream of bleeding, the initiating event.
journal: Haemophilia : the official journal of the World Federation of Hemophilia

title: Retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2): a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
abstract: Background: Retatrutide is an agonist of GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors, and is currently under investigation for the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other comorbidities, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnoea. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of retatrutide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Methods: TRIUMPH-2 was a double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial conducted at 92 medical and research centres and hospitals across eight countries. We enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or higher and type 2 diabetes (glycated haemoglobin [HbA1c] 6·5-10·5%) on stable treatment for type 2 diabetes for at least 90 days before screening (diet or exercise alone, or up to three oral glucose-lowering medications), and a history of at least one self-reported unsuccessful dietary effort to reduce bodyweight. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1), using an interactive web-response system, to receive once-weekly subcutaneous injections (self-administered) of placebo or retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg. The primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline to week 80 in bodyweight for the retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg doses versus placebo, with 4 mg versus placebo a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses included all randomly assigned participants, with missing data imputed with a primary multiple imputation strategy for the treatment regimen estimand. Safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of study drug. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05929079 (completed).

Findings: Between July 11, 2023, and Nov 1, 2024, 2047 participants were screened, and 1152 (mean age 55·1 years [SD 10·8], 554 [48%] females and 598 [52%] males, and 672 [58%] of White ethnicity) were randomly assigned to retatrutide 4 mg (n=292), 9 mg (n=284), or 12 mg (n=287), or placebo (n=289). At baseline, the mean BMI was 38·2 kg/m2 (SD 7·4), mean HbA1c was 7·71% (1·07), median duration of obesity was 21 years (IQR 11-31), and median duration of diabetes was 5·6 years (2·6-10·4). At baseline, 1055 (92%) of 1152 participants were on any oral glucose-lowering medication, including biguanides, SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and other oral glucose-lowering medications. Of 1152 participants, 965 (84%) completed the study drug. For the treatment regimen estimand, the mean percentage change from baseline in bodyweight at week 80 was -11·9% (SE 0·6) with retatrutide 4 mg, -16·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 9 mg, -18·8% (0·7) with retatrutide 12 mg, and -5·1% (0·7) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences compared with placebo for percentage change in bodyweight were -6·9% (95% CI -8·7 to -5·1) with retatrutide 4 mg, -11·8% (-13·7 to -9·8) with retatrutide 9 mg, and -13·8% (-15·8 to -11·8) with retatrutide 12 mg (p<0·0001 for all). The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal, which were more common in the retatrutide groups than in the placebo group (diarrhoea occurred in 80 [27%] of 292 participants in the 4 mg group, 95 [34%] of 284 in the 9 mg group, and 96 [34%] of 286 in the 12 mg group vs 38 [13%] of 287 in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 40 [14%], 59 [21%], and 80 [28%] vs 23 [8%]). Hypotension and dysesthesia were more frequent with retatrutide than with placebo (four [1%] in the 4 mg group, 14 [5%] in the 9 mg group, and 18 (6%) in the 12 mg group vs one [<1%] in the placebo group with hypotension; 13 [4%], 16 [6%], and 21 [7%] vs two [1%] in the placebo group with dysesthesia). Permanent treatment discontinuation due to adverse events or death was more frequent in participants treated with retatrutide 9 mg (33 [12%]) and 12 mg (22 [8%]) compared with retatrutide 4 mg (11 [4%]) and placebo (14 [5%]). Two participants died in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group, and one in the placebo group; all deaths were deemed to be unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator.

Interpretation: Treatment with retatrutide resulted in substantial improvements in bodyweight and was associated with improvements in glycaemic control in participants with obesity and type 2 diabetes, with a safety profile generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism. These results show that retatrutide might be effective for the treatment of obesity in people with type 2 diabetes.
