title: Bivalent gambogic acid-functionalized curcumin nanoparticles with insulin modulate the gut-liver-kidney network in type 2 diabetes
abstract: The gut-liver-kidney (GLK) network is a critical driver of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) complications, where gut dysbiosis triggers cycle of hepatic metabolic stress and subsequent renal dysfunction through a complex, bidirectional signaling crosstalk. Despite its importance, therapeutic strategies capable of addressing this multi-organ crosstalk remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that bivalent functionalized curcumin-encapsulating PLGA nanoparticles (nGA2-CUR) combined with subcutaneous insulin beneficially modulate the GLK network in obese T2DM mice. This combination therapy successfully stabilized systemic glucose homeostasis and restored essential endocrine signaling (insulin, GLP-1, and GIP) while significantly suppressing pro-inflammatory markers (MCP-1, haptoglobin). Microbiome profiling revealed a suppression of pathobionts alongside distinct sex-specific restorative responses, where males exhibited Muribaculaceae enrichment while females showed Bifidobacterium expansion. Integrated liver metabolomics associated these microbial shifts with unique organ-specific repair responses in each sex. Males showed elevated levels of purine salvage pathway intermediates alongside suppression of a specific pathobiont cluster (including Lautropia and Porphyromonas) correlated with oxidative stress, whereas females replenished aromatic amino acids, consistent with reduced predicted microbial proteolytic potential and lower markers of nephrotoxic uremic toxin production. Molecular analysis confirmed the downregulation of glucose-sensitive pathways (Chrebp/Srebp-1c). These systemic improvements were accompanied by an anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage profile shift, alongside suppression of renal fibrosis via the TGFβ/SMAD network and reduced injury markers (Cystatin C and Osteopontin). Our findings suggest that by reshaping the gut microbiome to alleviate upstream hepatic metabolic burden, this nanoparticle-enhanced therapy provides a sex-specific framework for attenuating irreversible diabetic renal injury.
journal: Journal of controlled release : official journal of the Controlled Release Society

title: Food noise among U.S. adults: Psychometric evaluation and prevalence estimates from a nationally representative sample
abstract: Background: Widespread use of GLP-1 medications has revealed not only their effectiveness in reducing food intake and body mass, but also the clinical relevance of a seemingly underrecognized cognitive-affective process, food noise, that may be highly distressing for some individuals. Although the concept has gained increasing attention in public discourse, empirical research on food noise remains quite limited. We aimed to provide an initial epidemiologic characterization of food noise among U.S. adults. Methods: Our study utilized data from a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults ( N =3 646) conducted in Fall 2025. Survey-weighted exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to evaluate the structure of the Food Noise Questionnaire (FNQ; ref. 1). Food noise endorsement was estimated using three operational definitions. Survey-weighted linear regression was used to examine associations between food noise and sociodemographic and weight-related subgroups. Results: Exploratory factor analysis supported a strongly loaded one-factor solution explaining approximately 80% of the variance. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the one-factor structure, with factor loadings and model fit broadly consistent with the original FNQ validation study. Depending on the operational definition, approximately 4% to 9.5% of U.S. adults met criteria for food noise endorsement. Among adults with obesity, prevalence ranged from approximately 6% to 14%. Food noise scores were higher among women than men ( B =0.18, 95%CI[0.09, 0.26], p <.001), higher among younger adults, and progressively increased across weight categories, from overweight ( B =0.23, 95%CI[0.13, 0.32], p <.001) to class III obesity ( B =0.61, 95%CI[0.46, 0.76], p <.001), relative to normal weight. Conclusions: These findings provide an initial indication of the potential scope and public health relevance of food noise, suggesting that its occurrence is not negligible but is far from ubiquitous among adults with obesity. Further research is needed to establish clinically meaningful thresholds, determine the overlap of food noise with related constructs, and examine its underlying mechanisms.

title: Periostin in diabetic kidney disease: mechanistic insights, biomarkers, and therapeutic perspectives
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is among the most common and severe microvascular complications of diabetes and represents a leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) worldwide. Currently, although strict glycemic and blood pressure control, together with the use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, and non-steroidal selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, can moderately delay DKD progression, the risks of progression to ESRD and cardiovascular events remain high, highlighting the urgent need to identify novel therapeutic targets. Preclinical and observational studies suggest that periostin (POSTN) is associated with DKD progression and may contribute to renal inflammation and fibrosis. POSTN expression is minimal in healthy kidneys but is markedly upregulated under conditions of renal injury and fibrosis. Cross-sectional clinical studies report that serum, urinary, and renal tissue POSTN levels are elevated in patients with DKD and correlate with proteinuria, the severity of renal fibrosis, and a decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR); these associations have not been confirmed prospectively. Preclinical studies indicate that POSTN promotes inflammatory cell infiltration, myofibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix accumulation, and it has therefore been proposed to contribute to the inflammatory and fibrotic progression of DKD. In preclinical DKD models, POSTN inhibition attenuates renal injury and fibrosis. No POSTN-targeted therapy has entered human clinical trials, so POSTN remains a promising preclinical candidate target. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis and recent advances in POSTN research in DKD, and further explores its translational potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: Tirzepatide versus other glucose-lowering therapies and risk of COPD exacerbations in patients with comorbid type 2 diabetes: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) frequently coexist, sharing inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Tirzepatide (TZP), a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, has demonstrated metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects. However, its impact on pulmonary outcomes in patients with COPD and T2D remains uncertain.

Methods: Using the TriNetX global research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with coexisting COPD and T2D prescribed TZP, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i), or glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA). Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed separately for each comparison. Primary outcome was COPD exacerbation; secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, acute respiratory failure, and lower respiratory tract infection. Outcomes were assessed during a prespecified observation period from day one through day 365 after the index date.

Results: Matched populations included 6,080 patients per group (TZP-SGLT2i), 4,684 (TZP-DPP-4i), and 6,727 (TZP-GLP-1RA). In the independently matched comparisons, median follow-up was 232 versus 365 days for TZP versus SGLT2i, 235 versus 365 days for TZP versus DPP-4i, and 233 versus 365 days for TZP versus other GLP-1RAs; incidence rates were expressed per 1,000 person-years. Compared with SGLT2i and DPP-4i, TZP significantly reduced COPD exacerbation risk (hazard ratio [HR] 0.73 [95% CI 0.64-0.82] and 0.72 [95% CI 0.63-0.82], respectively) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.30 [95% CI 0.23-0.38] and 0.24 [95% CI 0.18-0.31], respectively). TZP also reduced acute respiratory failure and lower respiratory tract infection risks. Outcomes were similar between TZP and GLP-1RA, except TZP showed lower mortality (HR 0.55 [95% CI 0.42-0.72]).

Conclusion: Among patients with COPD and T2D, TZP use was associated with lower risks of COPD exacerbations, respiratory complications, and mortality compared with SGLT2i and DPP-4i, findings that warrant confirmation through randomized clinical trials.

title: Oral Obesity Medicines in the Era of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome (CKM): Beyond Weight Loss Toward Disease Modification
abstract: Obesity is a major driver of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome and contributes to the development of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes. Historically, oral obesity pharmacotherapy was evaluated primarily according to weight loss efficacy. However, the emergence of the CKM framework has shifted therapeutic priorities toward modifying obesity related complications and improving long term clinical outcomes. This review summarizes currently approved oral obesity medications, including first generation agents (orlistat, phentermine/topiramate, and naltrexone/bupropion) and second generation incretin-based therapies (oral semaglutide and orforglipron), within the context of CKM syndrome. First generation agents provide modest-to-moderate weight loss and variable metabolic benefits, but evidence supporting cardiovascular or kidney outcome improvement remains limited and largely observational. In contrast, oral incretin-based therapies demonstrate broader effects across the CKM spectrum, including substantial weight reduction, improved glycemic control, favorable effects on blood pressure and triglycerides, and emerging kidney benefits. Among currently available oral agents, oral semaglutide has the strongest evidence, with the SOUL trial demonstrating a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk individuals with type 2 diabetes. Signals suggesting benefits in heart failure and atrial fibrillation are encouraging but remain exploratory. Orforglipron represents the first non-peptide oral glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist and offers simplified administration with promising metabolic efficacy; however, cardiovascular, kidney, heart failure, and arrhythmia outcome data are still awaited. Collectively, the role of oral obesity pharmacotherapy is evolving from weight management alone toward comprehensive CKM care.

title: Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction: Pathophysiology, Molecular Mechanisms, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD), which includes memory loss, executive dysfunction, attention, processing speed, and an increased risk of dementia, is a growing problem associated with diabetes mellitus (DM), especially type 2 diabetes mellitus. Due to a significant increase in the global burden of diabetes and population ageing, DACD is becoming an important public health issue. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the pathophysiology, molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, experimental models, and emerging therapeutic strategies associated with DACD. At present, it is believed that the multiple mechanisms associated with chronic hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and microvascular injury all contribute to the pathogenesis of DACD. These interrelated mechanisms are responsible for cognitive decline, synaptic dysfunction, and neuronal damage. Experimental research has shown that specific molecular pathways contribute to the pathogenesis of DACD, such as AGE-RAGE signaling, nuclear factor-κB activation, PI3K/Akt dysregulation, and inflammatory cascades. Emerging biomarkers including neurofilament light (NfL) chain, phosphorylated tau (p-tau), neuroimaging markers, exosomes, metabolomic profiles, and transcriptomic signatures may improve early diagnosis and risk stratification. Several therapeutic approaches, including GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, intranasal insulin, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, stem cell therapies, and bioactive compounds, have demonstrated promising neuroprotective effects in preclinical studies, although clinical translation remains limited. Finally, future studies should be directed toward the use of biomarker-driven diagnosis, clinically relevant disease models, and large-scale clinical studies in order to develop effective therapeutic interventions. Understanding more of the mechanisms that underlie DACD could help inform the creation of precision medicine strategies to prevent or delay diabetes-related cognitive decline.

title: The Effect of Exanatide on Recovery of the Facial Nerve Crush Injury in the Rat
abstract: Background: Exenatide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, has been shown to promote functional recovery and nerve regeneration after nerve crush injury. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of exenatide on facial nerve regeneration in traumatic facial paralysis.

Methods: This prospective, randomized animal study included 28 healthy female Sprague-Dawley rats divided into 4 groups of 7 rats each: control group, sham group, 2.5 μg/rat/day exenatide-treated group, and 10 μg/rat/day exenatide-treated group. Exenatide was injected subcutaneously for 14 days. Crush injury was applied to the left facial nerve in all groups except the sham group. Functional assessment, electrophysiological, histopathological, and immunohistochemical examinations were performed after crush injury.

Results: The blink reflex score was higher in 10 μg exenatide-treated rats than in other rats at week 1. At weeks 3 and 4, the vibrissae movement score was higher in exenatide-treated rats than in untreated rats. Electromyographic assessments performed at weeks 2 and 4 showed higher amplitude values and shorter latency periods in the exenatide treatment groups. Exenatide was found to have a dose-dependent effect on reducing the severity of vasoconstriction, and this effect was statistically significant. When comparing the exenatide treatment groups with the control group, a significant reduction in the incidence of severe macrovacuolation and an increase in myelin thickness were observed (P < .05).

Conclusion: Functional, electrophysiological, and histopathological evaluations have shown that exenatide treatment has a positive and accelerating effect on facial nerve recovery in traumatic facial paralysis.
journal: The journal of international advanced otology

title: Status Of GLP-1 drugs and their application in treating substance use disorders: A systematic review
abstract: Background/Objective: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have an exciting future potential beyond metabolic disorders. This review gauges their effectiveness, safety, and clinical role in the management of substance use disorders in diverse populations.

Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review searched PubMed, Scopus, WoS, CENTRAL and PsycINFO up to March 2026; 1641 records were identified, 11 included; screening, extracting and evaluating the efficacy, safety, and bias of the studies.

Results: 11 studies were selected out of 1641 records. Reduced substance-related outcomes were always observed with GLP-1RAs. In alcohol use disorder (AUD), there was a decrease in the risk of hospitalization (aHR 0.640.72), and reduced incident AUD (OR 0.260.71), but randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provided contradictory outcomes (p = 0.37; 29% reduction, p = 0.04). Semaglutide reduced the risk of tobacco use disorder (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.630.74). There was a great decrease in the risk of opioid overdose (HR 0.32-0.58). The incidence (HR 0.86), mortality (HR 0.50), and suicidal ideation were less in composite substance use disorder (SUD) outcomes (HR 0.75). Weight reduction was consistent (-2.9 kg; ≥16 kg in 37.5%), with HbA1c improvements (-0.25%). RCTs were found to be low-bias and the observational studies were moderate-bias. The safety profiles were positive, and there were no patterns of increasing serious adverse events (SAEs).

Conclusion: GLP-1RAs have good potential protective properties against SUD especially in observational research with good safety. However, robust randomized trials are needed to confirm causality and clinical applicability.

title: Reduced pancreatic responsiveness to glucose plus amino acids and incretins in early versus late lactation dairy cows
abstract: The action of insulin that influences partitioning of nutrients to milk in early lactation and to the body in later lactation is controlled by the effect of insulin on an array of insulin-dependent tissues and by pancreatic responsiveness to insulin secretagogues. To examine differences in pancreatic responsiveness between stages of lactation, pairs of cows in early (39 ± 24.3 DIM; n = 11) and late lactation (316.5 ± 77.3 DIM; n = 11) were feed restricted for 24 h and then subjected to a 2-h hyperglycemic, hyperaminoacidemic clamp (HGHAC) where glucose + 9 essential amino acids were infused intravenously to reach plasma concentration targets of 5 mM for glucose and 800 μM for branched-chain amino acids. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) were then added to the HGHAC for 2 more hours to isolate the pancreatic responsiveness to these incretins. Baseline, feed-restricted glucose and insulin concentrations before infusion were lower in the early-lactation group compared with late lactation, while baseline branched-chain amino acid and lysine concentrations were higher. Early-lactation cows needed 147 mmol/h more glucose to maintain hyperglycemia than those in late lactation, indicating a higher glucose disposition. The physiological basis for this response and for the low baseline glucose concentration is likely the high glucose uptake of the mammary glands of early lactation. In contrast, 224 mmol/h less amino acid was infused in early lactation to maintain hyperaminoacidemia, suggesting a faster endogenous entry of amino acid from body stores. Insulin concentrations during both sets of clamps showed that cows in early lactation exhibited reduced pancreatic responsiveness to glucose + amino acids and to incretins, compared with cows in late lactation. The opposing effects of stage of lactation on glucose and amino acid infusion rates reveal the existence of differences between glucose and amino acids in how the insulin sensitivities of their production and utilization are affected. Blunted pancreatic responsiveness may be more important than a decrease in insulin sensitivity for directing glucose and amino acids toward milk.

title: Digestive lipases as therapeutic targets in obesity: From Orlistat to next-generation inhibitors
abstract: Obesity remains a global pandemic and a major driver of metabolic diseases, with current pharmacotherapies often limited by modest efficacy, systemic side effects, high costs, and weight regain after cessation. Targeting dietary lipid digestion via the inhibition of gastrointestinal lipases offers a mechanistically rational and peripherally acting therapeutic strategy. This review provides an updated, quantitative overview of human gastrointestinal lipolysis, emphasizing the sequential and complementary roles of human gastric lipase and human pancreatic lipase in dietary triglyceride absorption. We critically analyze the clinical proof-of-concept provided by Orlistat, the only approved digestive lipase inhibitor, whose utility is constrained by limited efficacy, significant gastrointestinal intolerance, and rare but severe hepatotoxicity. While next-generation systemic therapies like GLP-1 receptor agonists show superior weight loss, their chronic administration and high cost underscore the need for safer, localized alternatives. We systematically review recent strategies for developing superior digestive lipase inhibitors, including structure-based drug design, in silico screening, and bioguided fractionation of natural products (e.g., flavonoid derivatives). Emphasis is placed on the critical design principles required for next-generation inhibitors, including strict luminal confinement, high selectivity for digestive lipases, and controlled, reversible inhibition to improve tolerability. By bridging biochemical insights with pharmacological challenges, this review outlines a roadmap for the development of safer, more effective lipid-targeted therapies to combat obesity.

title: A stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies in weight management
abstract: Background: Use of incretin-based therapies, including GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists, for weight management and related cardio-kidney-liver-metabolic comorbidities has expanded rapidly, yet real-world practice is challenged by inconsistent prescribing, access barriers, limited long-term safety data, low treatment persistence, and concerns regarding equity and financial sustainability. These gaps highlight the need for a structured, coordinated stewardship model to guide safe and evidence-based use of incretin-based therapies.

Objectives: To develop a scalable, multidisciplinary stewardship framework for incretin-based therapies that supports consistent and efficient prescribing practices, optimizes patient outcomes, strengthens medication access and safety monitoring, and defines the role of pharmacists in chronic weight management.

Methods: Two sequential expert workgroups were convened, composed of clinicians and pharmacy leaders from 21 health systems. Workgroup 1 identified foundational stewardship elements drawing from established antimicrobial and opioid stewardship models. Workgroup 2 applied these core principles to incretin-based therapies, informed by real-world challenges, emerging evidence, and clinical experience in weight and diabetes management. Consensus was established using a Delphi process, with ≥60% agreement required for inclusion.

Results: Workgroups reached consensus on a stewardship framework comprising multidisciplinary leadership, stakeholder engagement, pharmacy expertise, defined priorities, evidence-based interventions, education, data and reporting strategies, communication pathways, and mechanisms for feedback and continuous assessment. In addition, consensus-based pharmacist-led initiatives and metric categories were developed to support implementation and program evaluation across varied ambulatory environments, with pharmacists identified as central to therapy initiation and titration, adverse effect management, access navigation, patient education, and care coordination.

Conclusion: A structured stewardship model offers a feasible and scalable approach to optimize incretin-based therapies in weight management. By integrating multidisciplinary collaboration with pharmacy expertise and clinical and operational strategies, health systems can promote safe, equitable, and sustainable use of these therapies, improve population-level outcomes, and safeguard long-term value amid rapidly expanding utilization.
journal: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA

title: Association between Socioeconomic Deprivation and Clinical Outcomes of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Heart Failure
abstract: The impact of socioeconomic deprivation on the effectiveness and safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) in heart failure (HF) remains unclear. We evaluated GLP-1RA-associated outcomes across socioeconomic strata and quantified residual disparities among GLP-1RA users. Using the TriNetX Global Network (2020-2024), adults with HF initiating GLP-1RA therapy were categorized as socioeconomically deprived or non-deprived. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity-score matched within each stratum, enabling three comparisons: GLP-1RA users vs non-users in deprived patients, GLP-1RA users vs non-users in non-deprived patients, and deprived vs non-deprived among GLP-1RA users. Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for 12-month mortality and hospitalization outcomes. Among deprived patients, GLP-1RA users (n=22,585) were compared with non-users (n=194,967); among non-deprived patients, users (n=116,439) were compared with non-users (n=2,254,050). In a direct comparison restricted to GLP-1RA users, deprived (n=21,171) and non-deprived (n=104,887) patients were analyzed. GLP-1RA therapy was associated with similar relative reductions in all-cause mortality or hospitalization in deprived (aHR 0.68, 95% CI 0.66-0.70) and non-deprived patients (aHR 0.68, 95% CI 0.67-0.69). However, deprived users had worse outcomes than non-deprived users (35.5% vs 27.1%; aHR 1.50, 95% CI 1.44-1.55), driven by higher hospitalization (aHR 1.53, 95% CI 1.48-1.58) and mortality (aHR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02-1.24). HF exacerbation (aHR 1.11) and ischemic stroke (aHR 1.16) were also increased. GLP-1RA use was associated with similar relative reductions in adverse outcomes across socioeconomic groups; however, socioeconomically deprived patients continued to experience higher absolute event rates, likely reflecting persistent baseline disparities and residual risk.

title: Short-term clinical efficacy and recorded adverse events of semaglutide combined with dapagliflozin in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) complicated by chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with persistent hyperglycemia, progressive renal impairment, systemic inflammation, and an increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists have shown metabolic and cardiorenal benefits, but clinical evidence regarding their combined use in patients with T2DM and CKD remains limited. This retrospective observational study included 126 patients with T2DM complicated by CKD who were treated at our hospital between March 2023 and July 2024. Patients were identified through a review of electronic medical records and the application of predefined eligibility criteria. Treatment groups reflected the actual regimen documented in the medical record rather than random allocation. The final analytic cohort comprised 42 patients in each group; the equal group size reflected the eligible records with complete baseline and 8-week follow-up data available in each treatment category during the study period rather than a prospective 1:1:1 enrollment target. The treatment duration was 8 weeks. Glycemic indices, renal function-related parameters, inflammatory markers, clinical response, and recorded adverse events were compared among the 3 groups. After 8 weeks of treatment, fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour postprandial plasma glucose, hemoglobin A1c, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, 24-hour urinary protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, interleukin-6, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were significantly reduced in all 3 groups compared with baseline. The combination group showed greater short-term reductions in glycemic indices, renal function-related parameters, and inflammatory markers than either monotherapy group. The overall clinical response rate was significantly higher in the combination group than in the dapagliflozin or semaglutide group. In patients with T2DM complicated by CKD, semaglutide combined with dapagliflozin was associated with greater short-term improvements in glycemic control, inflammatory markers, and renal function-related indicators, as well as a higher exploratory clinical response rate, than either monotherapy. No increase in recorded adverse events was detected during 8 weeks of treatment. Because of the retrospective design, modest sample size, and short observation period, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating definitive long-term renal benefit or equivalent long-term safety. Further large-scale prospective studies with standardized renal outcomes are required.

title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension, Basic Concepts and Emerging Molecular, Genetic, and Immunological Therapies
abstract: Background: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is a chronic disorder characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) without an identifiable intracranial mass lesion or abnormal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) composition. Traditionally viewed as a disorder of impaired CSF absorption or venous outflow obstruction, IIH predominantly affects women of reproductive age with obesity and remains a major cause of preventable visual loss. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that IIH is driven by a broader biologic framework involving dysregulated CSF secretion, metabolic and endocrine dysfunction, immune activation, and genetic susceptibility.

Summary: This narrative review synthesizes recent advances in the molecular and cellular pathophysiology of IIH and examines emerging mechanism-based therapeutic strategies. Particular emphasis is placed on choroid plexus biology and hormonally regulated CSF hypersecretion mediated through glucocorticoid metabolism via 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1) and androgen signaling pathways that modulate Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity. Distinct metabolic features of IIH, including visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and adipose tissue inflammation, are integrated with evidence of systemic and central immune dysregulation. Recent genetic and biobank-based studies further support IIH-specific biological risk extending beyond obesity alone and implicate pathways involved in steroid metabolism, ion transport, vascular biology, and glymphatic regulation. We additionally review translational and clinical evidence supporting targeted therapies, including glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and 11β-HSD1 inhibitors, which demonstrate ICP-lowering effects that may occur partially independent of weight loss.

Key Messages: Accumulating mechanistic evidence supports a paradigm shift in IIH from a diagnosis of exclusion toward a biologically defined neuroendocrine disorder characterized by dysregulated CSF secretion, endocrine and metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and impaired glymphatic regulation. Advances in molecular biology and translational therapeutics are enabling the development of targeted, disease-modifying therapies and may facilitate future precision medicine approaches for IIH management.

title: A Microsimulation of Eligibility for Cardiorenal Combination Treatment and Potential Deaths Averted
abstract: Background: Clinical guidelines recommend combined use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASi), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RA) and nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (nsMRA) to reduce cardiorenal risk. However, eligibility for combination treatment and the potential effects of implementation on preventing mortality remain unclear.

Methods: We conducted a microsimulation study using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2007-2016 and 2017-2020). The model incorporated acute treatment effects of RASi, SGLT2i, GLP1RA, and nsMRA on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and serum potassium. Eligibility for combination treatment was assessed for each participant according to 73 clinical practice guideline recommendations and inclusion criteria from recently published clinical trials. Primary outcomes included: 1) the percentage of participants eligible for single or combination treatment with RASi, SGLT2i, GLP1RA, and nsMRA, and 2) the projected potential number of annually averted all-cause and cardiovascular deaths.

Results: Of 8,152 adults, 15% had type 2 diabetes (DM), 14% had chronic kidney disease (CKD) and 5% had DM and CKD (DKD). Among all U.S. adults, 19% were treated with RASi, 1% with SGLT2i, 1% with GLP1RA and none with nsMRA. The dual-therapy associated with the highest eligibility was RASi+SGLT2i, with 15% of the U.S. population eligible (DM subgroup: 70%; CKD subgroup: 50%; DKD subgroup: 84%). The triple-therapy with the highest eligibility was RASi+SGLT2i+GLP1RA, with 11% overall eligibility (DM: 69%; CKD: 33%; DKD: 83%). Eligibility for quadruple-therapy was 4% overall (DM: 22%; CKD: 17%; DKD: 40%). Based on our microsimulation model, fewer individuals with diabetes were eligible for triple-therapy with RASi+SGLT2i+GLP1RA compared to dual-therapy with RASi+SGLT2i, but triple-therapy was projected to prevent 2-fold more potential all-cause and cardiovascular deaths versus dual-therapy.

Conclusions: Under the assumptions of our microsimulation model, eligibility for combined treatment with cardiorenal protective therapies was prevalent, particularly in adults with type 2 diabetes and/or CKD.
journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN

title: Migraine and Obesity: From Shared Mechanisms to Therapeutic Strategies
abstract: Migraine and obesity are highly prevalent, chronic conditions that frequently coexist, presenting a significant clinical and therapeutic challenge. Their relationship is multifactorial and bidirectional, albeit with more consistent evidence supporting obesity as a contributor to migraine than the converse, driven by shared biological mechanisms that include systemic low-grade inflammation, adipose-derived adipokines, metabolic dysfunction, and insulin resistance. These systemic disturbances converge on hypothalamic dysregulation and altered neuropeptide signaling, notably involving calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), ultimately promoting trigeminovascular activation and migraine chronification. Clinically, excess body weight is associated with increased attack frequency, greater pain intensity, and higher disability, particularly in women of reproductive age. Conversely, migraine can indirectly influence factors contributing to weight gain, often compounded by psychological comorbidities. Management requires an integrated approach; traditional oral preventives that promote weight gain should be avoided, prioritizing sustainable lifestyle interventions alongside modern, weight-neutral or weight-reducing therapies. This article reviews the available evidence documenting the complex pathophysiological link between obesity and migraine, diagnostic and clinical implications across specific populations, and current management strategies. Emphasis is placed on novel therapeutic options, including CGRP-targeted agents and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, as well as future directions and unmet clinical needs in the management of comorbid migraine and obesity.

title: Neuroendocrine regulation of adipose partitioning in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: the gut-brain-adipose axis
abstract: Purpose: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), formerly polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is a common, complex, and heterogeneous endocrine disorder characterized by reproductive and metabolic dysregulation that significantly increases long-term cardiometabolic risk. Growing evidence indicates that dysregulated adipose tissue partitioning, resulting in preferential visceral and ectopic fat accumulation, is a major determinant of metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. The presence of metabolic abnormalities in lean women with PMOS further suggests that mechanisms beyond obesity and total fat mass contribute to disease pathophysiology. This review aims to examine the potential role of gut-brain-adipose signaling in adipose tissue distribution and insulin resistance in PMOS.

Methods: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the gut-brain-adipose axis and its potential role in adipose tissue distribution and metabolic dysfunction in PMOS, with particular emphasis on oxytocin, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), leptin, and other gut- and adipose-derived mediators.

Results: The gut-brain-adipose axis represents a neuroendocrine network regulating appetite, energy homeostasis, and adipose tissue function. Within this framework, oxytocin and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), alongside gut- and adipose-derived mediators including glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), leptin, and other adipokines, may also contribute to these processes. Evidence demonstrating altered fasting and postprandial oxytocin and GLP-1 responses in women with PMOS suggests that impaired neuroendocrine signaling may be associated with dysregulated adipose partitioning and could contribute to visceral and ectopic fat accumulation and increasing metabolic risk.

Conclusion: This review discusses the gut-brain-adipose axis as a conceptual framework for understanding how neuroendocrine signaling influences adipose tissue distribution and insulin resistance in PMOS. Further understanding of the gut-brain-adipose axis may help identify potential therapeutic targets for improving metabolic health in women with PMOS.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and serious adverse events: Evidence, uncertainty and clinical implications
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists provide benefits in weight reduction, glycaemic control in Type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Their widespread use has given rise to concerns regarding rare but potentially serious adverse events. This narrative review appraises evidence regarding seven serious adverse events linked to GLP-1 receptor agonists: thyroid cancer, non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION), suicidal behaviours and self-harm, diabetic retinopathy complications, acute pancreatitis, gallbladder and biliary disease and intestinal obstruction. Evidence from mechanistic studies, spontaneous reports, randomized trials and cohort studies is considered. Gallbladder and biliary disease has the most consistent evidence supporting a causal association. Worsening of diabetic retinopathy appears most consistent with early worsening after rapid glycaemic improvement in patients with pre-existing retinopathy. For thyroid cancer, NAION, suicidal behaviour and self-harm, acute pancreatitis and intestinal obstruction, evidence regarding causality remains uncertain. Rare events, incomplete ascertainment in trials and residual confounding in observational studies limit inference. Because these events are rare, even substantial relative risk increases generally correspond to small absolute risk increases in broad populations but may become relevant in patients with high baseline risk. Treatment decisions should consider the strength and uncertainty of safety evidence, individual baseline risk, expected benefits relative to available alternatives and patient preferences.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure in the periconceptional period and adverse obstetric outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses whether exposure to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) during pregnancy or the periconceptional period is associated with adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes.

Methods: Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for observational studies comparing pregnancies exposed and unexposed to GLP-1 RAs within 6 months before a positive pregnancy test. Outcomes included miscarriage, intrauterine death, congenital anomalies, preterm birth (PTB), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), fetal growth restriction (FGR), small for gestational age (SGA), large for gestational age (LGA), and excess gestational weight gain. Random-effects meta-analyses and subgroup analyses by indication were performed.

Findings: Ten studies included 2,118,215 women, of whom 8,325 were exposed and 2,109,890 were unexposed. Pooled estimates did not show a clearly detectable increase in miscarriage or intrauterine death, congenital anomalies, preterm birth, HDP, gestational diabetes, abnormal fetal growth, or excess gestational weight gain. A lower pooled estimate for preeclampsia was observed (odds ratio [OR]: 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78-0.98; p = 0.02), but this was based on two datasets and should be interpreted cautiously. Subgroup analyses showed no clearly detectable differences by indication. The exposure-window sensitivity analysis, covering 90 days before conception through the end of the first trimester, used the same four studies as the primary congenital-malformation analysis and therefore was not independent.

Conclusion: Available observational evidence did not identify a clearly detectable increase in adverse maternal or perinatal outcomes following periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 RAs. However, these findings do not establish safety because of heterogeneity, residual confounding, and limited datasets.
Funding: None.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and lymphedema: from weight loss to potential direct modulation of lymphatic function
abstract: Obesity and lymphedema are linked through increased interstitial fluid load, impaired collecting-vessel pumping, inflammation, and progressive fibro-adipose remodeling. This bidirectional relationship makes glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) relevant through two potentially distinct pathways. First, substantial weight loss may unload a compromised lymphatic system, improve mobility, and reduce adipose-driven inflammation. Second, GLP-1 signaling may directly influence lymphatic vessel function. Case reports and a retrospective cohort have described reduced limb volume, improved symptoms or imaging findings, and a lower incidence of breast cancer-related lymphedema among GLP-1RA users. Experimental work has identified GLP-1 receptors in lymphatic endothelial cells and shown that pharmacological activation with semaglutide increases the pumping capacity of isolated collecting lymphatic vessels. These findings support a potential direct lymphatic effect but do not establish clinical efficacy in human lymphedema. Improvement during treatment may instead reflect reduced fat mass, greater mobility, or changes in conventional care. Future studies should distinguish weight-loss-dependent unloading from weight-loss-independent effects by combining standardized clinical outcomes, functional imaging, body-composition measurements, and, where feasible, weight-matched comparison groups. The available evidence therefore supports prospective investigation rather than clinical adoption. Trials should assess early vascular responses before major weight loss, longer-term changes in tissue composition and inflammation, and durability after treatment withdrawal, while maintaining standardized compression, exercise, skin care, and other components of established lymphedema management throughout. Until such evidence is available, GLP-1RAs should be prescribed for established metabolic indications rather than lymphedema itself, and any lymphatic benefit should be regarded as a promising clinical signal rather than a treatment claim.

title: Real-World Anthropometric Outcomes, Safety, and Use Patterns of GLP-1 and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Obesity and Glucose Metabolism Disorder: A Nationwide Multicentre Community Pharmacy Study
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Although randomized clinical trials have demonstrated substantial weight loss and metabolic benefits with incretin-based therapies, real-world evidence is needed to characterize anthropometric outcomes, safety, prescribing patterns, and treatment use under routine clinical conditions.

Objectives: The objective of this study was to characterize real-world anthropometric outcomes, safety, and use patterns of GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with obesity or glucose metabolism disorder receiving treatment through Spanish community pharmacies.

Methods: A nationwide multicentre cross-sectional study with retrospective data collection was conducted between January and April 2026 across community pharmacies in Spain. Adult patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists or dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists were consecutively enrolled and classified according to therapeutic indication (obesity or glucose metabolism disorder). Changes in body weight and body mass index (BMI) were assessed using paired-sample t-tests, while multivariable linear regression explored independent determinants of weight loss. Crude safety signals were initially evaluated using exploratory crude safety association analysis based on Odds Ratios (ORs). Subsequently, multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of suspected digestive adverse drug reactions after adjustment for demographic characteristics, treatment-related variables, lifestyle factors, and concomitant glucose-lowering therapies. Baseline body weight was retrospectively reported by participants and was not independently verified against clinical records or other objective sources, whereas current body weight was measured by the pharmacist at the study visit.

Results: A total of 531 patients were included (52.2% with obesity; 47.8% were classified in the glucose metabolism disorder (GMD) cohort, comprising 200 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and 54 with prediabetes/fasting glucose disturbance; the mean age was 56.5 ± 12.5 years; and 66.7% were women). The mean observed reduction in body weight from treatment initiation to the study assessment was 12.17 ± 10.64 kg, corresponding to an 11.71% ± 9.40% reduction relative to retrospectively reported baseline weight. Overall, 73.9% and 54.1% of participants achieved ≥5% and ≥10% weight loss, respectively. No statistically significant unadjusted difference in relative weight loss was detected across treatment groups; however, equivalence was not formally assessed. Gastrointestinal suspected adverse drug reactions were the most frequently reported safety outcomes. Exploratory crude analyses showed nominal associations between Wegovy® and nausea/vomiting and between Mounjaro® and constipation, as well as between concomitant insulin and dizziness and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy and urinary disorders; however, none of these associations remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. In the exploratory multivariable linear regression model, treatment duration, treatment agent, dietary adherence, light physical activity, and age showed statistically significant adjusted associations with observed percentage weight loss. In the multivariable logistic regression model, increasing age was the only variable significantly associated with lower odds of reported suspected digestive adverse drug reactions (adjusted OR = 0.97 per year; 95% CI 0.96-0.99; p = 0.003).

Conclusions: Observed percentage weight loss varied across treatment groups, although between-treatment comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because of differences in treatment duration, therapeutic indication, sample size, and dose exposure. Given the retrospective ascertainment of baseline weight and the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as real-world estimates of observed weight change rather than causal estimates of treatment effectiveness. Reported suspected adverse drug reactions were common, particularly gastrointestinal events. Although several nominal associations were observed in exploratory crude analyses, none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings support the importance of individualized monitoring in community pharmacy settings. These findings provide a rationale for the prospective development and evaluation of a standardized pharmacy-led dispensing and follow-up protocol to support patient safety and treatment adherence.

title: A coordinated paracrine islet cell network regulating β-cell Ca2+ dynamics
abstract: Pulsatile insulin secretion originates from oscillations in cytosolic free Ca2+ in pancreatic islet β-cells. Decades of work have identified multiple determinants of these oscillations, including glucose metabolism, ion channels, ER Ca2+ handling, cellular heterogeneity, and paracrine and neurohormonal signaling. Yet their relative contributions under physiological conditions remain unresolved because each experimental preparation preserves only a subset of these regulatory layers. Here, we review evidence that intercellular paracrine signaling, in addition to cell-autonomous β-cell machinery, is an important determinant of oscillation frequency and coordination. Simultaneous Ca2+ imaging of α-cells and β-cells reveals tightly coordinated activity, with α-cells following β-cells after a conserved ∼20-s delay. Perturbation of glucagon signaling further indicates that α-cell signaling can modulate β-cell oscillation frequency. Complementing these findings, in vivo imaging of islets engrafted in the anterior chamber of the eye shows that α-cell expansion enhances β-cell Ca2+ coordination in a glucagon-receptor-dependent manner. Extending this circuit to δ-cells, somatostatin limits oscillation frequency primarily by suppressing α-cell glucagon release, thereby enabling the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell paracrine circuit to shift β-cell oscillations between fast, mixed, and slow regimes. Importantly, a glycemia-dependent slow-to-fast transition is lost in diabetic mice and rescued by GLP-1 receptor agonism. Under anesthesia-free conditions, however, islets in awake animals occupy a slow, highly synchronized oscillatory regime in which glucose modulates amplitude, period, and plateau fraction without altering network coordination. Together, these findings suggest that the δ-cell-α-cell-β-cell circuit represents an important regulatory layer shaping β-cell Ca2+ oscillations alongside intrinsic β-cell mechanisms and extrinsic physiological inputs. β-cell dysfunction may therefore involve not only altered oscillation frequency and coordination, but also disrupted paracrine regulation by glucagon and somatostatin.

title: Development and validation of qualitative methods for the detection of GLP-1 receptor agonists in serum and dried blood spots by LC-HRMS/MS for doping control purposes
abstract: The increasing use of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists for weight management has raised concerns about their potential misuse in sports, where effects such as weight loss, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, and enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis may offer performance advantages. Although currently not prohibited, semaglutide and tirzepatide have been included in the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Monitoring Program to assess potential misuse. In response to these concerns, this study aimed to develop detection methods for five GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as the endogenous metabolite GLP-1(9-36)-NH2 in serum and dried blood spot (DBS) samples by liquid-chromatography and high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS/MS). For analytes with expected low blood concentrations (exenatide, lixisenatide, GLP-1(9-36)-NH2), affinity purification using magnetic beads coupled to an anti-GLP-1 antibody and a GLP-1 receptor fusion protein achieved limits of detection (LODs) ranging from 9.4 pg/mL (exenatide) to 48 pg/mL (lixisenatide and GLP-1(9-36)-NH2) in 100 μL of serum. Serum analysis provided superior sensitivity compared to DBS and was therefore prioritized for these analytes. For higher-abundant, lipidated peptides (liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide), mixed-mode anion-exchange solid-phase extraction was employed, allowing for LODs ranging from 0.48 ng/mL (tirzepatide) to 4.7 ng/mL (liraglutide and semaglutide) in serum, and 0.95 ng/mL (liraglutide and semaglutide) to 3.8 ng/mL (tirzepatide) in DBS. Both sample matrices were suitable for reliable detection. In addition, post-administration samples from humans treated with semaglutide and tirzepatide, as well as murine samples following administration of exenatide, lixisenatide, and liraglutide, confirmed the suitability of the developed methods for sports drug testing.
journal: Journal of chromatography. B, Analytical technologies in the biomedical and life sciences

title: Values, preferences, and treatment burden for initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT-2 inhibitors, tirzepatide, and finerenone in adults with type 2 diabetes: systematic review
abstract: Objectives: To summarise existing evidence regarding the values, preferences, and perceived treatment burden of adults with type 2 diabetes when considering initiation of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i), finerenone, or tirzepatide.
Design: Systematic review.

Data Sources: Medline, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to 7 January 2025 (updating a previous systematic review that captured literature up to 23 May 2020).

Eligibility Criteria: Quantitative or qualitative studies were included if they reported patient reported values, preferences, or treatment burden among adults with type 2 diabetes and compared initiation of GLP-1 RA, SGLT-2i, tirzepatide, or finerenone with each other or with other glucose-lowering treatments.

Data Extraction And Synthesis: Paired reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Findings were synthesised narratively.

Results: Thirty four studies (15 656 patients) were included, 17 of which were new since the previous 2021 review (8360 patients). Of the newly included studies, 10 evaluated GLP-1 RA, seven evaluated SGLT-2i, and one evaluated tirzepatide; no studies evaluated finerenone (because several studies compared multiple drug classes, these categories are not mutually exclusive). Across comparisons, patients consistently reported glycaemic efficacy, cardiovascular risk reduction, and simplicity of administration as their priorities. Oral once-daily regimens and once-weekly injectable treatments with easy-to-use devices were generally preferred. Weight loss was valued but was typically secondary to glycaemic and cardiovascular benefits. SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA were often preferred over dipeptidyl peptidase 4-inhibitors (DPP-4i), thiazolidinediones, and insulins, but no consistent preference emerged for SGLT-2i over GLP-1 RA. Tirzepatide was favoured over semaglutide in a single study, largely due to greater haemoglobin A1c reduction and lower hypoglycaemia risk. Certainty of evidence for all comparisons was low or very low certainty.

Conclusion: Adults with type 2 diabetes prioritise treatment effectiveness and convenience among glucose-lowering treatments. Current evidence does not support a clear preference between SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA, and data for finerenone are absent. These findings underscore the importance of shared decision making informed by individual patient priorities.
Prospero Registration: CRD42023429170.

title: Short-Chain Fatty Acids as Endogenous Inhibitors of DPP-IV Enzyme: Implications in GLP-1 Stability and Metabolic Health
abstract: Dipeptidyl peptidase-IV (DPP-IV/CD26) is a circulating serine protease that rapidly degrades incretin hormones, including glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), limiting incretin activity and glucose homeostasis. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), major gut microbiota-derived metabolites, influence metabolic health through multiple mechanisms; whether they directly inhibit DPP-IV remains unknown. Here, we investigated the inhibitory activity and mechanism of acetate, propionate, and butyrate against recombinant human DPP-IV. All three SCFAs inhibited DPP-IV concentration-dependently, with an average IC50 of 0.62 ± 0.13 mM. Michaelis-Menten, Lineweaver-Burk, Dixon, and Cornish-Bowden analyses demonstrated reversible mixed-mode inhibition, whereas sitagliptin exhibited competitive inhibition (Ki = 2.6 nM). SCFAs protected GLP-1 from DPP-IV mediated degradation and preserved GLP-1-induced calcium signaling in INS-1 cells. Molecular docking indicated preferential SCFA interactions within the DPP-IV β-propeller domain. These findings identify SCFAs as direct, reversible DPP-IV modulators, providing a molecular link between gut microbial metabolites and incretin regulation.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

title: Combined empagliflozin and liraglutide therapy protects against tacrolimus-induced pancreatic and renal injury associated with oxidative stress reduction
abstract: Background: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are widely used in type 2 diabetes mellitus for glycemic control and organ protection. This study investigated whether the combined use of empagliflozin (EMPA) and liraglutide (LIRA) could protect against pancreatic and renal damage caused by tacrolimus (TAC).

Methods: Male Sprague-Dawley rats received TAC for 4 weeks, either alone, or in combination with EMPA, LIRA, or both. Metabolic, histologic, and molecular parameters were assessed in vivo and in vitro. TAC caused hyperglycemia, reduced creatinine clearance, pancreatic β-cell loss, renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and increased oxidative stress and apoptosis.

Results: Either EMPA or LIRA alone partially attenuated these changes, whereas their combination provided enhanced protection- improving kidney function, preserving islet integrity, and reducing fibrosis and cell death. In the kidney and pancreas, dual therapy restored antiapoptotic and antioxidant signaling while suppressing profibrotic pathways, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and injury. Cell-based experiments further confirmed that EMPA plus LIRA enhanced cell viability and reduced reactive oxygen species generation in TAC-injured HK-2 and INS-1 cells.

Conclusion: These findings indicate that combined SGLT2i and GLP-1RA therapy confers additive metabolic protection associated with attenuation of oxidative stress in tacrolimus-induced pancreatic and renal damage in this preclinical model, warranting further investigation of its potential as an adjunct strategy for posttransplant diabetes mellitus and nephrotoxicity.

title: Persistent Hyperinsulinemic Hypoglycemia After Insulinoma Surgery: Diagnostic Impact of GLP-1 Receptor PET/CT After Negative Conventional Imaging
abstract: Background: Localization of recurrent or residual insulinoma may be particularly challenging in postoperative setting, especially in the presence of postoperative anatomical distortion and inconclusive conventional imaging.

Case Presentation: A 71-year-old man developed recurrent endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia following apparently curative surgical enucleation of a pancreatic insulinoma. The postoperative course was complicated by intra-abdominal hemorrhage and pseudocyst formation, resulting in marked anatomical distortion. Despite persistent biochemical evidence of insulinoma recurrence, serial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) and 68Ga-DOTATOC PET/CT failed to identify residual disease. Subsequent glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) imaging with 68Ga-NODAGA-Exendin-4 PET/CT demonstrated focal tracer uptake in the pancreatic head, highly suggestive of recurrent or residual insulinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) subsequently confirmed a small lesion in the uncinate process, which was successfully treated with EUS-guided radiofrequency ablation (EUS-RFA). Following the procedure, hypoglycemic episodes resolved, with normalization of glucose, insulin, and C-peptide levels and no signs of recurrence at follow-up.

Conclusion: This case highlights the clinical value of GLP-1 receptor PET/CT for localizing insulinoma in the context of negative conventional or somatostatin receptor (SSTR)-based imaging. Accurate functional localization may directly guide minimally invasive therapeutic interventions and help avoid high-risk reoperative pancreatic surgery.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for Glucocorticoid-Induced Dysglycaemia: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background: Glucocorticoids (GCs) commonly induce glycaemic disturbance, from transient steroid-induced hyperglycaemia to steroid-induced diabetes and contribute to post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM). Insulin remains the standard treatment for GC-induced glycaemic dysregulation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have a mechanistic rationale here, but their efficacy and safety in GC-induced dysglycaemia have not been systematically appraised.

Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines (registration number: CRD420251183082). Embase, PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched up to May 2026. A structured narrative synthesis was the primary method.

Results: Thirteen studies were included, predominantly retrospective cohort studies; 10 enrolled solid organ transplant recipients with PTDM or pre-existing type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 RA therapy, either as monotherapy or as an adjunct to insulin, was associated with reductions in HbA1c and body weight, and a low rate of hypoglycaemia in the majority of included studies. GLP-1 RAs led to insulin dose reduction or discontinuation, reducing injection frequency and treatment burden. Five studies contributed to at least one pooled estimate, and no outcome was informed by more than three studies; given substantial heterogeneity and very low GRADE certainty, these estimates are exploratory and are presented in Supplementary Material 2.

Conclusions: Individual studies reported reductions in HbA1c, body weight and insulin dose, with a low rate of hypoglycaemia episodes. However, available data specific to GC-induced dysglycaemia remain insufficient. Prospective controlled trials with explicit characterisation of GC exposure are required.

title: Contraceptive use and GLP-1 receptor agonists: an intersection of metabolic and reproductive health
abstract: The growing overlap of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and contraceptive use in women of reproductive age warrants a comprehensive understanding of the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions of these two drug classes. Studies that evaluate the two are limited, and significant knowledge gaps remain regarding interactions. This narrative review synthesizes the current body of literature surrounding glucagon-like peptide receptor agonists and hormonal contraception and their effects on the female reproductive tract. It defines potential interactions between the two classes of medication across the female reproductive tract, and highlights gaps in knowledge. Lastly, this review underscores the need for healthcare providers to incorporate contraceptive counseling as a routine component of care when initiating glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists.
journal: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology

title: GLP-1 receptor biology and the therapeutic role of incretin-based agonists in metabolic diseases
abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and obesity represent a growing global health burden, sharing underlying pathophysiological mechanisms such as impaired insulin signalling and chronic low-grade inflammation. The discovery of the incretin effect opened the way for agonist therapies targeting the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) as therapies capable of addressing the metabolic dysregulation common to both diseases simultaneously. This review examines the biology of GLP-1 and the incretin system, with a focus on the structure and signalling mechanisms of GLP-1R, including biased agonism and receptor trafficking. The clinical effectiveness of stable, long-acting GLP-1RAs is evaluated across three therapeutic domains: T2DM management, obesity treatment, and emerging cardiovascular protection. Current evidence demonstrates that GLP-1RAs, which induce insulin secretion and suppress appetite, achieve superior glycaemic control and significant weight reduction compared with conventional therapies, with emerging cardiovascular benefits now extending to non-diabetic patients as well. The shift towards dual and triple receptor agonists, such as tirzepatide and retatrutide, together with biased agonist design, is a promising development for further improvements in effectiveness. Progress in oral formulations of GLP-1RAs may also improve tolerability and patient adherence. Nevertheless, important challenges remain, including gastrointestinal side effects, weight regain upon discontinuation, loss of lean body mass, and unresolved questions regarding long-term safety. In conclusion, while GLP-1R-based therapies represent a major therapeutic advancement, particularly for T2DM patients, their broader application in obesity management requires careful patient selection, continued long-term safety monitoring, and integration with lifestyle interventions.

title: Long-term injectable non-insulin antidiabetic drug use and in-hospital mortality in sepsis: A nationwide analysis of the 2023 National Inpatient Sample
abstract: Purpose: Injectable non-insulin antidiabetic agents have hypothesized antiinflammatory effects in sepsis, but no nationally representative US inpatient analysis has examined their association with in-hospital outcomes.

Materials And Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2023 National Inpatient Sample. Adults with any-listed sepsis and diabetes were included; exposure was documented long-term injectable non-insulin antidiabetic use (ICD-10-CM Z79.85). Survey-weighted logistic regression estimated adjusted odds of in-hospital mortality across three pre-specified comparators.

Results: Among 241,808 hospitalizations, 5238 (2.2%) carried Z79.85. Adjusted odds of death were 0.53 (95% CI, 0.45-0.63) versus the full cohort, 0.73 (0.61-0.87) therapy-matched, and 0.77 (0.64-0.93) versus oral therapy alone. The E-value was 1.61.
Conclusions: Exposure was associated with lower in-hospital mortality, attenuating under stricter comparators. Findings are hypothesis-generating and subject to residual confounding.

title: Olive Oil Before Oral Glucose Delays Gastric Emptying and Lowers Glycemia Through Partially Redundant Glucagon and GLP-1 Signaling in Mice
abstract: We undertook this study to define how fat consumed before oral glucose attenuates postchallenge glycemia. We asked whether olive oil reduces glycemia by slowing gastric emptying and investigated contributing endocrine and neural pathways. Olive oil increased glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, and glucagon-like peptide-1; slowed gastric emptying; and reduced early glycemia in mice. Glucagon and glucagon-like peptide-1 signaling acted redundantly, with vagal involvement. Nutrient timing integrates endocrine-neural regulation of gastric emptying and glycemia, supporting evaluation of meal sequencing in humans.

title: Exercise, Nutrition and GLP-1 Medicines to Improve Body Weight and Muscle Function in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
abstract: Purpose Of Review: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on lifestyle, pharmacological, surgical, and multimodal interventions targeting muscle strength, body composition, and functional capacity in HFpEF with sarcopenia and/or obesity.

Recent Findings: Exercise, particularly concurrent endurance and resistance training protocols, improve aerobic capacity, functional performance, symptoms, and quality of life in HFpEF. Protein supplementation may preserve muscle mass, while caloric restriction may enhance aerobic capacity and function butdecreases muscle mass. SGLT2i and GLP-1 medicines may reduce hospitalizations and improve symptoms, with GLP-1 medicines producing greater weight loss and performance benefits. Bariatric surgery may also achieve substantial weight loss and functional improvements, although evidence in HFpEF with obesity is limited. Obesity-related HFpEF may benefit from a combination of resistance exercise and adequate protein intake to preserve muscle during weight loss, while pharmacotherapy can be used to support cardiac function. Future trials should evaluate multimodal interventions to mitigate frailty risk in HFpEF.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in perimenopause and early postmenopause: clinical role, cardiometabolic benefits and knowledge gaps
abstract: Perimenopause and early postmenopause represent a critical metabolic transition with adverse changes in body composition, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism and cardiometabolic health, contributing to increased rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. As the prevalence of obesity continues to rise among midlife women, effective therapeutic strategies are increasingly needed. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have emerged as highly effective treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes through their effects on appetite regulation, weight reduction, glucose homeostasis and metabolic health. Beyond their established role, GLP-1 RAs have demonstrated favorable effects on visceral adiposity, glycemic control, lipid profiles, hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular outcomes. Preliminary experimental evidence also suggests possible complementary effects when combined with menopausal hormone therapy (MHT). However, menopause-specific evidence remains limited. This review summarizes the current evidence regarding the efficacy, safety and clinical application of GLP-1 RAs in perimenopausal and early postmenopausal women. Particular attention is given to their effects on cardiometabolic health, cardiovascular risk, bone and muscle health, cancer risk, cognition and potential interactions with MHT. Although GLP-1 RAs represent a promising therapeutic option for obesity and metabolic dysfunction during menopause, important knowledge gaps remain regarding their long-term safety, effects on menopause-related outcomes and optimal integration into comprehensive menopausal care. The efficacy, safety and potential interactions of GLP-1 RAs when used in combination with MHT remain to be determined.
journal: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society

title: Ischemic colitis associated with oral semaglutide with recurrence upon rechallenge
abstract: Ischemic colitis associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists is an exceptionally rare condition, with only a few cases reported in the literature. We present the case of a 46-year-old woman treated with oral semaglutide (Rybelsus®) for weight loss who experienced three episodes of abdominal pain and hematochezia temporally associated with drug exposure. The third episode, which occurred after semaglutide was reintroduced, led to a confirmed diagnosis based on computed tomography, rectosigmoidoscopy, and histopathological findings consistent with ischemic colitis. Permanent discontinuation of semaglutide was followed by complete clinical resolution without further recurrence. The temporal relationship, improvement after drug withdrawal, and recurrence upon rechallenge support a probable causal association. This case highlights the need to consider ischemic colitis as a potential rare adverse effect of semaglutide.

title: The Gut-Brain Axis in Parkinson's Disease: From Clinical Observation toward Mechanism-Based Precision Medicine
abstract: Gastrointestinal dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), affecting quality of life, nutrition, medication response, and potentially the earliest stages of pathogenesis. This perspective traces the evolution of the gut from a neglected source of non-motor symptoms to a central component of biological models of PD. Gastrointestinal manifestations are physiologically heterogeneous and require objective phenotyping to distinguish dysphagia, gastroparesis, slow transit, defecatory dysfunction, and overlapping mechanisms. The body-first/brain-first framework further suggests that Lewy pathology may follow distinct anatomical trajectories, with early enteric and autonomic involvement defining a subgroup in which gut-directed biomarkers and therapies may be especially relevant. Alterations of the gut microbiome are reproducibly associated with PD, although geography, constipation, medication, diet, disease stage, and reverse causation complicate interpretation. Emerging work is shifting from taxonomy toward microbial functions and host pathways, including barrier integrity, immune and enteroendocrine signaling, short-chain fatty acids, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), host genetic susceptibility, α-synuclein aggregation and propagation, and microbial levodopa metabolism. Trials of probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, and dietary interventions remain heterogeneous and have not established disease-modifying efficacy. Progress will require longitudinal studies in prodromal and subtype-defined populations, objective gastrointestinal measurements, integrated microbial, host-genetic and other multi-omics, mechanistic human and animal models, and clinical trials combining target-engagement markers with meaningful outcomes. Such an approach may enable precision gut-brain medicine for appropriately selected patients with PD. © 2026 The Author(s).
